+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Nine: The Star-and-Laurel** The transfer vessel's air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone. Arthur Neegan had been listening to it for the better part of a day, and in that time he had come to think of it as the sound of his old life leaving him. That morning—if morning meant anything on a trajectory to high orbit—three black skimmers had settled onto the claim road at Anseris Flats, raising the fine rust dust in slow, deliberate plumes. The captain who knocked wore dove-gray with the star-and-laurel of the Antares Diplomatic Corps on his collar, and his courtesy had been flawless. *Mr. Neegan? Forgive the intrusion.* Behind him a corporal held a rifle at exactly the angle of politeness. They had let Arthur lock his own dome. That was the frightening part. Men who are certain of themselves can afford manners. He turned his wedding ring once around his finger and watched Mars shrink in the porthole—a rusted coin spent on God knew what. The steward brought coffee in a squeeze bulb. The instrument panel was all brass-rimmed dials and trembling needles, the way ships had been built for a hundred years, and Arthur took thin comfort in it. Machines he understood. Needles pointed at truths. The docking clamps rang like a struck bell. Whatever they had mated with was on no registry he knew—a spindle of a station, unmarked but for the star-and-laurel, gleaming where the sun caught it. They walked him down corridors that smelled of ozone and machine oil, past pneumatic doors that sighed like tired clerks, and into a room that had no business existing in orbit: real wood paneling, a carpet, a desk where a telex chattered softly to itself beside a microfilm reader and a cut-glass decanter. Two ceramic cups. A window the size of a barn door, with Mars turning slowly beneath it like a patient etherized upon a table. The man behind the desk was fifty, gray, and unremarkable in the way that only very important men can afford to be. "Sit, Mr. Neegan. You'll forgive the theatricals. My name is Soren Harth." "Is that what we're calling kidnapping now? Theatricals?" "Come. You were invited. You came." "A man comes when the alternative is discussed in front of him." Harth smiled, and it was not unkind. "Then let me justify the discussion. Do you know what you have?" "A lease. Plot 114, Anseris Flats. Forty thousand tonnes of Azra, per the assay I filed." "The assay you filed. Yes." Harth slid a photogram across the desk—a gravimetric deep-scan, contour lines dense as a fingerprint. "Nine hundred thousand tonnes, running straight as a rule line beneath your plot. The largest single concentration yet surveyed. Held by a man who fixes his own pumps." He let that sit. "Consolidated Metals has filed three challenges to your claim since Tuesday. The Terran Procurement Office has a cruiser nine days out. The Kessel Combine will simply purchase the Colonial Authority outright—it has done so twice before. None of them will ask you for anything, Mr. Neegan. We are asking." Arthur kept his hands still, the way he did when a cutting head ran hot. "Ask, then." "First, understand the stakes." Harth poured the coffee. "Azra does one thing. It hurries the death of atoms. A drive pile doped with it burns in weeks what once burned in years. The Centauri run took our grandfathers eleven years; with Azra, a ship may do it in one. And a warhead—well. A warhead need not be large, if it is quick. Whoever holds this metal holds the pace of the age. And the age, sir, is impatient." He pushed a contract across, printed on actual paper, the kind used for things meant to outlast governments. "The Concourse will confirm your claim in perpetuity, against all challenge. We will buy out the indenture contracts of every lease-man on your section—" Arthur's fingers stopped on the paper. Dooley. The Vassko brothers. Men paying off passage debts with their lungs. "—and you will remain owner-operator at fifty-one percent. In exchange: exclusive offtake to Antares for twenty years, at a price you name today. Your silence regarding the core samples. And a small technical mission, housed on-site." "Observers." "Observers." Harth spread his hands. "You will be the wealthiest man on Mars, and the freest. We are prepared to be generous precisely because we cannot afford to be refused." "And if I refuse?" "Then we return you to your dome with our apologies. Within a month, men will arrive who will not ask. I shall read of you in the casualty columns—claim dispute, equipment failure, suit malfunction. Mars is a dangerous place, Mr. Neegan. It is about to become more so." Harth said it the way a man reports weather, and Arthur believed him completely. He looked down at the contract, then up at the seal on Harth's signet ring as the man lifted his cup. The star had eight points. The Corps' star, on every charter and every embassy plaque Arthur had ever seen, had seven. He thought of the captain at the airlock, saluting with the wrong hand. He filed it away the way he filed core samples—labeled, unexamined, waiting. "One more thing," Harth said, almost gently. "Ask your geologist friends how Azra came to be on Mars. Ores pool. They fold, they fault, they wander. Azra does none of these things. It runs in straight lines. Nine hundred thousand tonnes of it, under your tomato beds, true as a surveyor's transit." He set down his cup. "When you have explained that to yourself, you will understand why we came with guns." Arthur rose and went to the window. Somewhere down there was his dome, the frost on the regolith, the pump house with the valve he'd meant to replace. A small life, suddenly the center of the human universe. Behind him the telex chattered on, steady as a Geiger counter. "I want time." "You have until the Terran cruiser. Nine days. Think of it as a courtesy—we are the only ones who will give you any." Arthur drank the coffee. It was terrible, recaffeinated, twice-cooked. Somehow that was the worst of it—that the fate of worlds could be negotiated over coffee this bad. Aft, the filtration system hummed its indifferent note, and Arthur Neegan, who had asked only to be left alone with his claim, understood that he had just been handed the fulcrum of the age—and that fulcrums, as any engineer knows, are where things break.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of pastiche Asimov: the dialogue-driven negotiation, the big-picture geopolitics delivered through exposition-in-conversation, the retrofuturistic brass-dial-and-telex technology, and the engineer protagonist who thinks in mechanical analogies. The chapter fulfills the prompt's requirements: it opens aboard the transfer vessel, delivers the meeting with the unknown party, keeps the scene primarily dialogue with interspersed description, and sows intrigue (the eight-pointed star vs. seven, the wrong-hand salute, the "Azra runs in straight lines" mystery). Strengths: The dialogue is crisp and character-revealing. Harth's menace-by-courtesy is well drawn ("Mars is a dangerous place, Mr. Neegan. It is about to become more so"). The small details (Dooley, the Vassko brothers, the valve he'd meant to replace) ground the world effectively. The closing fulcrum metaphor is earned by Arthur's engineering identity. The wrong-star detail is a genuinely good clue—showing Arthur's observational competence rather than telling us about it. Weaknesses: "A patient etherized upon a table" is lifted directly from Prufrock—jarring in an Asimov pastiche and slightly purple. The exposition about Azra's properties is delivered somewhat baldly by Harth, though this is authentically Asimovian. The stakes laid out (Consolidated Metals, Terran Procurement, Kessel Combine) are efficient but a touch listy. The prose occasionally strains for aphorism ("Men who are certain of themselves can afford manners" works; "the sound of his old life leaving him" is a bit on-the-nose). The ending's "fulcrum of the age" line is a strong close but flirts with overwrought. Overall, however, this is competent, coherent, engaging genre fiction that captures the requested voice well. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 82.0
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations The safelight makes everything the color of a held secret. Third Thursday night in a row, Elliot and I alone in the campus darkroom, trays lined up like a science experiment, the enlarger humming its one low note. Fixer sharp in my nose. My whole world shrunk to a red room and a boy in smudged eyeliner. Elliot dresses like a thrift store dared him to—mesh sleeves under a Siouxsie tee, jeans held together by safety pins and spite, rings on every finger, black polish chipped to confetti. Nineteen, six years my junior, and the only person all semester who's made me feel like the student. I'm usually so much simpler than this. My history sorts into two clean piles: men built like monuments, women honed like switchblades. Definition—that's been my type. Edges you could cut your thumb on. And I'm the one who says *come here.* The one who leaves first. Fluent in pursuit, me. Elliot is teaching me a second language: waiting. "Test strip's lying," he murmurs, bending over the developer tray. His forearm brushes mine and neither of us moves away. He holds the tongs like a surgeon—precise, quiet, a stillness that makes my usual volume feel like a crime. Tonight the print sliding into the developer is his self-portrait—the one he shot last week in a mirror, in makeup that wasn't the usual smudged liner but deliberate, careful, *considered.* I watch his face surface out of the gray like a ghost agreeing to appear. "I don't know what I am," he says. To the tray, not to me—like the print asked first. "The eyeliner started as a look. Now it's the only honest thing in the mirror." A pause. The timer beeps; neither of us reaches for it. "He. For now, he. I think. I'm still—" He laughs once, wet and ugly, and it breaks something in me. Every instinct I own says *take over.* Say the right thing, name it for him, kiss him against the sink and make keeping up his problem. It's what I do. It's all I've ever done. Instead I ask, "What do you need?" Four words. Hardest print I've ever made. He's quiet so long the image goes past done, and I rescue it with the tongs, slide it into the stop bath. "That," he says finally. "Nobody's asked me that. People either look away, or they hand me a label like a coat that doesn't fit." Here's my confession, whispered only to the red dark: I don't know what wanting him makes me. I've built a whole self on the clean lines of who I desire, and now I'm standing in the fog between categories, heart hammering like the first time I watched an image bloom in the tray. What if I want the in-between and he becomes someone solid who doesn't want me? What if I'm just a tourist in his becoming? "You're doing the math face," Elliot says softly. "Stop doing math. It's just me." "I don't know what 'just you' is yet." "Me neither." He smiles—God, the first one all night that reaches his eyes. "We could not-know in the same room, though." That's when it happens. He turns toward me, I turn toward him, the air goes electric with everything neither of us will say first, and Elliot—flushed, flustered, reaching blind for the timer—slaps the wall switch instead. White light. Blinding, absolute. We freeze like caught animals. Then I see it: the fresh box of fiber paper on the counter, lid off, where I set it ten minutes ago. Eighty sheets. Four dollars a sheet. Our entire printing budget for the final, fogged to useless gray in half a second. "Oh *no,*" Elliot breathes, hand over his mouth. "Dani—your paper—I can pay you back, I can—" And I start laughing. It comes up out of me huge and undignified, and after a second he's laughing too, both of us wheezing under the merciless fluorescent truth of the room, three hundred dollars of ruined paper gleaming between us. "It's fine," I gasp. "It's—Elliot, it's *paper.*" "I ruined your—" "Some things can't be un-exposed," I say, and I mean the paper, and I don't mean the paper at all. He goes still. Looks at me—really looks, in white light, no red to hide inside, both of us exposed down to the emulsion. Then, slowly, deliberately, he reaches out and takes the tongs from my hand. Sets them down. Nobody takes anything out of my hand. Ever. His fingers stay on mine. Nineteen years old, doesn't know his own name for himself yet, and he's the bravest person I've ever met. "Ask me again," he says, "when I know what to call it. I'll tell you first. I want you to be first." I am the one who leaves first. I am the one who says *come here.* "Okay," I say, and let the picture come to me.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of short fiction that hits nearly all the prompt's requirements with craft and economy. The darkroom setting is used thematically throughout—exposure, development, "the red light creates a confessional atmosphere" is translated into "everything the color of a held secret." The white-light accident that fogs the paper is an excellent plot device: it literalizes the theme of exposure, breaks the tension believably, and generates the piece's best line ("Some things can't be un-exposed"). Dani's voice is consistent and distinctive: clipped, confident, self-aware, with a habit of aphoristic self-summary ("men built like monuments, women honed like switchblades"). Her internal conflict—wanting to take charge versus giving Elliot agency—is dramatized rather than merely stated, most effectively in the four-word question "What do you need?" and in her letting him take the tongs from her hand ("Nobody takes anything out of my hand. Ever."). The ending inverts her established pattern ("I am the one who leaves first") into "let the picture come to me," which is earned by the preceding beats. Weaknesses: the piece occasionally tips into over-cleverness. "Jeans held together by safety pins and spite" and "a thrift store dared him to" are the kind of quippy constructions that signal a writer performing wit. Some metaphors are stacked two or three to a paragraph ("heart hammering like the first time I watched an image bloom in the tray" is a doubled simile). The "math face" exchange is a touch convenient. Elliot's dialogue is slightly idealized—his lines ("We could not-know in the same room, though") are more polished than a flustered nineteen-year-old's speech would likely be, though it's within the register of literary dialogue. The word count is somewhat under the 1000-word seed (roughly 850), a minor adherence issue. The transformation of Dani's character is modest and plausible rather than unearned; Elliot's request for time is handled with restraint rather than rushing to a kiss, which is a mature choice. The prose flows well, the imagery is fresh and integrated, and the emotional complexity—Dani's confusion about her own identity as a desirer of "defined gender presentations"—is genuinely explored rather than glossed. It's not a masterpiece; it's a very good piece with a few overwrought flourishes and slightly too-neat dialogue. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma **8:47 — Fontana di Trevi** The guidebook insisted the fountain was best approached slowly, "savored." Ben was savoring it backwards, one eye on a paragraph about Nicola Salvi, when the world became a horn and a scream of Italian. "*Madonna santa, ma che fai?! Cammini o dormi?!*" The motorcycle stopped a breath from his hip. Its rider yanked off her helmet, unleashing dark hair and fury in equal measure. "*Cretino!* You walk like the street is a *library*—" "Mi scusi," Ben stammered. "Sono molto—*desolato*—I am so terribly—do you speak—" "English? Yes. Unfortunately for you." She dismounted, all economy and spark, and looked him over: the linen shirt, the sensible shoes, the book clutched like a life raft. "You have a death wish, *Professore*?" "How did you know I'm a professor?" "You dress like a funeral." He opened his mouth, apologized again, then noticed the motorcycle — a battered red Ducati with a jagged turquoise gash along the fairing, painted over in a color that matched nothing. "What happened there?" "An adventure." A beat. "You weren't invited." While he bent to retrieve his scattered pages, her hand drifted to the fountain's edge. A coin vanished into her fist, casual as breathing. Ben almost said something. He decided he'd imagined it. **9:15 — Same** "What were you doing today?" "The British School library. I'm researching funerary inscriptions of the late—" "Dead people's names. Tragic." She plucked the guidebook from his hands and stowed it in her top box. "Hostage. Now get on." "I beg your pardon?" "*Dai.* You came to Rome to read about it?" She tossed him a helmet. "Tieniti forte, Professore." Every sensible instinct filed a formal objection. Ben climbed on anyway, and apologized to her back as Rome detonated past them — marble, laundry, miracles. **11:03 — Mercato di Testaccio** She stole two peaches with a magician's ease, tossed him one. Ben fumbled it, horrified, and turned back toward the vendor, wallet out. "You can't just—" "They were going soft. I'm a humanitarian." She hauled him away by the collar, laughing. At a café they drank espresso standing up, the Roman way. When she set her cup down, the spoon had gone up her sleeve. "Did you just take that?" "Take what?" Her smile was pure innocent mischief. "So. Dead inscriptions. Seven years?" "Eight. My department head called it 'thorough.'" He said it the way other men said *heartbreak*. "And you? Courier, art school dropout." She shrugged. "They said I had no discipline." "Did you?" "None whatsoever," she said, with enormous pride, and stole his napkin. **13:52 — Il Buco, Aventino** At the keyhole on the Aventine she talked them past the queue with a burst of Italian so fast he caught only "BBC." "Did you tell them I'm with the BBC?" "Or the Vatican. I don't remember." She pushed him forward. "Look." Through the keyhole: green hedges, and floating at the end of them, impossibly, the dome of St. Peter's. "It's a stolen view," Ben said quietly. "Best kind." She stood closer than necessary. "You like rules, Professore. Queues. Permissions." It wasn't quite a question. "That sounds exhausting." He watched the dome tremble in its green frame. "It never occurred to me until today." **16:31 — A rooftop, somewhere off Campo de' Fiori** The key had been hanging on a nail behind a sacristy door. "Where did you get that?" "It was hanging there. Practically asking." The prosecco came from a crate outside a restaurant — she winked at the delivery boy as she took it. Now they sat among TV aerials and terracotta, the city's domes going honey-gold, and when a caretaker's voice barked below, they flattened behind a water tank, shoulder to shoulder, her hand clamped over his mouth, both shaking with silent laughter. "I haven't broken a rule since 2009," he whispered when it was safe. "What happened in 2009?" "I took the plastic off a library book." She laughed then — not the wicked laugh, a real one, surprised out of her — and for a moment something unguarded crossed her face before she put it away. **19:44 — Lungotevere** The river held the last light. She handed back his guidebook. "Page one-twelve." Then she pressed something small and round into his palm and closed his fingers over it: the fountain coin, warm from her pocket. "For your return. Don't say I never gave you anything." Then she kissed him — once, quickly, exactly, the way she took things — and was already swinging onto the Ducati. "The scratch!" Ben called, dazed. "What happened?" Helmet down. Engine alive. "Ask me tomorrow." Page 112 was the Trevi Fountain. Across Bernini's Oceanus she had scrawled a number and four words: *Per il Professore. Coraggio.* Behind him, somewhere, a coin hit the water. Ben hadn't thrown one. He didn't need to. He was already coming back.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a tightly structured day-in-Rome romance told in timestamped vignettes, which suits the "interconnected short scenes" instruction well. The opening collision crackles with personality contrast: Alessandra's rapid Italian insults versus Ben's flustered apologies. The kleptomania is handled exactly as requested — never named, shown through escalating small thefts (coin, peaches, spoon, napkin, key, prosecco), each rendered with casual sleight-of-hand. The pacing is brisk and the word count lands near the target. Strengths: The dialogue is consistently sharp and character-revealing ("You dress like a funeral," "I took the plastic off a library book"). The keyhole scene and rooftop scene build genuine intimacy and humor. The ending — the returned coin, the scrawled note, "Ask me tomorrow" — is a satisfying payoff that preserves Alessandra's enigmatic quality while giving Ben a clear emotional arc. The prose is economical and evocative ("Rome detonated past them — marble, laundry, miracles"). Weaknesses: Some beats are a touch predictable for the genre (the manic-pixie-courier leading a repressed academic astray is a well-worn trope; the "stolen view" line is a bit on-the-nose). Alessandra risks being a type — the quirky lawless woman who exists to liberate a dull man — and her interiority remains thin; we get one flicker of unguardedness but little else. Ben's transformation from rule-follower to willing accomplice happens quickly, though the "2009 library book" joke makes it charming rather than jarring. The queue-jumping via "BBC" lie is convenient. A few lines flirt with cuteness ("exactly, the way she took things" is clever but slightly showy). The Italian is used effectively but occasionally leans on stock phrases. Overall this is skilled, polished commercial fiction — engaging, funny, well-paced — that falls short of profundity due to familiar archetypes and a somewhat formulaic emotional trajectory. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Vega, Neat** The Last Outpost hums at a pitch I've learned to sleep to. Three years on this rock and the rattle of the grav-plates under the bar is as familiar as my own pulse. Friday—or what passes for Friday on an asteroid with no sun—and the usual drift of miners and merchants filters in, shedding vacuum-cold and bad moods at the door. "Nets!" Bram drops onto his usual stool, still gray with ore dust. "The tap. The good tap. Don't look at me like that, I've had a day." "You've had a decade," I say, and pull it anyway. In the corner booth, Mira and Sol are re-litigating their anniversary dinner for the third week running. Old Otta is teaching Gerald—my semi-sentient fern—to play tiles, which mostly means the fern bats the pieces onto the floor. Home. The word sneaks up on me sometimes. Then the door sighs open and everything in the room shifts half a degree. The stranger is tall, frazzled, their tentacled dreads askew like they've been running a hand—or the void—through them for six hours straight. They cross the room without looking at it and plop down at the bar. "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Behind me, glass shatters—Mira, mid-gesture, emphatic about appetizers. "That's coming out of your deposit!" I call, already reaching for the bottle. "Sol bumped me!" "Sol's half of your deposit, then." The stranger almost smiles. I set the glass down and watch them notice the label. "Huh. Dust on the bottle." "Nobody orders Vega neat. I keep it for the aesthetic." "Dust tastes like home." They drink half the double in one go, eyes closed, and some of the frazzle unknots. "You pour like someone from the Reach." "I pour like someone who owns the bar." I wipe down the counter, casual. "Name?" "Wren." "That your real name?" "Tonight it is." Fair. Half my register is aliases. "Rough crossing?" "Rough everything." They turn the glass in slow circles. "Can I ask you something, bartender? Anyone come through asking questions the last few days? Strangers. Clean ships. People who tip too well." "It's a bar on the outer rim. Everybody's running from something. Last week a man tried to pay me in emotional support worms." "I'm serious." "So were the worms." That gets the full smile, brief as a coin flip. Then Wren reaches into their coat to pay, sets a coin on the bar, and my whole chest goes cold. A heron, wings spread, stamped into old alloy. The Heron's mark. The Combine doesn't mint scrip anymore—they mint people, contracts, debts that outlive you. I know. I have a scar under my left sleeve shaped exactly like that bird, burned over and half-gone, and it picks now, of all times, to itch. I don't touch the coin. "We're credit-only." "Since when?" "Since about four seconds ago." Wren looks at my face, then at the coin, then back, and I watch understanding land. "You've seen the mark." "I don't pry. House policy." "You flinched." "House policy is also lying." They lean in, voice dropping under the music. "I walked off a contract. Navigator, eleven years, bonded since I was nineteen. Two weeks ago my ship docked at a waystation and I just—didn't go back aboard." A beat. "Their reclaimers were a day behind me. Maybe less now. I don't need much. A berth that isn't on a manifest. A name that isn't mine. A door they won't knock on." "And you came here. To a bar. With windows." "I came here because the freighter pilot who sold me this coat said there's a bartender at the Last Outpost who—" Wren stops, recalibrates. "Who used to be good at making people disappear." The bar noise goes on around us—Bram laughing too loud, Mira and Sol moved on to entrées, the fern cheating at tiles—but it all feels far away, like sound through hull plating. "Whoever told you that," I say, "is confusing me with somebody interesting." "Am I?" Their eyes drop, deliberate, to my left sleeve. I resist the urge to tug it down. Before either of us can say the next thing, the wall comm crackles. "Outpost, this is Dock Control." Dee's voice, bored until she isn't. "Nets, you listening? Got an unscheduled arrival requesting clamp at Bay Two. No transponder. No flight plan. They're polite about it, which I hate." Static. "Everything okay up there?" Wren has gone very still, dreads flattened tight against their skull—fear, I'd guess, in whatever bloodline they're from. "That's them. They're early." "Maybe it's a courier. Maybe it's a lost tourist." "Nobody's polite on the outer rim. Even you lied about being credit-only." A shaky breath. "I can go out the back. If there's a back." There's a back. There's a cellar, a crawlspace, an ore chute that drops to the old mining levels, and three years of me being very careful, very boring, very unremarkable, all of it stacked like glasses on a shelf—and this stranger with dust on their bottle has just walked in and bumped the table. Bram's shouting for a refill. The comm crackles again—"Nets? They say they'll only wait ten minutes"—and Wren is looking at me like I'm the last door on the station. I reach under the bar. Past the good whisky. Past the scattergun I keep for asteroids and tax collectors. My fingers close on the cellar key, cold as the void, familiar as a scar. "Finish your drink," I say. "Then start talking. And Wren—" I slide the heron coin back across the bar. "Whoever taught you to order Vega neat? I want the whole story." They pick up the glass. Their hand is shaking. Mine isn't, somehow. Not yet. Above us, through rock and plating and three years of quiet, I hear the docking clamps engage.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of cozy sci-fi that hits nearly all the prompt requirements: first person, present tense, roughly 1000 words, dialogue-heavy (probably 60%+), conflict established (Wren's past, the Combine reclaimers, Nets's hidden history) and left unresolved. The chapter ends on a cliffhanger with the docking clamps engaging, exactly as instructed. Strengths: The voice is confident and consistent—wry, guarded, warm underneath. Nets's characterization comes through in small actions (pulling Bram's beer anyway, the "emotional support worms" joke, the scattergun kept "for asteroids and tax collectors"). The worldbuilding is economical and effective: the semi-sentient fern Gerald, the Heron's mark, bonded labor, the scar under the sleeve. The reveal of Nets's past via the coin is well-handled—showing through her flinch and the sudden "credit-only" policy rather than exposition. The dialogue crackles with personality and subtext; Wren's "Tonight it is" and Nets's "House policy is also lying" are sharp lines. The cozy atmosphere is established before the disruption, giving the intrusion real weight. Weaknesses: Some elements are familiar to the genre—the mysterious stranger with a past, the bartender with a hidden history, the "reclaimers arriving" cliffhanger are all well-worn tropes, even if executed with skill. The scar that "picks now, of all times, to itch" is a slightly convenient device. Wren is somewhat thinly sketched beyond their function as plot catalyst. A few lines flirt with over-polish ("cold as the void, familiar as a scar" doubles the metaphor unnecessarily). The "everything in the room shifts half a degree" is a nice touch but borders on the formulaic. The ending is tense but the emotional stakes for Nets, while implied, could be deeper—her internal conflict between safety and compassion is stated more than fully dramatized. Overall, this is professional-grade commercial fiction with genuine charm, good pacing, and strong dialogue, held back slightly by reliance on genre conventions and a secondary character who exists primarily to deliver plot. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gone South **Chapter Two: When the Saints** The first thing I learn about New Orleans is that it smells like a frat house threw up on a swamp. Beer, powdered sugar, horse, and something fried that's been re-fried so many times it's basically a religion. The second thing is that a saxophone will follow you down a whole street like it's got legs. I'm walking down a wide avenue crammed with tourists in beads, even though it's nowhere near Mardi Gras, and some guy on the corner is playing something slow, all bent notes, like the song is too tired to stand up straight. I don't know what it is. It sounds like my insides. Inventory, because inventory is what you do when your whole life fits in a backpack: seventy-four dollars. A phone at eleven percent. Fourteen missed calls from Mom. A jar of peanut butter stolen from my own pantry — crime of the century — and Dad's Swiss Army knife from the garage, the one he taught me to whittle with, which I guess makes me a runaway *and* a monster. Plus my ID, with a name on it that isn't mine anymore and a picture of a girl I don't recognize, even though she's technically the reason I'm here. Forty-eight hours ago I said it out loud. Three years of rehearsing in the bathroom mirror and it still came out small, like a confession instead of an announcement. Mom went statue-still. Dad said, "We'll talk about this when you've had time to think." Like I'd asked for a puppy. Like three years of thinking was not-thinking. Then the school counsellor calls — Ms. Pritchard, voice like a customer service line for feelings — and suddenly I'm a "concerning behavioural pattern," and Mom's crying at the kitchen table like somebody died. I heard her tell Dad, when she thought I was upstairs: *I don't know where my daughter is.* And I stood on the stairs thinking, right here. I have been right here the entire time. You just never once looked up. My phone buzzes. Fifteen missed calls. I can't listen to the voicemails. I can't delete them either. Somebody should study me. Oh wait — Ms. Pritchard already does. I give out around a square with iron balconies and music leaking from every doorway, and I sit on the curb because my feet are screaming and the light is doing something gold and forgiving off the buildings, and for about ninety seconds I forget to be afraid. Then this guy stops in front of me. Forties, clean shirt, smile like a realtor. "You look lost, sweetheart. Hungry? I've got a place nearby if you want to clean up, get a meal. No strings." He squints. "What are you, anyway? A boy or a girl?" And my brain does this disgusting split-screen, because part of me clocks the question as dangerous while another part is pathetically busy being *relieved he even asked*, like being a puzzle to a creep counts as progress. I say nothing, which apparently is an answer, because he steps closer. "There you are." A hand drops on my shoulder. "I've been looking everywhere, you idiot." Short braids. A jacket way too nice for this curb. A voice like she's already bored of rescuing me. She looks at the man with completely flat eyes. "They're with me." He raises his hands, backs off, dissolves into the crowd, and the adrenaline drains out of me and leaves pure shaking behind. "Rule one," she says, dropping down beside me like we planned this. "Don't sit still looking new. That's how guys like that find you. He wasn't offering food. He was shopping." "I wasn't going to—" "Rule two. Don't lie to the person who just saved your ass." I shut up. "Saint." She holds out a fist. I stare at it. "It's a fist bump, not a marriage proposal." I bump it. "Taylor." No pause. No "is that a boy name or a girl name." No squinting at me like a math problem. She just nods, like I said something ordinary, and I have to look away at the saxophone player down the block because my eyes are doing something I did not authorize. "Like the football team?" I manage. "Like the church kind. My mama had a drinking problem and a sense of humor." Flat, like a weather report. "You eaten?" And here's the concerning behavioural pattern, Ms. Pritchard, write it down: every documentary ever made says a stranger offering food is step one of vanishing. But Saint is the first person in two days to ask me a question and actually wait around for the answer. "...No." "Cool. Come on." She buys me a po'boy and pays out of a roll of bills thick enough that I stare, and she catches me and says, "Tips," in a tone that ends the conversation forever. On the stoop, a cop car rolls past slow and Saint goes very still and very interested in her shoes until it's gone. Her phone lights up twice. She flips it face-down without looking. *File all of that away,* says the smart part of my brain. *Shut up,* says the rest of me, which is chewing. "You got people looking for you," she says. Not a question. "You going back?" "No." It comes out fast and hard, and then, traitorously, my throat does the thing. "They didn't hit me or anything. Everybody wants it to be hitting. My mom just — she looked at me like I was a stranger who murdered her kid. While I was standing right there." I shred the wrapper into strips. "So I left before she could do it again." Saint chews for a while. "I had a home too," she says finally. "Ask me about it in a week." "Why a week?" "That's how long I take to decide if I like somebody." She stands, brushes off her jeans. "There's a spot. Other kids, a floor, a lock on the door. You can come or not. Rule three: I don't chase." The sun's going down red over the river and the saxophone guy has shifted into something new, and I swear to God it's *When the Saints Go Marching In.* I look at her. "You have got to be kidding me." First time she smiles. "Told you. Mama had a sense of humor." Every alarm bell Ms. Pritchard ever installed is ringing. This is the exact scene — kid meets kid on a curb, follows her into the dark. But here's what nobody tells you: the people who were supposed to be safe did the most damage, so maybe my instincts are wired backwards. Maybe backwards is how you survive a place like this. I shoulder my backpack. My hand finds Dad's knife in the side pocket, and I leave it there, unclipped. Just in case. "Lead the way, Saint." And the horn follows us down the street like it's got legs.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter is a strong execution of the prompt. Taylor's voice is consistent, wry, and wounded; the first-person mixed-tense narration works, blending present scene with past-tense backstory. The internal monologue captures conflicting emotions well — the split-screen reaction to the predator's question ("relieved he even asked") is a genuinely nuanced, uncomfortable insight. Saint is an engaging foil with plausible mystery (cash roll, cop flinch, face-down phone) and sharp dialogue ("He wasn't offering food. He was shopping"). The predator scene is realistic and handled without melodrama. The "When the Saints" musical callback is a bit on-the-nose but earns a smile. Taylor's caution (leaving the knife unclipped) shows believable, non-naive characterization. Minor flaws: some quips are overly polished for a 16-year-old in crisis ("customer service line for feelings" is great, but the density of cleverness occasionally feels authorial); the ending's optimism is slightly convenient, though Taylor's ambivalence keeps it grounded. Prose is clean, imagery evocative without purple. Word count near target. No meandering; tight structure over one day. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The end of the world arrived on a Tuesday, which surprised nobody who knew Tuesdays.* Ten years on, in the shell of the Gilded Wombat — a pub with no beer, which its inhabitants regarded as the more permanent apocalypse — Midas and Chewy held the morning briefing. "Right," said Midas. "Filter cartridge. The still's clogged again." "Model K-nine," said Chewy. "Or compatible." "You memorised the manual?" "I *contain* the manual. It isn't the same thing, and I'd thank you to remember it." Chewy was a Companion Koala (Series 3), grey, round, approximately the size of a suspicious watermelon. Under his left ear, in faded silver, it said GENUINE ANIMO-TRONIC PAL. He had a bald solar panel on his head and forty-seven pre-recorded phrases,† of which he used about six, dryly. He had been Midas's buddy for eleven years, nine longer than anyone else had managed, because the end of the world had killed fewer people than Midas had. Midas was named, his mother claimed, for the golden touch. It was true that everything he touched changed value. It was the direction that was the issue. They set off along the old highway, and that was where they found it, stencilled on a collapsed billboard: **SANCTUARY — 6 KM. WATER. POWER. FAMILY. FOLLOW THE GREY FACES.** Beneath: a stencilled koala face, pointing north. Chewy stopped walking. Companion Koalas did not, as a rule, see their own face on the ruins of the world. "Coincidence," said Midas. "Obviously," said Chewy, in the voice of someone checking exits. The filter depot was east. Sanctuary was north. "Six kays," said Midas, "is basically next door, by current standards." "That's the spirit," said Chewy, "that got you bitten by the library." The grey faces recurred — on a burnt-out bus, on a roundabout, once, memorably, on a cow. The mission went sideways shortly after, in the traditional manner, by which is meant: all at once and forever. First, the toll bridge demanded four dollars fifty, accepted their hoarded before-time coin with a pneumatic sigh, and rose majestically to reveal a bridge that ended mid-creek. They waded. Chewy deployed phrase thirty. Then the shopping centre, which had been claimed by geese. The geese had a complex society based on hatred, and were negotiated with at the standard rate: everything in the left-hand pocket. And then the source of the stencils hove into view, sun-bleached and still faintly cheerful: **WALTZING MATILDA KOALA KINGDOM — FAMILY SANCTUARY.** "Ah," said Chewy. "Sanctuary in the *before-time* sense." Inside, the entrance avenue was lined with animatronic koalas, sun-cracked, eyes like dull marbles. One was still ticking its head left, right. Left. Right. "They're sleeping," said Midas. "No," said Chewy quietly, "they aren't." The residents wore ranger khakis looted from uniforms and were led by a woman called Margaret, who had the patient stare of someone who had survived the apocalypse on annual leave and spite. Three years ago the park's solar-powered PA system, senile but operational, had crackled out the words "WELCOME… THE… CHOSEN… MATE," and theology had done the rest. Now here was a grey brother from the wastes who *spoke*. They garlanded Chewy in plastic eucalyptus and seated him on the coin-op ride, now a throne, and asked him to Say the Words. "Let's be mates!" said Chewy, in the manner of small gods everywhere. The crowd wept. They declined to let him leave. Gods who can leave are, theologically, staff. Midas negotiated. Midas's negotiating style was that he leaned on things. He leaned on the master control console. "Do not lean on th—" The park woke up. Every dead koala's head began to turn. The fountain gurgled something black. The PA announced, at full volume, what was either the End Times or a 1987 fire drill. The animatronic chorus, forty years un-oiled, ground into the Welcome Song at half speed, and the faithful, concluding reasonably that the apocalypse had come *twice* and they were not sitting through another one, scattered. Margaret hit Midas with a commemorative tray. In the confusion, Chewy was rescued from godhood. "I had it under control." "You were about to issue a tithe." "A *small* tithe." They left through the gift shop, grabbing what was grabbable, and exited through the geese (right-hand pocket; the geese knew their names now). They returned to the Gilded Wombat worse for wear in the following ways: physically — one boot, two buttons, and a hand bandaged with a commemorative tea towel; materially — the good crowbar, both pockets' worth of currency, and the day's dignity; spiritually — Chewy had lost an ear and gained a voice-chip stutter, so that in quiet moments he now murmured *"Let's be… mates… mates… mates"* like a tiny grey curse. What they had gained was four hundred commemorative spoons, a crate of plush keyrings, one ceremonial garland, and — produced by Chewy after a spiteful hour's silence — a Model K-9 filter cartridge, still boxed, $24.95, Special Offer. "So," said Midas, fitting it into the still. "It went sideways." "It went sideways *onto* the objective. That still counts." Behind the bar, the still began, heroically, to drip. Tomorrow's mission: salt. Margaret's lot had salt. Margaret also had a tray, and now a grudge. "Same time tomorrow?" said Midas. "Obviously," said Chewy. "Let's be mates." "I know," said Midas. "It's the only plan we've got." --- *\* It was officially designated the Great Unravelling by people with time for that sort of thing, and "that thing with the power" by everyone else.* *† Number twelve was "Let's be mates!" Number thirty was "Please do not immerse me in water." He deployed both with the same weary sincerity.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, disciplined piece of comic apocalyptic fiction that hits the brief with impressive precision. The structure follows the prompt exactly: morning deliberation at the Gilded Wombat, a mission (filter cartridge) that goes sideways via the koala sanctuary cult, and a return home "worse for wear in multiple ways" — which the story delivers literally as a list (physically, materially, spiritually), a nice Pratchett-ish enumeration gag. The word count is roughly on target. The Pratchett influence is handled with genuine skill rather than pastiche: the footnote jokes, the dry parentheticals ("which surprised nobody who knew Tuesdays"), the anthropomorphised geese with "a complex society based on hatred," and the theological satire of the "CHOSEN MATE" PA announcement are all in the right register. Chewy is the standout — a deadpan animatronic with forty-seven phrases of which he uses six, and the closing stutter ("Let's be… mates… mates… mates… like a tiny grey curse") is a genuinely earned comic-dark payoff. Midas's "everything he touched changed value; it was the direction that was the issue" is an economical character joke that does real work. Weaknesses are modest. The middle section compresses events into summary at times ("The mission went sideways shortly after, in the traditional manner") — a deliberate stylistic choice, but it occasionally tells rather than shows, and the geese and toll bridge are dispatched in a sentence each where a Pratchett would have lingered. Margaret is a sketch rather than a character; the cult could bear more texture. The emotional range is narrow — wry amusement throughout, with little genuine poignancy or menace, though the "No, they aren't" beat and the dead koalas ticking their heads hint at darker territory the story doesn't fully explore. The ending's "It's the only plan we've got" lands softly but appropriately; no false uplift. Prose is clean, rhythmically controlled, and the dialogue is consistently sharp and characterful. Nothing purple, nothing overwrought. The piece is coherent, tightly structured, and engaging throughout. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 89.3
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Love in the Limelight — A Scene: Penmorfa, Wales** The bell over the door of Rees & Daughter had two settings: a polite jingle and panic. This was panic. A man shouldered in out of the rain, flattened himself against the Welsh-language fiction, and said, "Please tell me you're closed." "We're open," said Elin Rees. "That's generally why the sign says open." "Then I'm not here." "I can see that. It's the sort of not-being-here that drips." He was dripping — onto the floor her grandfather had laid, onto a display of walking guides. Beyond the steamy glass, three men with cameras went past at a trot, lenses like gun barrels, heading down toward the harbour. "You're him," she said, before she could stop herself. *Duw.* So much for strategy. His whole face lit. "You've seen—" "I said you're him. I didn't say which him." "Oh." The light dimmed, then rallied. "Theo Marlowe. And you are—" "Busy." "Lovely shop, Busy. Is it a chapel? It feels like a chapel." "It was. We knocked the sin out of it. Mostly." She should put him out. The photographers would be back. She flipped the sign to CLOSED instead and went to put the kettle on, furious at her own hands, which had gone trembly as though she were sixteen. He was Theo Marlowe. She had seen that face on a billboard in Cardiff the size of a hay barn. It was smaller in person, and wetter, and it had read three poetry spines and one of her dust-jacket blurbs while she wasn't watching, and she didn't know what to do with that at all. "I'm being hounded," he said, accepting the tea towel she threw him like an honour. "There's a thing filming up at the castle, and a woman I had dinner with twice has told the *Sun* something that isn't strictly— it doesn't matter. The point is, I am a blameless man in a damp country." "It's Wales. There's no such thing." "Ha." He toweled his hair and grinned — *the* grin, the one from the posters, deployed like a cavalry charge. "You know, most people have asked for a photo by now." "Most people must be very tiring to carry around." Something crossed his face — quick as cloud off the sea. Then the grin again, wider, which told her more than the cloud had. "You've really never seen anything I've done? Not the Roman one? People like the Roman one." "I'm sure it's very loud." "You could just say. I've won—" He stopped. Recalibrated. "I was nominated." "There's modest." "I *was*," he said, stung. "Twice." Elin poured the tea and did not smile, which cost her something. The truth was she had seen the Roman one twice and told her sister once, and had thought about the battlefield goodbye rather more often than was sensible for a woman of thirty-four with stock to price. "They'll be drinking in the Dragon till the rain stops," she said. "So will you be." "Then I'll buy a book. Recommend me something. Nothing about acting." She looked him over — the expensive coat, the ruin of a haircut, the eyes that kept checking her face like a man checking a mirror — and reached, on instinct, for the R.S. Thomas. "He's Welsh. Austere. Miserable as November. He'd have taken one look at you and prayed for your soul." "Will I like him?" "No. That's why you should have him." He laughed — really laughed, not the poster laugh — and then, because the rain was hammering the old chapel roof and there was nowhere, for the moment, for a famous man to go, he told her something. "Opening night of my first proper job. Touring *Lear*. Mold. I was nineteen and had one line: 'My lord, the horses are ready.' I walked on, there were more people than I'd ever seen in the dark, and I said it to the wrong king." "Were there two kings?" "There weren't any kings. I said it to Gloucester. Gloucester doesn't ride." He turned the poetry book over without reading it. "One man laughed. Just one, not even cruelly. And I've heard him ever since. Every theatre, every premiere — twenty years of people clapping, and I can still find that one laugh in the dark like a loose thread. If a room goes quiet, I have to—" He gestured at himself, the towel, the whole wet performance. "You see. It's not attractive. I know it's not attractive." The shop ticked with rain. Elin thought of the billboard over the A470, forty feet of confidence, and of the small damp man in front of her checking her face to see if the laugh was there. "My father could charm the birds off the hedges," she said. "Charmed a rep into stocking five hundred copies of his own poems. Charmed himself out of a marriage before I was ten. Charm's a pickpocket, Mr Marlowe. It takes something off you and smiles." She pushed the R.S. Thomas across the counter. "So I don't pay in that currency. Nothing personal." He was quiet a moment — genuinely, she thought, the first unperformed quiet since the bell had panicked. "The horses were ready, though," he said at last. "That part was true." "There's something." "Elin." He'd read the till receipt she'd tucked in the book; he said her name carefully, like a line he meant to keep. "Do you ever leave Penmorfa?" "There's a question a man with a helicopter asks." "I'll come back. Thursday." "It's a day of the week. I've no opinion on it." The rain had thinned; the Dragon's door stood open and empty of photographers. He paid with a note far too large, refused the change, and at the door he turned — and the cavalry-charge grin started up and then, interestingly, was stood down. "*Diolch*," he said, murdering it gorgeously. "Go on with you. And Mr Marlowe." "Theo." "The Gloucester in that play. Blinded, wasn't he? Maybe he needed a horse more than the king did. Maybe you were the only one in the building who'd read it properly." He looked at her a long moment, as though she'd handed him back something he'd lost in Mold twenty years ago. Then the bell jingled — politely, this time — and he was gone. Elin stood a while in the chapel quiet. On the counter he'd left the tea towel, folded badly, and one of her bookmarks, on which he'd written, in a hand too grand for the message: *For the towel — T. xx* She put it in the drawer, not the bin. For stock purposes. Obviously.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This scene is a polished, confident execution of a demanding brief. The prompt asks for something quite specific — a rogue actor with a fragile ego whose charm offensive derails against an outwardly immune but inwardly flustered bookstore owner — and the response delivers every element with precision while adding texture the prompt didn't require. Strengths: The dialogue is the engine of the piece, as instructed, and it's genuinely distinctive in both voices. Elin's dry Welsh wit ("I said you're him. I didn't say which him"; "It's a day of the week. I've no opinion on it") is crisp and characterizing. Theo's voice shifts subtly between performance and confession — the grin "deployed like a cavalry charge," then "stood down," tracks his arc through the scene physically rather than through narration of feeling. The Gloucester/Lear anecdote is an excellent device: it shows his fragility concretely, gives Elin the material for her final grace note ("Maybe you were the only one in the building who'd read it properly"), which lands as an earned emotional beat rather than sentimentality. The interiority is handled economically and mostly through action: Elin flipping the sign to CLOSED "furious at her own hands," the admission of having watched "the Roman one" twice, the bookmark "put in the drawer, not the bin. For stock purposes. Obviously." — that final line is the kind of closing gesture that shows rather than tells her flustered interior while maintaining her surface immunity. The Welsh setting is integral, not wallpaper: the converted chapel, the Welsh-language fiction section, R.S. Thomas ("Miserable as November"), Mold, the Dragon pub, the mangled "Diolch." The setting informs the theme — chapel, austere poetry, a culture suspicious of charm. Weaknesses, mostly minor: Theo's confession about Mold arrives fairly easily; a rogue with a fragile ego might resist revealing it so promptly to a near-stranger, though the framing ("there was nowhere, for the moment, for a famous man to go") partially justifies the openness. The trajectory — famous actor rendered vulnerable, leaves smitten — is a familiar romance beat, though the execution freshens it. One or two images strain slightly ("lenses like gun barrels," "quick as cloud off the sea" is good but "like a loose thread" is a touch convenient). The chemistry, while present, resolves somewhat fast for one scene, though the prompt explicitly demands mutual attraction within the scene, so this is fidelity rather than fault. The prose is elegant without being purple; the sentences have rhythm and variety; the tonal control (wit carrying real feeling underneath) is maintained throughout. The ending's lightness is well-earned — the folded towel and grandly-written bookmark are earned by the scene's logic. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door opened on warmth, and that was the first wrong thing. Aya had expected cellar breath — cold stone, the dry whisper of the wards. Instead lamplight spilled across the threshold, sweet with spermaceti smoke, and beneath it tobacco, and beneath that, faint as gossip, the sea. The underhold was no vault. It was a long, low hall of blackened oak and scrimshaw, lit by a dozen whale-oil lamps, and at its far end — where the relic should have stood alone under spell and key — someone had set a counting table like a throne. Behind it sat Marena. The Drowned Woman of Morska. Mother-of-knives. Decidedly *un*-incarcerated, grey braid over one shoulder of her oilskin coat, a ledger open before her. They said she'd been keelhauled under a whaler in her youth and come up the far side smiling — that the sea had given her back. Around her stood guards. Aya's heart did arithmetic: eight. No, nine. Crossbows. The brass mouth of a harpoon-pistol. One vast, silent man honing a flensing knife. Out beyond the guild walls, down in the harbor, a foghorn sounded — one long note, mournful as something grieving in the murk. "Wren," Marena said, almost gently. "There she is. Come in, come in. You've caught me at my accounts." "You're supposed to be in irons," Katra said, flat as a slap. "Am I?" Marena turned a page. "The constabulary and I keep an understanding. They wanted a morning's headlines; I wanted a quiet season. The cove they carried out of my rooms answers to my name in bad light and owes me his teeth besides." She looked up, and her eyes were the color of harbor water. "Then I let it be whispered about that Morska stood headless, and I sat in the dark, like a spider. It's a marvel, what crawls to the web when the spider plays dead." *A snare. All of it.* Aya reached inward for the cold place, the door behind the door — and found it smothered. Her own knotwork, thrice-turned, tied into that lintel three months past for a purse of silver, lay over the threshold like wet wool over a fire. Below the world, the whispering congregation pressed flat against it, and could not rise. *She had taught them how to hold the knife. The edge was at her own throat.* Katra's hand drifted toward her gutting knife. A crossbow string drew taut. "Ah-ah," Marena said. "Hand away, sweetheart, or you'll be haddock before you hit the floor." "We're caught, girls." Simeon's voice was tired, old. He set his jimmy down with terrible gentleness and knelt. "Put it away, Kat." They were disarmed in silence, made to kneel on the cold stone. Aya's mask suddenly itched like a lie. Marena beckoned. "Let's see the Wren's true feathers." Her hooked fingers took the mask at its edge and peeled it away like skin from fruit. The foghorn sounded a second time. Marena studied her, tilting her chin to the lamplight. "Soft hands. Straight teeth. Quality." Then stillness. A long, drowned stillness. "God below. I *know* this face." Her grip tightened. "Twenty years gone I stood in the rain at Gallows Steps and watched a woman with your chin refuse the hood. Spat in the bishop's eye before they sprang the trap. Vask. You're the Vask girl. Lady Aya Vask, as I live and breathe." The name landed in Aya like a dropped bell. She saw it all in merciless sequence: the *Gazette* by noon, set in great fat type — LORD'S DAUGHTER TAKEN MASKED IN THIEVES' DEN. Her father at breakfast, the paper slipping from his hands. Twenty years the family had spent drowning that name in consecrated silence, and here was the daughter to dredge it up — thief, witch, unmasked. They hanged witches still. She had warded this very room. *I am bargaining with the rope already round my neck*, she thought, and underneath the thought, faint and patient, something below the stones knew her name. "Gentry." Katra spat it like a fishbone. "You eat gutter bread with us by night and go home to silk. All this time, you were slumming on our lives." "Stow it, Kat—" "She *used* us, Sim—" Aya said nothing. It was true, all of it, and there was no soap for it. So she lifted her chin — her mother's chin, curse it — and did the coldest arithmetic of her life. "Then you know what I'm worth," she said, and some distant part of her was proud that her voice came out level. "Dead, I'm a scandal and a magistrate's questions. Alive, I'm the Vask purse. My father would empty his coffers to keep my name out of the papers." Marena leaned back. "Your father would pay to have you sunk in the harbor with your ankles wired to a try-pot. You're the family shame, girl, come home to roost." "A trial," Aya pressed. "A hanging. Think of the broadsheets. He sits on the Admiralty Board — he has elections to buy and daughters to marry off. Every day I breathe *quietly* is worth more than your treasury." Marena laughed then, genuinely, delighted, and addressed her guards. "Hear her? The little witch thinks she's an annuity." Her gaze came back, sharp as a flensing blade. "And so you are. Why sell the cow when she'll keep for years? A lord's daughter on my hook and a witch in my pocket, all in the one skin." She tapped the table. "Did you think I'd let a witch knot my locks and never ask her name? I've been *keeping* you, Wren. Like a coin for a rainy day." "And us?" Katra said. "You? You're worth your wages and nothing more. You'll live because corpses are paperwork." Marena lifted the relic then from its cloth beside the ledger — the Scythan crown, the gutter's seat of power. Up close it was an ugly little thing: a circlet of black whalebone set with amber, ancient as sin. In the largest stone hung a small dark shape, and it was not an insect. She turned it idly in her hands, like a washerwoman wringing cloth. "You came for this," she said. "Try it on someday, if you're very good." She rose. "Take them below. The lord's daughter gets her own cell — she's porcelain now." As the guards hauled Aya past the table, the amber caught the lamplight, and she would have sworn — God below help her — that the dark thing in it turned to watch her go. Out beyond the walls the foghorn sounded a third time: three notes across the black water, like a bell counting the drowned. The sea kept its accounts. And below the world, pressed flat beneath her own knotwork, the congregation that knew her name settled in, patient as the tide, to wait.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of genre fiction that hits nearly all the prompt's beats with confidence and style. The whalepunk/Victorian-gothic aesthetic is vividly rendered through details like spermaceti lamps, scrimshaw, flensing knives, try-pots, and the foghorn motif. Marena is a compelling antagonist with a distinct voice — the "keeping you like a coin for a rainy day" reveal that she always knew Aya's identity is a satisfying twist that recontextualizes the power dynamic. The unmasking scene lands well, with the Gallows Steps recognition tying Aya's mother's execution into the plot organically. The internal monologue is present and effective, particularly "I am bargaining with the rope already round my neck." The dialogue is largely excellent — Katra's bitterness ("You eat gutter bread with us by night and go home to silk") and Marena's mercantile menace feel authentic to the world. The immateria congregation waiting "patient as the tide" provides a strong gothic undertow and forward hook. Weaknesses: the story beats requested (trio captured, unmasked, hostage negotiation) are delivered, but the negotiation resolves a bit too smoothly in Marena's favor without real tension of Aya nearly failing — Marena capitulates to the hostage logic almost instantly, deflating some suspense. Simeon is underdeveloped, a near-silent third wheel. A few phrases flirt with overwriting ("her heart did arithmetic," "the name landed in Aya like a dropped bell"), and the foghorn-as-omen device is repeated perhaps once too often. The "corpses are paperwork" line is great, but some of Marena's aphorisms crowd one another. The ending's darkness is earned and consistent with the gothic tone. Prose is polished, coherent, and controlled throughout; no meandering.
