# The Last Outpost ## Chapter One: The Knot in the Bar The knot in the bar top is the oldest thing on this rock that isn't rock. Real cedar, which out here costs more than the still it sits under. When I'm listening, I wipe it. When I'm worrying, I wipe it harder. Tonight I'm only listening, so the knot gets a gentle polish while Pru Vann explains her marriage to me for the fortieth time. "All I'm saying, Nets, is if she loved me, she'd sell the skiff." "If she sold the skiff, sugar, she'd have no way to visit the woman she sold it for." I top her glass. "Buy her a heater for the cab. Apologize for the thing about her mother." "How d'you know I said something about her mother?" "Everybody says something about the mother." The Last Outpost: a lazy hub bolted to an asteroid in the far belt, Andromeda's outer rim, where miners drink their ore money and merchants drink their margins. I tend bar. They tolerate my flaws; I keep the flaws in equilibrium with my talents, mostly by knowing everyone's business before they do. Then the door chimes, and the evening tilts. She's reefborn, off some water moon — tendril-dreads where hair should be, and every one of them askew, frizzed like she stuck her head in a thruster. Dust on her coat. She plops down at the bar, quiet as a dropped wrench. "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." I pour the good blue stuff — distilled in orbit, tastes like someone set fire to honey. She pays in coin. Hard coin, no chip. She's checked the door four times since sitting down. "Running from or running to?" I ask, rag moving on the knot. "Does it matter?" "Only for the tab." That almost gets a smile. Her tendrils loosen a quarter inch. "Nettle," I say. "Nets, to my friends. The bar decides who's friends." A pause. Half a breath too long. "Sorrel." Half the belt names themselves after things that grow. It's a wish. I know, because I did it too. "Pru," I say, not turning, "take the skiff problems to the other end." "Ears are closed," Pru announces loudly, relocating. Dempsey, bless him, cranks the jukebox without being asked. That's the Outpost's version of shutting a door. Sorrel wraps both hands around her glass. "You ever hear of thread-listening?" "Something with gravity?" "Grav-shear. The drift sings, if you've got the tendrils for it." One of hers curls around the glass stem, all on its own. "Combine bonded me at nineteen. Family debt, three generations deep. I chart approach threads through the belts, and they own the charting." "Owned," I say, wiping the knot. "Past tense. I can hear it." "Three weeks back, out past the cold belt, we struck an ark. First-generation seeder, pre-Compact. Read dead on every scope." Her voice drops under the jukebox. "It wasn't dead. It was sleeping. Two hundred thousand seed cultures — a whole terraforming library. Orchard worlds that don't exist yet. The Combine logged it as salvage. Strip the vault, sell it by the kilo." "And you?" "Filed the approach thread wrong. On purpose. Wiped our nav logs at Ferris Gate and walked off with the only copy." She taps her temple. "It's up here. Only one anywhere." The rag stops. I make it start again. "That's a burn-your-bond crime," I say. "Reclaim writ." The words come out flat, practiced, like she's said them to herself a lot in the dark. "There's an agent out there with my face in a folder. Combine doesn't chase coin. They chase precedent." I know what it is to be paperwork somebody wants back. I don't say that. I wipe the knot instead, which is the same thing. "Berth nine's mine," I hear myself say. "The lock's honest, and—" She's on her feet before I finish. Tendrils gone wire-tight. "Why would you do that? You don't know me." "Sit down, Sorrel." "People don't just— why?" "Because somebody did it for me once," I say. "And because meddling is my worst quality. Ask anyone." "Worst quality," Dempsey confirms, not looking up. "Tragic," Pru agrees. Sorrel stands there a moment, out past the edge of her own map. Then she sits. Slow. Like the stool might bolt too. "First rule of the Outpost," I say, refreshing her glass. "Nobody runs on an empty tab." "What's the second rule?" "Haven't needed one yet." The comm crackles before she can drink. Pip's voice, young and apologetic, straight from the dock: "Nets? Got an independent cutter off the cold-belt lane requesting berth. No manifest filed. And, uh — they're asking for our arrivals log?" Sorrel's tendrils flatten against her skull. All the looseness, gone. "That's them," she whispers. Outside, there's a ship hanging off our rock with a writ in its pocket and her face in a folder. That's a real thing now, in my bar, between the jukebox and last call. "You going to answer that?" she asks. "Nets?" Pip says. "They're asking again." I look at the coin on the bar. At the door. At the knot, worn smooth as river stone under my rag — I've polished this one spot through two owners and one past life, and my hand is steady, which is more than I can say for the rest of me. "Pip," I say, keying the comm, "tell them the dock computer's down." "It's not down." "It's a moody machine. Tonight it's moody in your favor." I set the rag over the knot like a flag over a country I'm not done defending, and pour her the second double before she asks. "Drink your whisky," I tell her. "Around here, holding the door is the whole job. The whisky is a garnish." She drinks. The cutter waits. And I keep wiping the same warm spot of cedar, because tomorrow is going to need me steady — and nobody, but nobody, docks at the Last Outpost without buying a round first.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong execution of the prompt. The piece hits the cozy sci-fi register well: warm, wry first-person present tense, a bar with personality, low-stakes banter (Pru's marriage) opening before the stranger arrives. Dialogue percentage is roughly 60% as requested. The conflict — Sorrel carrying the only copy of a stolen nav thread to a sleeping ark, with a Combine cutter now docking — is established and left unresolved, per instructions. Strengths: The voice is consistent and distinctive ("The bar decides who's friends," "It's a moody machine. Tonight it's moody in your favor"). The cedar knot motif is a nice throughline — wiping as emotional barometer — and pays off at the end. Supporting cast (Pru, Dempsey, Pip) get quick, characterful beats. Nets' hinted past ("paperwork somebody wants back") is shown obliquely rather than explained. The worldbuilding (reefborn tendrils, thread-listening, reclaim writs, plant-names as aspiration) is economical and evocative. Weaknesses: Some lines flirt with cuteness and quip-fatigue — "Tragic," Pru agrees / "Worst quality," Dempsey confirms is a sitcom beat. The "somebody did it for me once" reveal is a bit pat. The ark discovery is delivered as a fairly long expository monologue by Sorrel — the one place the piece tells rather than dramatizes. The ending's "nobody docks without buying a round first" is charming but slightly glib against the armed-cutter threat, edging toward incongruous lightness, though it fits the cozy genre contract. A few metaphors ("quiet as a dropped wrench," "like a flag over a country I'm not done defending") are serviceable but occasionally strain. The plot itself — fugitive with secret in her head, pursuers arriving — is a familiar shape, though the texture redeems it. Overall: competent, warm, well-paced, with minor quip-overload and one expository sag. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Two: Where You Got Your Shoes Morning tastes like pennies and bus exhaust. I slept — if you can call it that — on a bench in a park by the river, and somewhere upriver an invisible madman is playing scales on what sounds like a haunted calliope. My whole body is one long bruise shaped like a bench slat. The strap slips off my shoulder for the fortieth time since Memphis. The pack is Dad's old hiking one, army green, one buckle held together with a hair tie. Everything I own weighs eleven pounds. I know because I weighed it on the bathroom scale at 1 a.m. while the whole house held its breath. That was *last* night's disaster. The disaster before that: me, at the dinner table, saying the truest sentence I've ever said out loud. *I'm trans. My name is Taylor.* Mom went grey. Dad went somewhere behind his own face and didn't come back. Forty-eight hours of careful, awful quiet, and a guidance counselor's voice on the phone saying *concerning behavioral patterns* like I'm a weather system. So. New Orleans. I have $36.40. I have a phone at nine percent with fourteen missed calls. I have a T-shirt stuck to my back because apparently the air here is soup. At Café du Monde I spend $3.85 on beignets because you can't come to New Orleans and not, even if you're a fugitive. Powdered sugar gets everywhere. I look like a crime scene at a bakery. Around me, tourists take photos of their coffee while I do math in my head — at this rate I'm broke by Thursday. Unless I stop eating. Don't think about that. I turn the phone on. It buzzes so hard it nearly jumps off the table. **Mom:** *please just tell us you're alive* **Mom:** *taylor please* **Mom:** *we can figure this out* She used the right name. She used it twice, which means she's practicing, which means she has to practice. I don't know if that makes me want to scream or crawl home. Both. That's the thing nobody tells you — you can be one hundred percent right and still want your mom so bad it feels like drowning. I type *im alive* and delete it. I type *im alive dont look for me* and delete that too. I turn the phone off before it can betray me with more hope. Outside, a guy with a gap-tooth grin steps into my path. "Bet you five dollars I know where you got your shoes." "Um. A strip mall in—" "Don't answer that." A hand closes around my arm — not grabbing, just *there* — and suddenly there's a girl beside me, my age or a little older, all elbows and dark braids, sunglasses pushed up into them. "Now you owe him five bucks. That's the whole trick. The answer is 'on your feet.'" "You got 'em on your feet," the guy says, shrugging, delighted. "On your feet, on Decatur Street." "She's new, cut her slack," the girl says, and steers me away. To me: "Rule one. Nobody here bets you anything unless they already won." She says her name is Wren. Probably. "Real names are a luxury," she tells me, walking backwards like the street owes her money. "You've got that look, by the way." "What look?" "Fresh off the truck. Sleeping-bench posture. Counting-your-money face." She taps her own cheekbone. "I've been out here since March. So let me save you some time. Don't sleep in the same spot twice. The river cops clear the park at five a.m. And if a guy named Church ever offers you a shower and a hot meal, you run. The shower has a price." "What kind of—" "Run," she repeats, flat, and something behind her sunglasses goes somewhere I don't want to follow. "Free is the most expensive word in this city." The sky, which has been blue all morning, simply gives up around two o'clock. The rain doesn't fall so much as arrive, all at once, like somebody upending a bucket over the entire Quarter. Wren grabs my sleeve and we cram under an awning on Royal with three street musicians and a bride in a ruined sash. "So," Wren says, hugging her knees. "What's yours?" "What's my what?" "Your thing. Everybody out here has a thing. Mine's—" She pulls out a phone with a shattered screen, checks it, flips it face-down like she's smothering it. She's done that four times today. "Mine's classified. Yours?" "My parents and I had a difference of opinion," I say, "about whether I exist." Wren goes still. Then she nods, once, like I've passed a checkpoint. "Yeah," she says. "Mine too." We don't elaborate. It's the most honest conversation I've ever had. Later — after the rain quits, after she shows me which church actually feeds kids without a sermon and which alley the rats have claimed as sovereign territory — Wren stops me mid-stride. "Your strap's doing the thing again." "It's doing its best." "Mm." She unhooks a safety pin from inside her jacket cuff, threads it through the strap webbing, and crimps it shut with her teeth. "There. Now it'll only betray you sometimes." She says it so casually, this small competent kindness, and I have to look hard at a balcony full of ferns because kindness is somehow harder to survive than cruelty. Cruelty, I've got armor for. "There's a place kids crash," Wren says, not looking at me now either. "Two blocks. It's not great. It's dry. You don't have to." And here it is, the whole day rolled into one moment: is she the trap? Is *this* how it works — the shoe guy, the pin, the dry floor? Or is she exactly what she seems, a kid with a dead phone she can't stop checking, handing out rules like spare ribs because nobody handed her any? "One night," I say. "One night," she agrees, like it's a contract. I follow her down the darkening street. The strap holds. Somewhere behind me the calliope starts up again, and for the first time in two states, I'm walking toward something instead of away.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong YA chapter with a distinct, consistent first-person voice. Taylor's internal monologue is wry, wounded, and specific ("kindness is somehow harder to survive than cruelty"), and the mixed-tense, digressive narration matches the prompt's request. The New Orleans setting is well-researched and textured: the shoe scam on Decatur, the calliope, the sudden rain, Café du Monde beignets. Wren is a believable fellow runaway with hints of secrets (the shattered phone she keeps checking, the warning about "Church") without over-revealing. Dialogue is mostly natural, though Wren occasionally tips into overly polished aphorism ("Free is the most expensive word in this city") — a touch writerly for a street kid, but it fits the genre's stylization. The mother's texts using the right name is a genuinely affecting detail, and the emotional conflict (wanting to go home while fleeing) is earned rather than stated flatly. The ending's cautious hope ("walking toward something instead of away") is modest and earned — one night of shelter, not a transformation. Minor flaws: some metaphors strain slightly ("the street owes her money," "handing out rules like spare ribs" is odd), and the pacing compresses the afternoon. Word count is roughly on target. Overall a polished, engaging chapter with only small craft blemishes. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The end of the world came about, as these things do, because of an update. Nobody remembered what was being updated, or why. There had been a message — *Do not turn off your device* — and humanity, tired and three-quarters asleep, had turned off its device. When they turned it back on, everything was gone: the lights, the money, the little maps that told you where you were. It turned out civilization had lived in something called the cloud, which was not a cloud at all but other people's machines, and the other people had gone home. That was sixty years ago. Midas wasn't counting. Midas had other problems. "You're going to die," said Chewy, conversationally. "Thanks." "Statistically." Midas had been named by a mother who had only heard the first half of the story. He had a talent for finding trouble the way some people have a talent for the violin: without visible effort, and to the distress of everyone in earshot. He sat on the roof of Bloomin' Marvel's Garden World, wrapping his hand in curtain fabric, while his best friend offered a second opinion. Chewy was an animatronic koala* from the Before Times, when people had so much electricity they used it to make toys that were annoying in six languages. He ran on a proprietary power cell guaranteed for two hundred years. The box had also said he was fun for ages three and up. Both claims were being tested. "It's a small cut," said Midas. "It's gone the color of a sunset," said Chewy. "The bad kind. The kind that means locusts." So that was the mission, deliberated and agreed: the SuperSaver MegaCentre, four miles east, where the pharmacy aisle remained mostly unlooted on account of the locals. Go at dawn, back by lunch, get the good pills. Nothing would go wrong. "Terms and conditions apply," said Chewy brightly. No one knew what it meant. Everyone understood. --- The MegaCentre loomed out of the ivy like a beached ship. The sign promised EVERYDAY LOW PRICES, and beneath it someone had added, in careful paint: THE MANAGER IS WATCHING. The locals found them in Aisle Three. They were called the Greeters — descendants of the staff, still wearing the vests, vestments now — and they surrounded Midas with the serene menace of people who have found religion in an employee handbook. "Do you have," said their high priest, "a Club Card?" "No?" "Then that," he said, pointing at Midas's satchel of scavenged tins, "is shoplifting. The penalty is to be *Returned*." He gestured toward the Returns Desk, beyond which, legend said, none returned. It was Chewy who saved them, or at least postponed the disaster in a novel direction. The Greeters' most holy relic was the Catalogue — a thousand glossy pages of the world as it was, wept over nightly — and on page 214, between a bread maker and a gazebo, was Chewy's own face. *The Small Friend of Aisle Nine. He Sings. Batteries Not Included.* They fell to their knees. They gave him a tiny paper hat. "He has come," whispered the high priest, "to sing the Song of Restocking, and summon the Trucks." "Fifteen minutes could save you fifteen percent or more," said Chewy. "A prophecy!" "Maybe she's born with it," Chewy added, "maybe it's—" He never finished. Theology, like pottery, only needs one crack. Half the congregation declared the second utterance blasphemy — a rival brand, the scriptures of the False Aisle — and within a minute the MegaCentre was a war between the Rollbackers and the Everyday Low Priests, which was exactly the sort of sentence that would have made no sense before the world ended and made perfect sense now. Midas ran. He lost a boot in the escalator, which had stopped working decades ago and been demoted to stairs but still, clearly, hungered. A Greeter shot him with a pricing gun as he passed; he would find the sticker later, on his own back: MANAGER'S SPECIAL, 50% OFF. Then Barry found them. Barry the Bear had fronted the store's in-house band, six feet of moth-eaten fur and jammed servos, eternally grinning, built to make children happy in a way that had clearly curdled. He blocked the doors, raised one paw, and played his only chord. Chewy lost an ear to that paw. Midas got them both through a fire exit by main force and the timely collapse of a display of lawn furniture, and Barry, mid-lunge, simply stopped — his capacitor spent, his grin undimmed — and the last thing they heard behind them was the high priest screaming that the Small Friend had been, and gone, and it was *them*, they were the chosen— "I'm lovin' it," said Chewy, faintly, from under Midas's arm. --- They got home at dusk, worse for wear in the following ways: one boot, one ear, one graze from a ceremonial box-cutter, one pricing sticker, and one satchel that contained, instead of antibiotics, a bottle of dinosaur-shaped gummy vitamins and a garden gnome Chewy had refused to abandon. "Fruit-flavored," said Midas, reading the label on the roof. "My hand is going to fall off, but at least it will fall off with the complete daily requirement of vitamin C." Chewy said nothing. He was turning around and around, like a dog settling, and then with a sound like a cough he opened the little velcro pouch in his back — the battery hatch, long since repurposed — and produced a dusty foil blister pack. Amoxicillin. Expired, but then, so was everything. "A little girl's mother put it there," Chewy said, "in the Before. In case." He paused, searching himself. "I forgot I was carrying it. I forget a lot of what's in me." Midas held the pills up to the sunset — the good kind, the kind that means nothing — and was quiet a moment. "Tomorrow," he said, "we go back for your ear." "Same time?" "Dawn." "Just do it," said Chewy, and nobody knew what it meant, and everybody understood. --- *\*Strictly speaking, koalas are not bears. People in the old world mentioned this constantly, at parties, unprompted. It is entirely possible this is what brought the old world down.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of comic post-apocalyptic fiction that captures Pratchett's register well: dry asides, footnote humor, institutional satire (the Greeters, a cargo cult of retail religion), and a warm undertone beneath the jokes. The premise — civilization ended via a software update — is economical and funny. The retail-theology set piece (Club Card, the Catalogue, schism over advertising slogans) is genuinely inventive and the strongest section. Strengths: The voice is consistent and confident. Chewy's glitch-speech (recycled ad slogans as prophecy) is a clever device that pays off structurally — the final "Just do it" mirrors the opening "Terms and conditions apply," giving the ending a satisfying circularity. The ending's emotional beat (the forgotten antibiotics in Chewy's battery pouch, "I forget a lot of what's in me") is understated and earned, avoiding sentimentality. The footnote about koalas-not-bears is a good Pratchett homage. The "worse for wear" inventory list is a tidy fulfillment of the prompt's requirements. Weaknesses: The plot is somewhat episodic and the Barry the Bear sequence, while fun, arrives and resolves quickly, feeling like a set piece rather than an organic development. The Greeters' schism resolves the escape a bit too conveniently. Midas himself is thinly characterized beyond "hapless" — Chewy carries the story's personality. Some jokes are near-misses ("demoted to stairs" is great; the escalator "hungered" is a bit easy). The emotional complexity is present but modest; this is comedy first. The prose is clean but occasionally leans on list-like joke construction rather than flowing description. Imagery is functional rather than vivid — the world is sketched in jokes more than rendered. The prompt's requirements (deliberation, mission going sideways, return home worse for wear, ~1000 words, wry dry tone, both characters) are all met, and met well. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Love in the Limelight** — *a scene* --- The bell over the door of the Drowsy Dragon gave its tired little clang, and a man in a waxed jacket and a flat cap pulled low burst in out of the October mizzle, shut the door behind him, and leaned against it like the tide might follow. "Sorry," he said. "Hide me." Lowri Davies did not look up from her invoices. "We're open till five. Everyone's welcome. Even the hunted." Something in the voice made her glance up — and there was the face, the same one on the magazine a customer had abandoned on the counter that morning, under the headline RHYS MARLOWE: HOLLYWOOD'S MOST WANTED? She'd read the first paragraph. Only the first. "Oh," she said. "It's you." His grin arrived like a stage light coming up. "It's me," he agreed, as though this were good news for everyone. Outside, three men with cameras the size of small dogs were pressing their noses to the glass of the empty café across the lane. "Get away from the window, then. Unless you want to be a display." He moved fast — credit where due — ducking into the poetry alcove with the ease of a man who'd spent twenty years finding his light. One of the photographers cupped his hands to the Dragon's window. Lowri met his eye over her reading glasses and held it, flat and unhurried, the way she'd look at a dog considering her flowerbeds. The man moved on. "They've gone up toward the castle. You've got five minutes before they work out they've lost you." "You're wonderful." He emerged from poetry, cap in hand, and gave her the full wattage — the smile that sold out cinemas, apparently, according to the magazine's second paragraph, which she had not read. "I owe you. Dinner. Name the place." "You don't owe me. I just don't like men with cameras blocking my door." "Dinner," he said again, undeterred. "There's got to be somewhere half-decent—" "There's a chippy in Brecon." There it was — the flicker. She watched it cross his face like cloud over a field: the tiny recalibration of a man who'd aimed his best arrow and hit a wall. She shelved a paperback to hide that her hands weren't entirely steady, and hated herself for it. "I'm Rhys," he said, offering the hand, tilting the head, doing the voice — low, warm, faintly Welsh in a way it hadn't been when he came in, she noticed. Turned up like a dial. "I know who you are." She shook his hand once, firm, and let go. "Gareth." The dial snapped off. "Nobody calls me— How do you know that?" "You're Gareth Jones from Talgarth. My mam taught you English." "Mrs. Davies? You're Mrs. Davies's— God." Something happened to his face; the charm didn't fall so much as step aside, and for a second he looked younger, caught out, almost pleased. "She made me read *Under Milk Wood* aloud. The whole of First Voice. I was brilliant." "She says you were a show-off then, too." Lowri paused. "Her favourite pupil was Nerys Hughes. You were 'a caution.'" He laughed — a real one, startled out of him — and she felt it low in her stomach, infuriatingly, like a coal catching. "Right," he said, dropping into the chair by the stove without asking. She let him, which she would examine later, at length. "I'm here filming, up in the hills. Dragons." "Come home to Wales to make up dragons. Original." "You don't watch it, I suppose." "I've read the books. You were better cast than I expected." "That," he said, pointing at her, "is the nicest thing anyone's said to me in a year, and it was barely a compliment." "I expect you've got people to tell you you're brilliant." "Rooms full," he said. "That's the trouble. You stop believing them." It came out before the charm could catch it; she heard him hear it. He reached for the nearest thing on the table — the new walking guide to Offa's Dyke — and turned it over like a shield. "Is this any good? I'm going mad in that hotel. I need to disappear for a weekend." "Hills are good for that. Nobody follows you up a hill with a long lens." "You walk it? The Dyke?" "Every year. A section. Hay to Kington, usually, spring. The ridge, if the weather's kind." "Hay Bluff." The accent deepened, going broad and local as a gate. "My grandfather used to take me up there in any weather. He'd say, 'A proper mountain day, this, boyo.' I used to know every name on that ridge better than my times tables." "Lord Hereford's Knob," Lowri said. "Don't. Don't pretend that's a real place." "Twmpa, to us. Best view in the Black Mountains. Second-best name in Britain." "What's the first?" "Lord Hereford's Knob," she said, deadpan. "To you." He laughed until he had to sit back, and the shop felt smaller for it, warmer, and Lowri busied herself with the till drawer that did not need counting, because he had forearms, apparently, rolled out of that jacket, and a laugh that knew its way home, and none of this was relevant to anything. "Go up from the Gospel Pass," she said. "Early. Take the ridge along to the Bluff, drop down into Hay by evening. I'll mark it." She took the guide from him — his fingers were warm; the rain hadn't been — and drew the route in pencil, quick and sure, aware of him watching her hands instead of the map, aware of herself being aware. "There. That'll be nine ninety-nine." He put a twenty on the counter. "Keep the change. For Mrs. Davies's girl." "Lowri," she said. "Lowri," he repeated, like he was learning his lines. He didn't move to go, though the lane was empty and the light was going gold on the wet cobbles. "You never asked. For a photo. An autograph. Most people—" "I'm not most people." "No." He tucked the guide inside his jacket, over his heart, which was a ridiculous thing she saw him do and would remember. "I'm starting to get that." At the door he stopped, cap back on, and tried one last time, softer: "Dinner? The chippy in Brecon?" "I close at five," she said, which was not an answer, and they both knew it, and the bell gave its tired little clang, and the mizzle took him. Lowri stood very still in her quiet shop. Then she picked up the abandoned magazine, looked at the photograph a moment, and turned it face down on the counter. "Rubbish photo," she told the empty room.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, well-crafted scene that hits nearly every brief requirement with precision and charm. The Welsh setting is not wallpaper — Offa's Dyke, Hay-on-Wye, the Gospel Pass, Twmpa, "Lord Hereford's Knob" (a real and beloved local joke) ground the piece authentically. The actor-as-rogue-with-fragile-ego is rendered well: his charm is performed ("the dial" of his accent, the "full wattage" smile), and his vulnerability leaks out believably ("Rooms full. That's the trouble. You stop believing them"). The bookseller's superficial immunity combined with inner fluster is shown through action — counting a till drawer that doesn't need counting, turning the magazine face down — rather than told, which is exemplary. The dialogue is the engine, as instructed, and the voices are distinct: Rhys is all performance and quick recalibration; Lowri is dry, clipped, deflecting with wit. The reveal that her mother taught him English (his real name Gareth) is a clever device that derails the charm offensive exactly as prompted, forcing genuine interaction. The escalating chippy/Brecon dinner negotiation and the non-answer ending ("I close at five... which was not an answer") land the unresolved chemistry perfectly. Weaknesses: the piece leans on familiar romance beats (celebrity hides in small shop, spunky local unimpressed by fame) — the premise is given by the prompt, but some individual beats (keeping the change, "over his heart") are slightly stock. A couple of metaphors are borderline cute ("cameras the size of small dogs" works; "like the tide might follow" is fine; "cloud over a field" is good). The interior narration of Lowri's fluster occasionally verges on self-aware cuteness ("because he had forearms, apparently"), though it's intentional and mostly earns its tone. The transformation is modest and earned — no one changes wholesale, which is right for a single scene. The ending's warmth is congruent with the material. Prose is controlled, rhythmically varied, shows rather than tells, and never purple. Emotionally, it's engaging and has genuine complexity beneath the banter. This is professional-grade commercial romance writing. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 85.9
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## The Underhold The door swung inward before her knuckles grazed the iron, and the draught that breathed up from below was cold as a held breath. No lamps. No ward-glow. The famous lock — seven geared teeth of brass the guild had paid a king's ransom for — hung open like a slack jaw. And the witch-chalk across the lintel, the ward nobody was permitted to name aloud, had been scuffed through by a deliberate boot. Aya felt the old bitterness rise. They hanged women like her mother in Gallowgate Square by day, and bought their charms by night. "Someone's come ahead of us," Simeon whispered. His watch ticked like a small hammer in the hush. *Tick. Tick.* "The wards are dead, Aya. I trust brass, I trust a gauge, I trust a rivet. I don't understand this, and I don't care to." "Then we go back," Katra said, lantern shuttered to a coin's width of light. "We go back right now." "Back to what?" But her skin knew what her pride refused. Since she was nine years old the immateria had murmured at the edge of her hearing — a drowned choir under the floorboards of the world. Down here, there was nothing. It was like going deaf. She went down anyway. Pride was a rope of its own. The underhold was a cathedral of salvage: riveted walls weeping rust, bollards from scuttled ships, and at its heart the reliquary — a cage of baleen and black iron, and inside it, the thing three generations of the Morska had killed for. A fang of green-black bone, long as her forearm, etched in a script older than lungs. Scythan. Older than the whales it somehow resembled. Then, one by one, gloved hands unhooded the lamps along the walls. At the far end, in a captain's chair mounted on try-pot rivets, sat Mother Morska. She was meant to be in a cell. Instead she looked like a tide going out — patient, grey, inevitable — a harpoon-pistol across her knees and six of the old guard around her, hull-guns levelled. "Four bells they took me," Mother Morska said, her voice a rope drawn over a cleat. "And by six, my own children come creeping down my stair to pick the corpse. Punctual as hunger, thieves." "The Watch took you," Katra said. "Half the hall saw the wagon." "The Watch takes who it's paid to take." She smiled with the left half of her mouth. "It costs a fortune to be arrested properly, girl. Worth every barrel of oil, to see who'd swim up my stairs while the water was muddy." Aya's mind did its arithmetic. Six guns. One stair behind. Simeon's breathing gone shallow, his watch a hard little metronome counting what remained. And the silence — the great drowned silence pouring from that cage. Nothing in the immateria would come near this place. Her one weapon, the current that had carried her up through the ranks, was a dead lantern. She had never stood in a room with no whisper in it. She had never been so afraid. "You." Mother Morska lifted her chin. "The masked one who rose so fast. Broll. Take them." Katra's knife came half out of its sheath. "Katra. *No.* Six guns." A beat. Then the gutting knife clattered to the stone, followed by the scrimshaw knuckles. They patted Simeon down and found gears, a wrench, the watch. The guard weighed it in his palm. "Leave him the watch," Mother Morska said. "A man should hear it." Then she crossed the floor herself, hooked one finger beneath Aya's mask, and pulled the ribbon loose. The silence that followed had teeth. Then she exhaled, long and delighted. "Well. Lady Aya Ambrose. Ambergris money. Your house perfumed half the continent, and here's the daughter, slumming in my bilge-water." The floor seemed to tilt. Aya saw it all in an instant — her father's name dragged through the scandal sheets, the family seat, the servants whispering. And beneath it, colder: if they ever learned *how* she had risen, none of it would matter. They had hanged her mother in Gallowgate Square with half the quality in attendance. The rope had not cared about breeding. "Then you know what I'm worth alive," Aya said, and lifted her chin, and auctioned herself. "My father would pay in oil-shares. In fleet contracts. Whatever figure you're imagining, double it — a dead Ambrose fetches nothing but vengeance, and you've seen this morning how thoroughly the Watch can be bought. Harm me, and I promise you'll meet them again." "Ransom." Mother Morska turned the mask over in her hands like a curiosity. "Ransom is a wage, girl. Paid once and spent. But an exposed lady — a lady whose mask sits in *my* pocket — that pays quarterly." She leaned in close. Her breath smelled of spermaceti and black tea. "And you can drop the bluster. You think I didn't know what rides you? I smelled the hollow on you that first night, under the pier, when you called that drowned thing up out of the dark and it *obeyed*. I let you rise, little witch. A leviathan on a leash is still a leviathan." Aya said nothing. There was nothing. Every road out of this room ended at a leash or a rope. "So here are my terms. You'll go home. You'll dine at your father's table and wear his pearls and be my hand inside House Ambrose. Or the Wick receives an anonymous account of a certain masked aristocrat and her unholy talents — and you may explain your pedigree to the noose." "And my friends?" "Insurance. They live as long as you're obliging." *Tick. Tick.* Simeon's watch, unbearably loud. Katra caught Aya's eye, jaw tight, a question in it. *Do something. Do the thing you do.* Not here. Not in this dead, silent water, with witnesses, with everything she was already laid bare. To call the dark now would only hand them the rope faster. "Not now," Aya said quietly. "We live first." "Live first," Mother Morska agreed, pleased, gesturing to the guards. "Welcome to the deep water, my lady." As they were marched past the reliquary, bound wrist to wrist, Aya glanced once at the green-black fang in its cage. The etched script seemed almost to *listen*. And faint beneath the great silence — so faint she might have imagined it — something down there whispered her name.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the prompt's story beats faithfully: the trio enters the underhold, confronts the un-incarcerated guild leader, Aya is unmasked, captured, and negotiates her hostage value while grappling with exposure of her magick. No fight scene occurs, dialogue is heavy, third person past tense with internal monologue, and the whalepunk/Victorian/gothic aesthetic is strongly rendered (baleen cages, try-pot rivets, spermaceti, spermaceti-scented breath, Gallowgate Square hangings, witch-chalk wards). The prose is confident and controlled, with strong imagery ("a tide going out — patient, grey, inevitable"; "Pride was a rope of its own"). The dialogue voices are distinct: Mother Morska's maritime menace, Simeon's brass-and-gauge pragmatism, Katra's terse survival instinct, Aya's aristocratic auctioneering. The ticking watch as a recurring motif is effective. Minor criticisms: the ending whisper of the artifact ("whispered her name") is a slightly convenient hook, and Mother Morska's omniscience ("I let you rise") is a familiar trope, though plausible. The negotiation resolves a touch easily in the leader's favor without much back-and-forth. Some metaphors are near-purple but mostly restrained. Word count is close to the 1000-word seed. Overall a polished, atmospheric, professionally executed scene. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 85.0
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gunpowder Rendezvous The Yellow Flag smells of rum, gun oil, and blood that's been mopped but never quite cleaned, and Spike Spiegel decides he could learn to like it. He takes a stool, knocks a cigarette loose, flicks his Zippo. A ring of rust bands the lighter's waist; it's been dropped in water more than once — a harbor, a toilet, a gutter on some moon he's since forgotten. It still works. That's the only quality he asks of anything anymore. Three stools down, a woman is watching him. She's all sharp edges. Short shorts, black crop top, boots. A dragon winds down her right arm in faded ink, and two pistols ride under her shoulders, grips worn smooth as old soap. Her eyes hold the bored brightness of someone who has already decided how she'd kill everyone in the room. "You're not from Roanapur," she says. "Nobody's from Roanapur." Spike exhales smoke at the ceiling fan. "That's the point of the place." She laughs — short, mean, genuine — and the bartender flinches like it's a gunshot. "You a cop?" "Do I look like a cop?" "You look like nothing," she says. "That's what worries me." He lets the silence sit, then slides a folded printout from his coat and smooths it on the bar. A fat man's sweaty face. Shen Wei-long, late of the Red Dragon syndicate, currently selling their ledgers to anyone with cash. Eight million, dead. The woman looks at the photo, then at him, and produces the same face from her own pocket, printed off a different wire. "Small world," Spike says. "Roanapur," she corrects. "Where rats wash up." She drains her glass and signals for two more. "Name's Revy. And before you get ideas, pretty boy — I don't split." "Spike. And I was about to suggest exactly that, but I like the way you refuse things." "Don't flirt. It'll get you shot." "Not the worst way I've almost died." The drinks come. She studies him like an appraiser — the loose limbs, the lazy sprawl, the eyes that don't quite match, one of them glass-calm in a way that has nothing to do with temperament. "Who are you?" she asks. "Really." "A dead man, mostly." He shrugs. "You?" "I'm not a good person," Revy says. "Not a bad one either. I'm just here." Spike raises his glass to that. It's the first true thing he's heard all year. Then the door opens, and Shen Wei-long walks in with four bodyguards and a briefcase cuffed to his wrist, because the universe has a sense of humor and Spike has learned to laugh along. Shen sees them. Fat men survive by recognizing predators, and he's spotted two at once. His hand is still moving when Revy kicks off her stool, both pistols clearing leather, and Spike is already sideways, the table coming up as a shield and then as a weapon. The bar becomes noise. Revy shoots like she's conducting — two guns speaking in alternation, never wasting a word. Two Hands, they call her, and the room learns why. A bodyguard folds over the pool table. Another takes both her bullets and one of Spike's, and she snarls at him for it. "That one was mine!" "Then aim faster." He's lazy about it, almost graceful — a heel into a knee, a gun twisted from a hand that won't hold one again, his Jericho coughing once, twice. Shen bolts for the back hall, briefcase swinging. Two guns come up. Two shots land as one sound. Shen drops at the threshold, a bullet in his head and one in his heart, and neither of them will ever know whose was whose. "Mine," Revy says. "Whatever happens, happens," Spike says. The bartender is screaming about his bar. Revy kneels, works the cuff off Shen's wrist with a knife, and holds the case up like a trophy. "Wire just wants proof and this. My contact pays at dawn." She grins, all teeth. "My motel's around the corner. Come wait for it, cowboy. Or trust me to cut you in later." "I don't trust anyone," Spike says, and follows her out. The room is a bed, a lamp, neon bleeding through broken blinds. The case sits on the bedspread between them. Revy pulls a bottle from her bag, drinks, passes it. He drinks. Their fingers don't touch. Both of them notice. "Your eye," she says. "One of them's lying." "Long story." "I've got till dawn." "No," Spike says, gently, and it's the gentlest thing in the room, including the light. She looks at him a moment too long. Then: "You'll move for the case before dawn. I can smell it on you." "Maybe. Or maybe I just like the view." That's when it happens — no signal, no count. Her hands are full of steel, his Jericho is level, and they are suddenly very close, muzzles crossed in the narrow space between their bodies. Close enough to share breath. Close enough that he smells rum and cordite and her, that she sees the faint seam at his temple where the false eye was fitted by someone underpaid. Her heart is going hard. So is his. Both of them can tell. Neither moves. "I will kill you," Revy says, not quite steady. "You'll have to," Spike says. Her mouth is right there. The muzzle under his jaw is right there. The neon buzzes. Somewhere a boat holds a horn like a low note played too long, and neither of them pulls a trigger, and neither lowers a gun, and both understand — with the intimacy of people who will never say it aloud — that they were never going to. "Whatever happens," Spike murmurs, "happens." Dawn is still hours away.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of fan fiction that hits nearly all the prompt's requirements: seedy bar (the Yellow Flag, a nice Black Lagoon touch), drinking, gunplay, mutual attraction complicated by trust issues, and a motel room standoff with unresolved sexual tension. Third person, present tense is maintained throughout. Length is roughly at target. Character work is the standout. Spike's fatalism, laziness, and prosthetic eye are woven in naturally ("A dead man, mostly"; the seam at his temple). Revy's quote is deployed organically rather than pasted in, and her appraisal of Spike ("You look like nothing. That's what worries me") is exactly her register. The dialogue crackles — clipped, flirtatious-hostile, character-consistent. The shared-kill resolution (neither knowing whose bullet killed the bounty) is an elegant, thematically apt device that mirrors their standoff: neither yielding, neither knowing. The prose is confident and controlled, with strong imagery (the Zippo's rust ring, "the room becomes noise," the boat horn "like a low note played too long"). It flirts with over-stylization in places ("conducting — two guns speaking in alternation, never wasting a word") but mostly stays on the right side of the line. The ending is appropriately unresolved — guns crossed, neither pulling the trigger — which suits both characters and the prompt's demand for unresolved tension. Minor criticisms: the bodyguards are pure furniture; the fight resolves a bit too smoothly and quickly for the buildup. The "fingers don't touch. Both of them notice" beat is a touch on-the-nose. The mutual standoff is somewhat predictable given the prompt, though the execution redeems it. Some lines edge toward aphorism-heavy noir pastiche ("It's the first true thing he's heard all year"). The bartender flinching at Revy's laugh is a nice show-don't-tell detail, though. Overall: professional-grade genre writing with authentic voices, tight pacing, and a satisfyingly ambiguous ending. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 85.7
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Útiseta I was fifteen the autumn we moved north, and I have spent thirty years deciding what actually happened on that mound. My father's transfer to the sawmill took us from Södermalm to Granhäll, four hundred people folded between the lake and the treeline, where the dark arrived before dinner by October and everyone already knew who I was. I hated all of it until Astrid. She sat beside me in class and borrowed my Discman and spoke about her grandmother's teachings the way other girls spoke about pop lyrics. The old woman up the valley had passed things down to her, she said — small things first. Knotted grass buried at a doorstep to end a quarrel. Salt on a windowsill to make Johan Lindqvist turn and look at you in the corridor, which he did, which he *did*, though I grant you we wanted him to. Every game had rules, and Astrid recited them like a recipe, half rebellion, half liturgy. We were stealing her brother's cigarettes and calling down the old world in the same breath, and I never once thought about what we were doing. "My grandmother won't teach me this one," she told me in September, like that was a selling point. "It's in the old laws as forbidden. *Útiseta.* Sitting out. You sit on a grave mound from midnight until the birds wake, and the land tells you what it knows." She said the old law banned it not because it didn't work, but because it did. I said yes because I was fifteen and from Stockholm and terrified of being boring. We met at the crossroads by the closed kiosk. I'd told my parents I was sleeping at hers. Astrid checked my pockets like a customs officer: iron nail, left side. Salt in a film canister. Wool blanket. Matches, but no flashlight — "light offends," she said, flicking my Maglite back at me. No food. Don't say your name or anyone's. Don't sleep. Don't answer anything you hear. Leave nothing of yourself — no blood, no hair — and don't thank anything, whatever happens. "And if something sits down between us," she added, unwrapping a piece of gum, "don't look at it. Look at the flat stone." The mound stood on a ridge above the lake, pines crowding it like mourners who'd arrived early. Kids at school said a giant was buried there. Astrid said no — a woman, a seeress, which was why we sat facing the flat stone on its flank. "That's the door," she said. The wind moved through the pines as we climbed, a rustling that was almost — I told myself *almost* — like faint whispers. We poured the salt in a circle and sat down back to back, wrapped in the blanket. Midnight came and went. The cold worked up through the ground. I know now how the mind behaves in silence, how it manufactures what the dark withholds, and I have explained it all to myself a hundred times. But sometime past two, the whispering in the pines began to shape syllables, and the syllables became my name, spoken in the voice of Johanna — my best friend in Stockholm, who did not know where I was that night, who could not have known. "Linnea." I opened my mouth. Astrid's hand found mine behind us and crushed it. Then the wind stopped. Completely. Silence arrived with weight, the kind that presses on your eardrums, and Astrid — calm all night, bored all night — went rigid against my back. "It's here," she whispered. And then she broke her own rule. She asked out loud, in a voice I'd never heard from her, small and nine years old: "Is my mother coming back?" Her mother had left when Astrid was nine. She had never once mentioned her to me. I understood then what she'd actually brought to the mound — that the games had never been games for her, only practice. The wind rose all at once, and in it, or in the pines, something like a crowd murmuring very far away. Footsteps circled us — slow, outside the salt — or pinecones dropped in a pattern my fear arranged into steps. The smell of wet, turned earth rolled over us though nothing moved. The edge of the blanket pressed down between us, gently, as if something had sat. "Don't turn around," Astrid breathed, though I hadn't planned to. And into my head came — not a voice. A memory arriving that wasn't mine. *She isn't coming back. She tried once. There's a man in Östersund. A new baby. A daughter with your friend's eyes.* I hadn't asked. It was placed in my hands like something I was expected to carry. Or my sleeping mind built it out of village gossip I'd absorbed without noticing. I've never been able to decide, and deciding is the whole of it. A bird called once in the dark, and the pressure lifted like a released breath. "Stand up," Astrid said, her voice hers again. "Don't look at the mound. Walk." We walked. On the path down, footsteps matched ours a half-beat late until we passed the road sign, and then there were only our own. Two weeks later her grandmother stopped me on the road. She looked at me a long time. "You're the Stockholm girl," she said. "Don't sit out again. It answered her through you, and you carried it off the mound. You should have left it there." Astrid could have told her, of course. I know that. I also know we never played another game, and Astrid never spoke her mother's name to me again. Fifteen years later, Astrid's half-sister found her on Facebook — a girl with Astrid's eyes, living in Östersund. Villages keep their own records; I'd surely heard things, half-things, and the night assembled them. That's what I tell people. But my office window looks out on a stand of pines, and on still evenings the wind moves through them like faint whispers, shaping a name in a voice that belonged to a girl I grew up with, and I do not answer. I don't answer.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of folk horror that fulfills nearly all prompt requirements: rural northern Sweden, mid-90s texture (Discman, Maglite, Facebook later), the reluctant move, Astrid's matter-of-fact ritual instructions mixing teen rebellion with specific traditional elements (iron nail, salt, no names, no thanks, "light offends"), and sustained ambiguity between psychological and supernatural explanations. The frame of present-day recollection is handled transparently, with the narrator explicitly offering rational alternatives ("pinecones dropped in a pattern my fear arranged into steps") while letting the uncanny details stand. The strongest choice is Astrid's mid-ritual break — asking "Is my mother coming back?" — which reframes the games as her private grief-work rather than entertainment, deepening the "dangerous line" theme. The grandmother's later warning and the Östersund half-sister payoff give the ambiguity a satisfying, earned structure: the "knowledge" received could be gossip-assembled, and the narrator says so, yet the ending's whispering pines keep the wound open. Weaknesses: the word count is somewhat under 1000 (roughly 850-900), a minor adherence issue. Some images are familiar to the genre — whispering pines, the blanket pressing down, footsteps matching on the path — competent but not fresh. The final paragraph's repetition ("I do not answer. I don't answer") is effective but borders on a stock horror cadence. Dialogue is sparse but well-judged; Astrid's rules are the best lines. Prose is controlled, largely show-don't-tell, with a consistent retrospective voice that never slips. The emotional complexity — grief, guilt, complicity, thirty years of indecision — is genuinely earned, and the darkness lands without overwrought inflation. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 85.7
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Therapeutic Boundaries** The letter from the insurers used the word *mandatory* twice. Sixteen documented sessions, or the settlement reverts — as if my body were a claim to be adjusted instead of the ruin I actually live in. So twice a week I present myself at the clinic on Deansgate, and twice a week Wren destroys me kindly. She is charting at the desk when I limp in, and I see the sleeves before I see her: compression sleeves in a screaming teal-and-magenta zigzag, the same pair from the summer we trained under Okafor, the summer she ran 11.28 and I ran 9.97 and we both believed the future was a straight lane. She's the only physiotherapist in Manchester who wears old track kit under the polo. It unnerves me more than her beauty, and her beauty unnerves me plenty. "Cole." Not Mr. Adeyemi. We've agreed, without agreeing, that formality would be the bigger lie. "Shoes off. Face down." The plinth is papered and still warm from the last body. I lie prone, face in the horseshoe of the cradle, ankles off the end, and stare at the floor between my forearms. This is the arrangement: she gets the leg. I keep the rest. She bends my right knee to ninety and cups my heel; her other hand spans my forefoot, fingers across the metatarsals, and she eases my toes toward my shin. Dorsiflexion — the angle my tendon no longer makes. The pull climbs the back of my ankle like a drawstring, and somewhere between her counting and my breathing it stops being stretch and becomes threat. "Number." "Four." "Liar." She backs off a degree. She always knows. The goniometer's arms are cold where she seats the fulcrum on my lateral malleolus and lines the moving arm along my fifth metatarsal. "Eight degrees. Last week was six. Try to look less furious about improving." Then the scar. Her thumbs find the pink seam on the inside of my ankle and work across it — not along it, *across* it, short perpendicular strokes, cross-friction, ungluing whatever is healing wrong underneath. The skin there went numb in patches after the surgery, so sensation arrives doubled and wrong: pressure I can't feel at the surface, and beneath it a deep electric ache I feel too much. My toes curl. My hamstring knots of its own stupid accord, guarding, and she presses my thigh flat with a palm. "You're doing it again." "I'm lying still." "That's the problem." Her hand stays on the back of my thigh a second longer than the sentence requires. Or I invent that. I have stopped being certain which. "Bolster." The foam roll slides beneath my right shin so the knee softens and the calf lets go, and she lays her forearm into the belly of the muscle and lets her body weight do what her hands are too kind for. Gastrocnemius first, one long slow strip toward the knee; then deeper, soleus, dense as wet rope. The pain is a clean dark line drawn up the back of my leg. My fingers whiten on the cradle. Gooseflesh rises on the thigh she just touched; sweat beads at my hairline — involuntary, all of it, my body answering her in a language I have formally renounced. "Six," I admit. "I know." In Zurich, at sixty meters, somebody kicked me in the heel. I turned around to fight them. The track was empty. That's how an Achilles goes: shot by a bullet made of your own body. Wren got her wreckage a year before I got mine, and she built a life out of it — the degree, the licence, this room with its one good window. I took my wreckage and moved in. "Over." I turn supine; ceiling tiles; the hiss of the paper sheet. She sits low at the foot of the plinth, cradles my heel in one palm, hooks the web of her other hand over the front of my ankle, and leans her weight back — drawing the talus posterior in its mortise, oscillating at the edge of resistance. Rock, hold, release. Her shoulder hovers inches from my foot; the zigzag sleeves blur at the edge of my vision, and I can see the pale line on her forearm where somebody's spikes opened her in a fall in 2016. She is close enough that I count her breaths to avoid counting ceiling tiles, and then I count ceiling tiles anyway. "Breathe," she says, on an exhale she didn't take. Our eyes meet. It lasts one oscillation too long. She looks down first and narrates the ankle like a textbook paragraph — this is what she does when it's closest. This is what I do: recite old splits. 9.97. 10.04. 9.98. Then she makes me earn it. Seated, towel looped around my forefoot — her hands over mine to set the angle, then gone. Standing at the wall, right leg back, heel down; she kneels and pins my heel with a palm when it lifts, hair falling forward, thirty seconds knee-straight for the gastrocnemius, thirty bent for the soleus, and I watch the clock over her shoulder and do not watch her at all. Last, the step. Four inches of laminated birch. Rise on both feet, shift, lower on the right alone, heel sinking below the stair while the tendon loads as it lengthens — pain to a five, no more, her rule, the controlled infliction we have agreed to call medicine. By the ninth rep my whole leg is trembling. She steps in to spot me, both hands at my waist. My hand lands on her shoulder for balance. Neither of us moves it. The zigzag under my palm is a dozen years old and warm. "Fourteen. One more." The goniometer says eleven degrees when we're done. Eleven. A number that says the ruin is habitable, and I hate it, because I don't want to get better — getting better is the official admission that the old life is over, and the limp is my last evidence it happened. She writes it in the chart like it's nothing, like eleven degrees isn't a door. "Same time Thursday, Cole." In the doorway I look back. She's already charting, the past on her arms and the future in her hands, and I am counting in both directions: eight sessions down. Eight to go.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of controlled, restrained prose. The physical therapy details are anatomically precise (goniometer placement, dorsiflexion, cross-friction massage, soleus vs. gastrocnemius stretching, eccentric loading on a step), satisfying the prompt's demand for physical coherence. The tension between the characters is conveyed through touch, counting, and withheld eye contact rather than stated outright—effective show-don't-show. The narrator's resentment toward recovery ("the limp is my last evidence it happened") is the emotional core, and it's genuinely insightful. Voice is consistent: clipped, sardonic, athletic. Minor weaknesses: the "she's attracted to him" side of the tension is thinner than his side; a few lines flirt with over-polish ("a bullet made of your own body"), and the ending is slightly neat. Dialogue is sparse but authentic. Overall an excellent, disciplined execution. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# King's Business The sentry's fist on my door kept the same hour as the tide — too early and deaf to argument. "Eight bells, sir. Mr. Callow's respects, and you've missed muster. Again." I lay a moment tasting copper, as if I'd slept with a penny under my tongue. The cough came up out of me like something pumped from the bilge. Callow was at the taffrail with his coffee, the river behind him the colour of weak tea with the leaves left in. "Captain wants the tide-log fair by noon, Merrick." "He'll have it." He studied my face the way he studied soundings. "You look like boiled sin. That cough—" "Sea air," says I. "This is a river." "It hasn't had the chart read to it." He let it go. They always did. Drink they could smell, and forgive; this carried no smell a gentleman would name. I meant to copy that log. The river had other claims. I went ashore at the company stairs through the usual consort: the pork-boat's gong, a woman frying cakes in oil gone old, night-soil buckets shouldered past with the bearer humming. A kingfisher sat on a mooring line like a dropped jewel, the only clean thing in Canton. Ah-Tung found me under the colonnade, fanning himself with sandalwood against air you could have wrung out. "Merrick-sar. You late. Late is a kind of weather with you." "What's the work?" "Two chest. Honam side, up the creek past the customs hulk. My man rows. You sit in the stern and be the King of England." He grinned with gold. "Hoppo soldier see the coat, he look at the sky. Six dollar." "Ten." "Six. The coat earns it, not you. A clerk would do it for four." The fast crab was forty feet of tarred pine and twenty oars, narrow as a lie. Kwang, her master, said nothing to me the whole way, which I liked about him. Beneath the floor mats the chests shifted and knocked like something trying to be born. We passed godowns breathing tung oil and camphor, sparrows racketing in the rafters, a child on a barge gutting fish into the river and the river taking it all the same. At the customs hulk a soldier with a matchlock older than the dynasty stood up and struck a gong once. "Hei! What boat?" I stood. The coat did its work — the gilt, the white duck — but the cough chose that moment, and I had to swallow it whole, eyes streaming, copper bright in my throat. "King's business," I called when I could. "This gentleman for the joss-house at Honam." My Cantonese ran to about that much, and the fellow's contempt for it served as a passport; he waved us on rather than hear more. Kwang's oarsmen took us past with their faces emptied of everything, the way men row while listening to their own hearts. At the far stairs the mats were lifted, the chests shouldered, and I was paid in dollars chopped and tooth-marked like a dog's bone. Yap kept his divan behind a mat-shed off a lane I will not name, up a stair smelling of cat and joss ash. He weighed my dollars on his little steelyard and pursed his mouth as though all six were bad, which two of them were. "Four good, two so-so. You smoke three, keep one." "Smoke four." "You English want the ship and the anchor too." But he set the lamp, and I lay down on the matting beside a comprador from Dent's who had the look of a letter interrupted. Yap cooked the bead over the chimney flame, rolling it on the needle till it swelled and went the colour of strong tea. The first pipe tastes of scorched plum; the second tastes of nothing, which is the point; by the third the cough lay down like a dog told to, and I thought, not for the first time, that here was the only surgeon in China whose physick worked. Yap watched me with his hands folded. "Friday," he said, "one keg King's powder come off your ship. Ten tael silver." "No." "Friday," he agreed, and refilled my pipe. I crossed the river after dark among the lantern-boats, the water chopping black and bronze, some woman singing on a flower boat in a key that made the night feel older than the empire. One dollar left. Tomorrow I'd copy the tide-log fair, dine at the captain's table, stand a watch like a whole man. At the ladder the cough came back up on schedule, faithful as the tide, and left its penny on my tongue. "Sea air," I told the marine on watch, and went below before he could ask what sea.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a disciplined, atmospheric piece that executes the brief with notable skill. The day-in-the-life structure is honored precisely: waking late, shirking duty, a smuggling job to fund the habit, a transaction at the opium den, a hollow promise of reform at the end. The first-person past tense is maintained, and the prose is grounded in period-appropriate texture — "eight bells," taffrail, godowns, hoppo, comprador, steelyard — without tipping into costumed exposition. The sensory instruction is well served: the copper taste under the tongue recurs as a motif for the cough/addiction, the river "weak tea with the leaves left in," dollars "chopped and tooth-marked like a dog's bone." Some similes are genuinely fresh ("late is a kind of weather with you," "narrow as a lie," the comprador "with the look of a letter interrupted"). A few flirt with cleverness — "narrow as a lie," "the only clean thing in Canton" — but the register mostly earns them; the voice is wry, self-aware, self-loathing in a controlled, period-plausible way. Dialogue carries much of the narrative as requested, and it's strong: clipped, transactional, characterful. Ah-Tung's haggling ("The coat earns it, not you") and Yap's sly bargaining over powder theft are particular highlights. The Yap exchange — "No." / "Friday," he agreed — is a chilling, economical beat showing Merrick's corruption running ahead of his stated will. That refusal-then-inevitability is the story's best psychological touch: he doesn't transform, he decays on schedule, "faithful as the tide." Weaknesses: the plot is thin and predictable in outline — a fact the prose mostly disguises. The supporting figures are vivid but sketched; Yap and Ah-Tung function as functional acquaintances rather than layered characters. The opium den scene risks romanticism ("the only surgeon in China whose physick worked") though the closing irony re-covers it. The sentry's early-morning summons and the "I'll be a whole man tomorrow" ending are the most conventional beats, though the final line's deflation ("before he could ask what sea") lands well and avoids false redemption. Cohesion is tight, the piece never meanders, and the word count is in the right region. It is very good work — short of a masterpiece only because its architecture is familiar and its secondary characters remain types.
