+ Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 85.9
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Sisyphus Gives Advice The hill had not changed in three thousand years, which was more than could be said for Sisyphus.* "First one again," he said, palms on stone. Crow rode his left shoulder, stylus in beak, the morning's mail in a waxed pouch. On the descents Sisyphus read the letters himself; on the ascents he dictated, Crow taking it down in claw-footed cursive with punctuation that was frequently editorial. What had begun as a punishment had become, somewhere around the second millennium, a production schedule. --- *Dear Sisyphus,* *My wife claims I never listen. This is false. I can repeat everything she says, word for word, sometimes years later, at dinner parties. What more does the woman want?* *— Misunderstood of Megara* "Dear Misunderstood," said Sisyphus, leaning into the grade. "She wants the kind of listening where there's a chance it might change you. Repeating is storage. Listening is risk. Tonight, ask her a question you don't know the answer to, and put your hands somewhere they can't busy themselves defending you. Report back. Crow and I are invested." Crow ate a fig from the payment pouch and added an exclamation mark that had not been requested. --- *Dear Sisyphus,* *My husband has asked that I wear his old war helmet to bed. He calls it "the full Achilles." Is this normal?* *— A Respectable Wife of Athens* "Dear Respectable — three thousand years, and no one has yet shown me normal. Consent, enthusiasm, and a secure chin strap are the only commandments worth chiseling. If you both laugh, it's a success. If only one of you laughs, that's a conversation. Oil the cheek-pieces. They pinch." --- It was around here that the god Momus† descended in a smell of wet feathers and litigation, and stood with his arms folded until acknowledged. "So," he said. "An advice column." "Mmf," said Sisyphus, mid-push. "Don't you feel it rather undermines the punishment?" "Take it up with management." "And your advice. You told a man to ask his wife a question. Where are the steps? The numbering? A diagram, at minimum?" "He wanted help, not homework." Momus circled the boulder, searching for purchase. "It's looking shabby. When did you last polish it?" "Tuesday." "Hm." A critic requires resistance the way fire requires air; Sisyphus offered him a warm, well-ventilated nothing. Momus waited for the boulder to crest, watched it roll down, and announced, "Told you it wouldn't stay up." "You always do," said Sisyphus. "It's nice, having company for the descent." Momus left shortly afterward, to find fault with the Fates' weaving. Bit samey, he felt. --- *Dear Sisyphus,* *I make lamps. There is always one more order, and I tell myself I'll stop at sundown, but sundown keeps moving. My daughter is seven. My wife has stopped setting my place at dinner. Everyone says I'm a great success.* *— Overwicked of Corinth* "Dear Overwicked. Sundown has never once moved. It keeps the same appointment every day; you keep standing it up. The shop will always want one more lamp — that is what shops are for. Your daughter will be seven exactly once. Choose a quitting hour and guard it like a vow the gods will smite you for breaking. After a while they won't need to. You'll smite yourself." --- *Dear Sisyphus,* *Every visit, my brother and I have the same argument — our father's farm, who did more, who cared less. Twenty years of it. I have prepared new points. How do I finally win?* *— Tired of Argos* "Dear Tired. Burn the new points. You cannot win, because your brother is playing a different game — one he has already won, in which you are being offered a chance to apologize. You cannot set a person where you want them and expect them to stay there. Trust me on this. Say 'you may be right,' and mean it; he may be, about some of it, and it costs you nothing but a victory you were never going to collect. Then ask about his figs. Everyone longs to be asked about their figs." Crow made a noise like a hinge opening an envelope, which meant: *true about figs.* --- *Dear Sisyphus,* *I am nineteen. Father wants me to take over the inn; Mother wants me married well; my friends seem to have been issued instructions I never received. What is the point of a person? How do I find mine?* *— Unmoored of Ithaca* Sisyphus read this one twice on the way down, and let the boulder rest a moment at the bottom. "Dear Unmoored. No one is issued instructions. Your friends are guessing with confidence, which is not the same thing. Purpose is like sleep — chase it directly and it leaves the room. It accrues, instead, from small use. This week, do one useful thing for one specific person. Fix something that isn't yours. Feed someone. Then notice where your mind goes quiet. That quiet is the start of the trail. Follow it for thirty years or so and report back. An inn is not a bad place to begin, by the way. Everyone else's journey passes through one." --- Down at the bottom, the evening mail waited, damp with footprints. Sisyphus read the last letter walking, smiled once, and tucked it into his belt. The boulder would keep. Boulders are good at that. The boulder, he had long ago decided, was the day job. "Right," he said, flexing his hands. "Who's next?" --- *\*The column had begun eleven years earlier, when Crow — then operating under the standard avian arrangement of shiny objects for crumbs — misdelivered a widow's letter intended for her late husband in Asphodel to the wrong eternal penitent. Sisyphus, who had time between ascents, answered it. The widow told her friends. There was now a shrine in Corinth, a waiting list, and a small economy in figs, most of which Crow ate. This was listed as distribution costs.* *†God of censure and unfair criticism, late of Olympus, from which he was expelled for suggesting that Zeus's thunderbolts were "a bit much." He once reviewed Aphrodite. The best he could find was that her sandals squeaked.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a disciplined, genuinely Pratchett-adjacent execution of a demanding brief. The epistolary structure is handled cleanly, with letters and replies interleaved against boulder ascents and descents, and the running conceit that dictation happens on the way up and reading on the way down is a lovely structural joke that is shown, not explained. Sisyphus's voice is warm, practical, and understated; his advice is surprisingly concrete ("ask a question you don't know the answer to," "guard it like a vow," "ask about his figs") rather than the expected boulder-metaphor or stoicism homilies, exactly as instructed. The single sanctioned boulder metaphor — "You cannot set a person where you want them and expect them to stay there. Trust me on this" — is subtle and earned. The Momus interlude is the strongest section: the god of unfair criticism reviewing the boulder ("Told you it wouldn't stay up") and Sisyphus answering with "a warm, well-ventilated nothing" captures Pratchett's comic-theological register without pastiche. The footnotes are used in a properly Pratchett manner, with the fig economy as "distribution costs" being the best gag in the piece. The risqué letter (the war helmet) is handled with tasteful wit. Weaknesses: the word count falls short of the 1000-word seed (roughly 750-800 words), though not egregiously. The "purpose" letter to Unmoored of Ithaca drifts closest to the sentimental ("that quiet is the start of the trail"), and "Purpose is like sleep" flirts with the aphorism-density the prompt warned against, though it stays practical. The Overwicked lampmaker reply is strong, but "You'll smite yourself" is a hair clever-clever. Crow is charming but slightly underused as a character; his editorial punctuation is a good running joke that could bear one more payoff. The final beats — "The boulder, he had long ago decided, was the day job" and "Who's next?" — are light and earned, though the "boulder would keep. Boulders are good at that" line is the one moment that risks cuteness. No purple prose, no meandering, dialogue is crisp, show-don't-show is consistently honored, the voice is confident and uniform throughout. This is a high-level execution with only minor reservations. + Coming of age: Lost & Found in Osaka — Score: 79.3
Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Lost & Found in Osaka ## Track One: A Quarter Tone Sharp *Den Den Town, Nipponbashi, Osaka — Saturday* Rin had been pretending to compare prices on a used MicroKorg for twenty minutes when the guitar cut through the street like a dropped power line. She followed it out of the shop, past the capsule machines and retro-game bins, toward the arcade on the corner where the claw machines sang their three-note jingles to no one. A crowd had pooled around the entrance, and at the center of it— The melody hit her before the girl did. "A Cruel Angel's Thesis," faster than the original, harmonics sparking off the main line. The girl playing it was maybe eighteen, nineteen, boot braced on a little red amp, fingers moving like the song had personally offended her. Second chorus. The tapped harmonic at the end of the phrase went up when it should have come down, and before Rin could stop herself, she winced. The song ended in a scream of a bend. Applause. Coins rained into the open case. "You." The girl pointed the headstock straight at her. "Glasses. You winced." "I—what?" "Second chorus. The little harmonic. You went—" She mimed a full-body flinch. "In front of everyone. I'm wounded." "I didn't—I mean." Rin's face was doing something hot. "You bent it. The harmonic. You bent it up a quarter tone, and it—it wants to resolve the other way. Down. Sorry. Sorry, I don't—" The girl stared. Then she laughed, one loud crack of it that made a salaryman flinch. "It *does* want to resolve down. I know. String's two days old, won't hold pitch. You heard that? From back there? Over the claw machines?" Rin nodded. Then, because nodding felt insufficient: "I have... a thing. With pitch." "A thing." "Perfect—" She swallowed it. "Relative. Relative pitch. But strong." "*Strong relative pitch.*" The girl grinned like she'd found money in a jacket. "That's the most humble-brag thing anyone's ever said to me. Kaede." She stuck out a fist. Rin stared at it until Kaede opened her hand and waved instead. "You're in high school." "Second year," Rin managed. "Rin." "One syllable. Efficient. I like it." Kaede's eyes dropped to the charm on Rin's bag. "What's that." "It's—a volca. Not a real one. A keychain of one. The real one is a bass synthesizer, it has a sequencer and you can—" The words were coming too fast; she shut the door on them. "Sorry. It's a keychain." "Why do you keep apologizing? You haven't done anything wrong." "...Sorry." A beat. "That one was a joke." Kaede's second laugh was even better. "Oh, you're *sneaky*. You look like a library book and you're sneaky funny." "I don't—I'm not really funny. I make sounds. Patches. I program them and then I just... keep them." "You keep them." "They're mine." "You're the first person my age I've ever heard say the word *patches*, and I've met three DJs." Kaede crouched and started coiling her cable. "You hungry?" "I—" "Rhetorical question. There's a kaitenzushi around the corner where the cheap plates are actually cheap and the ginger is unlimited. I'm buying—no, I'm not, we're splitting, but you get my company, which is priceless." "I should get home—" "You should eat salmon and tell me more things I'm doing wrong. This is Osaka. We eat till we drop. It's the law." She hefted the case. "Come on. It fits in the booth. I've done the research." --- The restaurant was all conveyor belt and color-coded plates, vinegar rice and green tea in the air. Kaede stacked as she went—tuna, corn mayo, something unidentifiable with cheese on it—while Rin took the same egg nigiri twice, at careful intervals. "You had headphones around your neck the whole time back there," Kaede said, working the hot-water tap. "What were you listening to?" "Nothing." Rin turned her cup. "They—people talk to you less." "That is the saddest and smartest thing I've ever heard. Tea?" Rin nodded, and that was when she saw it—wedged beside the booth, the guitar case, and among the stickers one small round one: a doll's face, half-melted, ringed by a marching parade. She stopped breathing. "Your case. The sticker." "Oh, this?" Kaede followed her look. "You know it? Nobody ever knows it." "*Paprika.* The parade. That's—Susumu Hirasawa did the soundtrack. He recorded the vocals with an Amiga. For a 2006 film. On *purpose*, because—" "There she is." Rin stopped. "...What?" "The real you. She was back there the whole time. She only comes out for Hirasawa." Kaede leaned in, chopsticks raised like a fencing foil. "Favorite track. Go. No thinking." "'Parade.' The vocoder line under the second—no. 'Mediational Field.' No—" "You can't have two." "You can if the vocoder line—" Rin heard herself and nearly derailed, but Kaede was grinning so hard it steadied her. "The vocoder line in 'Parade' is the melody and the harmony arguing. It sounds like a crowd that's happy in a scary way. Like the movie." "Like Osaka at festival time. Happy in a scary way." "Yes." Rin laughed, surprised by it. "Yes, exactly." "I watched it when I was fourteen—my brother's DVD—and I've been trying to arrange 'Parade' for solo guitar for a year. It doesn't work. It needs everything. It needs the machines." "I could make the backing track." Kaede looked at her. "I mean—I recreated some of the stems. For practice. The sequencer part, and the choir synth, and the—" Rin stared down at her egg nigiri. "If you wanted. For your arrangement. I could send you—" "Phone." Kaede held out her hand. "Before you combust." "I wasn't—" "You were combusting. I could see the smoke." Kaede tapped her own contact in with great ceremony and slid the phone back. "There. Now you owe me a vocoder line, synth girl." "It's—my name is Rin." "I know. It's been in my phone for four minutes. Keep up." Outside, the street had gone neon. Kaede counted their plates—her tower against Rin's modest stack—and shook her head in mock grief. "Six plates. Beginner number. Next time I'll teach you how to eat." "Next time?" "Same spot, Saturday. I'll have the harmonic fixed. You'll have the stems." Kaede slung the case over her shoulder and pointed the headstock at her one last time. "This is a business arrangement now, Rin. Very serious. Bring egg nigiri money." Rin watched her go, the crowd parting around her like weather, and realized her hands had stopped doing the sleeve-pulling thing somewhere around the third plate. Her phone buzzed. A message from Kaede: a firework emoji, and— *happy in a scary way*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of dialogue-driven slice-of-life writing. The scene fulfills the prompt's requirements: Den Den Town setting, shy synth-nerd protagonist, confident busker playing an anime theme ("A Cruel Angel's Thesis"), awkward-to-easy conversational arc, and the kaitenzushi invitation. The word count is roughly on target. Strengths: The dialogue is the standout. Rin's hesitant, self-correcting speech ("I have... a thing. With pitch.") and Kaede's rapid, playful banter are distinct and consistent. The "strong relative pitch" humble-brag exchange, the fist-bump misread, and the "sorry—that one was a joke" beat are all well-observed character comedy. The Paprika/Hirasawa sticker is an excellent plot device—it gives the characters a genuine shared passion that justifies the connection, making the friendship feel earned rather than arbitrary. The recurring "happy in a scary way" motif pays off in the closing text message, a satisfying structural echo. The ending's small transformation (Rin noticing she stopped her sleeve-pulling habit) is appropriately modest for a first-connection scene. Weaknesses: Kaede occasionally tips into quirk-machine territory—every line is a zinger, which flattens her slightly and makes her feel more like a device than a person with interiority. The "There she is. The real you" moment is a bit on-the-nose, telling us about Rin's authentic self rather than letting it emerge. The transition into the sushi restaurant is handled with a scene break that slightly cheats the "surprisingly easy conversation" development—much of the easing happens off-page or in shorthand. Some jokes ("You look like a library book") are clever but feel writerly rather than spoken. The prose is clean and controlled, occasionally stylish ("the crowd parting around her like weather") without becoming purple. The plot beats are somewhat predictable—awkward nerd meets cool mentor-figure is a familiar template—but the specificity of the music detail (quarter-tone bends, Amiga-recorded vocals, vocoder lines) keeps it fresh. Overall, this is skilled, polished commercial fiction with genuine charm, held back from excellence by a slightly too-perfect dynamic and minor tell-don't-show moments. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter One: Time Flies The package came on a Tuesday. That's important, because by Friday, I didn't exist anymore. No return address. Just my name — MILO GRANT — printed in blocky letters that looked like a machine had written them. A machine that had never met a human. Inside: a smart watch. Matte black. No brand. No charger. The second my finger brushed the screen, it lit up. HELLO, MILO. "Free watch," I told Mom. "Probably a promo thing." She squinted at it. "Don't talk to strangers and don't wear mystery electronics." She said it like a joke. We both laughed. We shouldn't have. The watch did everything — texts, steps, weather. But the little crown on the side was strange. It only turned one direction. Backward. I found out what that meant on Wednesday, when I tripped over Sam's backpack and dumped an entire tray of spaghetti down Becca Marlowe's white sweater. The cafeteria went silent. Then it exploded. Becca looked at me like I was something she'd scraped off her shoe. I wanted the floor to open up and swallow me whole. That night, lying in bed and reliving it for the nine-hundredth time, I fiddled with the crown. Backward. Backward. Backward — The world *hiccupped*. And I was standing in the cafeteria. Tray in my hands. Sam's backpack at my feet. The clock on the wall said 12:14. I stepped *over* the backpack. No spaghetti. No laughter. Becca smiled at me. Actually smiled. I should have been terrified. Instead I thought: *Do you know what I can DO with this?* Thursday, I rewound a wrong answer in algebra, and suddenly I was "on fire today, Milo!" I rewound a bricked foul shot in gym — swish. I rewound an awkward silence with Becca three times until I found the joke that made her laugh. The watch face flickered sometimes, when it thought I wasn't looking. Numbers. 23:58:11. Then gone. I ignored it. You can ignore a lot when you're winning. Then my voice dropped. Not cracked — *dropped*. I said "hey" to Sam and he goes, "Why do you sound like my dad?" My jeans got short. My shoes pinched. I woke up Friday with a dark shadow on my upper lip that I had to shave. *Shave.* I'm twelve. I don't even own a razor. I used Dad's and took off half my face doing it. At school, the secretary asked for my hall pass and called me "sir." A substitute asked if I was the new student teacher. Becca crossed the hall when she saw me coming. In three days I'd gone from seventh grader to the guy your mom warns you about. Mom took one look at me over breakfast and dropped her coffee. "Growth spurt," she kept saying at the doctor's office, while the doctor checked my chart, then me, then my chart again. "His bone age reads about sixteen," the doctor finally said. Sixteen. I'd rewound maybe four minutes of my life. Total. The watch wasn't giving me time. It was *charging* me for it. With interest. That night the face flickered again: 11:04:53. Lower than before. A countdown. And suddenly I understood — not what it was counting down *to*, exactly. Just that I did not want to find out. I had to undo it. All of it. I gripped the crown and spun backward — past the shot, past the test, past the spaghetti, all the way to Tuesday. Before the package. The world screamed. Everything went white. When it stopped, I was standing on my own front porch. Trash cans at the curb. Tuesday. I nearly cried with relief. I rang the bell. Mom answered. She looked at me. *Through* me. "Can I help you?" "Very funny," I said. "Mom." Her face changed. "I think you have the wrong house." "Mom, it's ME. It's Milo!" She started closing the door. "I don't have a son," she said. "I have a daughter. I'm calling the police." The door slammed. Through the side window I could see the family photo over the fireplace. Mom. Dad. June. Three people. No me. I'd gone too far, or wrong, or the timeline had simply closed over the space where I used to be — like water swallowing a stone. On my wrist, the watch flickered: **00:09:41.** And that's when I got it. The countdown wasn't my doom. It was my *window*. My last chance to take it all back before it became permanent. I'd been spinning the crown backward this whole time — rewinding, stealing time from myself like a thief. The only way back was forward. I grabbed the crown and wrenched it clockwise. It fought me. Then it gave. The world lurched into fast-forward. Every second I'd ever stolen poured back into me at once, and it *hurt*. I shrank. My voice climbed the ladder back up to twelve. The stubble melted off my face. The watch face spun like a slot machine. **00:00:10.** **00:00:07.** **00:00:03.** Zero. Dark. I woke up in my bed. Tuesday morning. Downstairs, the doorbell rang. The mail. I got there first. I didn't open the box. I carried it to the storm drain on the corner and dropped it in, and the splash it made was the most beautiful sound I'd ever heard. At breakfast, Mom made pancakes. Sam texted me a meme. Becca waved at me in the hallway. I was short and squeaky and twelve years old, and nobody called me sir. Perfect. Fixed. Done. Except. Last night, my wrist started itching. Right where the watch used to sit. There's a pale band of skin there I've never had before, and when I scratch it, something *underneath* flickers green. Numbers. Counting down. And this morning, June came to breakfast wearing a brand-new watch. Pink. No brand. "Look what came in the mail!" she said. "There's a note. It says, 'Time flies!'" I couldn't breathe. I couldn't move. Because under my skin, my countdown hit 00:00:00 — — and paused — — and then three new words scrolled across my wrist, soft as a whisper: **READY WHEN YOU ARE.**
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of the prompt: a middle-school narrator, Goosebumps-style chapter structure, the rewind watch, the aging consequence (accelerated puberty handled with humor — shaving with Dad's razor, being called "sir"), the timeline shift (erasure from existence), and the ambiguous final fix that may not be a fix at all. Length lands near the 1000-word seed. The first-person voice is consistent, wry, and age-appropriate, with strong short-sentence rhythm and effective chapter-ending hooks ("That's important, because by Friday, I didn't exist anymore"). Strengths: pacing is tight; the countdown mechanic is introduced early and paid off; the "forward is the only way back" reversal is a satisfying logical twist; the ending's transfer of the watch to June and the "READY WHEN YOU ARE" under the skin is a genuinely creepy, earned final beat. Show-don't-tell is mostly strong (the doctor checking chart-then-boy-then-chart; Mom dropping coffee). Weaknesses: the mechanism by which spinning forward restores the original timeline is hand-waved — the story gestures at "stealing time from myself" but the physics is fuzzy even by Goosebumps standards. The June reveal is a familiar trope (cursed object passes to sibling), though the under-skin countdown partially refreshes it. Dialogue is functional but thin; Mom and Sam exist mostly as reaction shots. Some emotional beats (Milo's terror at erasure) resolve a bit quickly. Minor typo ("bricked foul shot" should be "bricked" as a verb is fine, but "bricked" reads oddly). The "I have a daughter" twist is effective but the daughter is never foreshadowed, making it feel slightly arbitrary — though the ending retroactively justifies it. Overall: a polished, engaging, genre-faithful chapter with a strong hook and ending, held back from masterpiece level by thin secondary characters and some convenient mechanics. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Carnival of Dangerous Intentions** He was already there, leaning on the gallery counter as if he had bought the hour outright, watching the tin ducks waddle their circuit. Along the midway the lights were coming on one by one and then all at once, and the heat lay over the boardwalk like a held breath. In that first electric flush he looked like something the carnival had made and might, without apology, unmake. "You're late." "I'm not late. I nearly didn't come at all." "But you did." He straightened, unhurried. "I counted on it." "That's arrogance." "That's arithmetic." "And if I'd stayed home?" "Then I'd have shot five ducks alone and gone home." "That's supposed to flatter me?" "It's supposed to be true." *His locks.* There it was again, that absurd old-fashioned phrase — curls gone damp at his collar in the heat, as though she were a heroine in a ten-cent serial and not a married woman with dinner going cold in Brooklyn. A girl drifted past trailing cotton candy, and the smell — spun sugar, hot machine oil — caught her wrong. The midway tilted. Striped canvas. A calliope slowing like a toy running down. Heat on her face, smoke threaded through the sweetness, somebody's arms around her ribs lifting her, a voice crying *again, again* — hers, perhaps; she couldn't say. Then it was gone, the way dreams go when reached for. She gripped the counter. "You've gone white," he said. "It's the heat." "It isn't." Gently, which was worse. "You looked like someone remembering a fire." "Is that your gift? Reading strangers?" "Only the ones who want to be read." "I don't want to be read." "Then stop leaving your pages open." He nodded to the barker, who handed her a rifle. It was heavier than she expected, smelling of gun oil and old pennies. "Have you ever held one?" "No." "Good. No bad habits." He came around behind her — not touching, a parenthesis of warmth — then touching, his hands over hers. "Loose shoulders. You're holding it like it's going to bite." "Isn't it?" "Only the things in front of it. Mind your thumb, Evelyn." She went still. "I never told you my name." "No." "Then how—" "I asked after you." "Of whom?" "Everyone." His breath was at her ear. "Fire when ready." She fired badly and knew she would; the ducks sailed on, smug as landlords. But her fourth shot clipped one, and it flipped backward with a tinny clatter, and she laughed — startled, unguarded. *How long*, some accountant in her wondered, *since I made a sound like that?* Harold was in Chicago until Saturday. She had told the housekeeper she was visiting her sister in Inwood. She was going to hell in a nickel-plated rowboat, and the evening was warm, and the ducks kept coming. "Your turn," she said. "Show me how it's done." "You'll be disappointed." "I doubt it." He took the rifle. Five shots, five ducks; the small crowd went quiet the way crowds do when a trick stops being a trick. The barker swallowed. "Mister, where'd you learn that?" "Spain," he said, and set the rifle down like a closed door. The barker gestured weakly at the shelf — kewpie dolls, celluloid charms, a fan of tin rings. The stranger took a ring, no bigger than a lie. "Aren't you going to win me a doll?" she said. "You don't want a doll." "You don't know what I want." Something moved behind his eyes. "No. But I'm learning." He took her left hand as if he had asked and been answered. "Your husband minds you out at night?" "My husband is in Chicago." "That isn't what I asked." He turned the gold band once with his thumb, like a man checking a lock, and slid the tin ring on above it — cheap metal kissing wedding gold. "There. Now you're married to the evening." "That's the worst line I've ever heard." "You'll remember it." That was the trouble. She would. "What do you do," she said, "when you aren't winning tin rings at the seaside?" "I acquire things for people." "What sort of things?" "Things people want very badly and shouldn't have." His smile never reached the dark of him. "Your hand is trembling, Evelyn." "It's the rifle." "You've put it down." "I should go." "Yes," he said, and didn't step back. "I won't come back here." "No?" "I mean it." "Thursday. Same hour. The light's best at dusk." She walked away into the crowd, past the Cyclone's wooden thunder, past a newsboy shouting about the lost aviatrix, and the cotton candy found her again — sugar and smoke and *whose arms, whose voice, again, again* — and she let it go, because some doors open onto rooms with no floor. At the seawall she stopped, meaning to fling the tin ring into the black water. She stood a long moment, feeling it warm against the gold. She was still wearing it on the train.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of period romantic-suspense writing that largely delivers on the prompt's demands. The scene sustains a 1937 Coney Island atmosphere with period-appropriate details (Cyclone, calliope, newsboy, celluloid kewpie dolls, the "lost aviatrix" — likely Amelia Earhart, a nice touch given the July 1937 date). The dialogue is crisp, clipped, and carries the flirtation-with-menace dynamic well; lines like "That's arrogance." / "That's arithmetic." and "Now you're married to the evening" have a hard-boiled economy that suits the era. The dialogue-heavy structure meets the ~50% target, and internal monologue ("She was going to hell in a nickel-plated rowboat") is threaded in effectively. The prose is elegant and controlled, with memorable images: "a parenthesis of warmth," "smug as landlords," "set the rifle down like a closed door," "a ring no bigger than a lie." The recurring cotton-candy/fire memory fragment is an intriguing ambiguity — though it risks being under-explained, it works as atmospheric mystery rather than confusion. The stranger knowing her name and marital status is a well-judged escalation of danger. The ending — keeping the tin ring on the train — is a restrained, earned beat that shows her complicity without melodrama. Minor criticisms: the "Spain" marksmanship reveal edges toward genre cliché; the "I acquire things for people" line is a touch on-the-nose for moral ambiguity; and the stranger occasionally tips from mysterious into authorially convenient (knowing her name, her husband). The heroine's name "Evelyn" is never established before he speaks it, which is intentional but slightly disorienting. Some metaphors ("something the carnival had made and might, without apology, unmake") strain slightly. Overall, however, the piece is coherent, tonally consistent, emotionally layered, and genuinely engaging — well above average craft with only small lapses. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Two** The guide's name was Henri Boudreau, and in thirteen autumns JT had never known him to stop talking for longer than it took to swallow a mouthful of coffee. Henri had stories—the winter of the big ice, the bear in the town dump that had learned to open car doors, the cousin who drowned and came home three days later not knowing he was dead (that one he told only after the third beer, and JT had never been sure it was a joke). He talked to the truck. He talked to the caribou while he gutted them, a low steady murmur, half apology and half ballgame. The old joke at the lodge was that you could find Henri in the dark by following the sound of Henri. This year Henri had said maybe forty words since they'd pulled in, and half of those had been about where the herd was running. He took his meals standing at the stove with his back to the room. He'd started driving home at night—twenty-two miles of washboard road—though the bunk over the woodshed had been his since before JT was born. When JT's father came into the kitchen, Henri remembered urgent business in the shed. Even his dog had changed. Bishop, a chewed-looking old hound who'd slept beside that stove every October of his life, now refused to leave the cab of Henri's truck, and sat there whining through the cracked glass at the trees. On the third evening JT came around the corner of the lodge with an armload of firewood, heard voices, and stopped without ever deciding to stop. "You've got your meat, Ray." Henri's voice, low and flat, stripped of everything JT knew it by. "Load up and go on home, all of you. Before the moon comes full." His father laughed, the big easy laugh he used on waitresses and game wardens. "Henri. You've gone superstitious on me." "You ever seen them stand like that? You ever once seen one wait for it?" A silence. Then the truck door squawked, and Henri said, maybe not to Ray anymore, maybe not to anyone, "I'm telling you what I'm telling you." The engine caught. JT backed a step into the shadow of the woodpile, but not fast enough. Henri's eyes found him over the hood and held, and what was in them wasn't embarrassment at being overheard. It was worse than that. It was recognition. "You," Henri said, quiet, through the open window. "You keep to the lodge after dark." Then the taillights were bumping down the lane, and JT stood there with the firewood biting into his arms until they went numb, telling himself the man was old, the man had been drinking, telling himself a whole list of things. At supper his father told it, just as JT had known he would, ladling beans like it was any year. "Damnedest thing I ever saw in the woods," he said. "Buck come right up to me. Another step and I could've touched him." He said it the way a man says a thing he's been turning over in his pocket, feeling its weight, and the regulator clock over the door ticked too loud in the quiet after. "I had the shot," Mike said, almost to himself. He hadn't touched his plate. "I had it the whole time. Never once thought to take it." He said it the way you'd report a misplaced set of keys. "Shame," JT's father said, and then his eyes came around the table and stopped on JT. "You were right behind us. You see him?" "Bootlace," JT said. "I was tying my bootlace." "Huh." His father let that sit awhile, and then he smiled. It was his father's smile, all the right parts in all the right places, and JT would think about that later, lying awake: how it was all the right parts. Before bed he carried the scraps out, because that was his job and had always been his job, and he stood a minute looking at the shed where the caribou hung in the dark with its neat opened throat. He thought—he could have sworn—for one breath, two, that its sides were moving. In and out. Slow and deep, like something resting. Then he blinked and it was only meat turning on its rope in the wind off the lake. He went inside. He did not hurry. Hurrying would have meant something was wrong. He woke with the moonlight lying across the floorboards in a long bright plank, and the sound. The sound was breathing. A great many breaths, slow and deep, drawn and let go together, like a congregation. *Stay in bed,* he thought, and his feet found the floor anyway. The yard lay silver. The trees stood black. And his father was in the yard in his long underwear, barefoot on the frost, facing the treeline with his head tipped back a little, as if listening to something lovely. Along the whole length of the trees the caribou stood shoulder to shoulder, more than JT could count—he got to forty and stopped counting—all of them facing the lodge, motionless, their antlers raised like the limbs of a leafless orchard. No wind moved them. No ear flicked. His father lifted one trembling hand, palm out, the way he had in the clearing. And from the dark between the trunks the big buck stepped forward into the moonlight, and lowered its head. As if to be touched. As if to give something. As if to take it. JT never remembered getting back into bed. In the morning his father's boots stood by the door, dry, the laces neat. At breakfast his father said "Sleep good?" the way he said it every morning of every year, and outside the window the moon hung pale over the lake in the early light, three nights shy of full. Two, maybe. JT's head felt strange around numbers lately. He said he'd slept fine. Always safer that way.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This continuation is a strong piece of surreal horror writing that captures the Stephen King register well: grounded, colloquial detail (the regulator clock, beans at supper, washboard road) layered against mounting wrongness. The introduction of Henri the guide is an effective device—the once-talkative man gone silent is a classic King-style signal of dread, and the overheard conversation ("Before the moon comes full") builds tension economically. The dialogue is largely strong: terse, character-revealing, with Mike's "I had the shot... Never once thought to take it" delivered with chilling flatness. The father's smile described as "all the right parts in all the right places" is an excellent, subtle wrongness beat. The hanging caribou appearing to breathe, the moonlit yard of motionless caribou "like a congregation," and the father's sleepwalking vigil all pay off the first chapter's setup. The ending—JT's denial, "Always safer that way," echoing the first chapter—provides satisfying circularity while deepening ambiguity. The unreliable narration is maintained well ("JT's head felt strange around numbers lately"). Minor criticisms: the "congregation" simile and antlers "like the limbs of a leafless orchard" flirt with overwrought imagery, though they mostly land. The buck's final gesture ("As if to be touched. As if to give something. As if to take it.") is a touch on-the-nose but effective as a chapter-ending sting. Henri's warning is a somewhat familiar trope (the knowing local), though executed with enough texture to feel earned. The piece occasionally tells rather than shows JT's rationalizations, but this fits the unreliable narrator. Word count and instruction adherence are solid; tone, POV, and dread escalation all match the prompt. Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Hell Is Other Demons Hell does not have mornings. Mornings imply a sun, and the sun keeps its distance. But Lucifer Morningstar had been the light-bringer once, and old habits were the only things in Hell that never died, so each day at seven he made his own dawn—a small one, the size of a grapefruit—which hung above the penthouse windows and glowed until he told it to stop. He ironed his shirt with the palm of his hand. He brewed coffee from beans grown, per his own design, in the ashes of a burnt offering, which gave it what the *Infernal Times* called "a note of remorse." He made two cups. He had lived alone for three hundred years and he made two cups every morning, and every morning he regarded the second cup as though it had personally betrayed him. Then he drank them both. Business began at eight. The damned started their shift; the screaming was piped through the building at a tasteful volume, like a water feature. Belial, who handled scheduling and had asked twice to be called Barry, brought the morning's reports. Three tormentors had exceeded quota, which was technically impossible and therefore a paperwork problem. The lake of fire needed skimming again—no one knew where the debris came from. Hope, probably. Lucifer signed forty documents. Hell had discovered paperwork in the third century and had never recovered. Lilith arrived at noon the way weather arrives. The hellhound heard her first. All three heads lifted. Two of them growled. The third, which had always been the optimist, wagged its entire body. "I've come for my knife," she said. "Good afternoon to you as well." "The one I threw at you in Lisbon." "1762," said Lucifer. "It's in the study." She followed him in, wearing the scorched leather purse the way other women wore perfume. The scorching was historically significant, though they disagreed about the details. She said Salem. He said she had not been within four hundred miles of Salem. She said that was exactly what she wanted people to think. The knife was in the desk drawer, with the good stationery. "You kept it," she said. "You have excellent aim. It would have been a shame to waste the craftsmanship." Everything in Hell required a signature—it was the only damnation that truly stuck—so she produced a transfer-of-property form and began digging through the purse for a pen. What she found instead was: a snow globe containing a seaside town that had burned down in 1911. A key card for a hotel demolished in the '80s. A cassette labeled ROAD TRIP '86 in mortal handwriting. A single boarding pass, unused. A plastic flamingo of no clear provenance. And a matchbook from a club on the South Side of Chicago, the kind of place that had a piano and an understanding. It had closed in 1958. He had played there four times. She had been there once. He did not ask about the matchbook. She did not explain it. These were the terms on which they currently operated. She found a pen. She signed. Then, because the form had taken all of forty seconds and neither of them mentioned the door, she reached back into the purse and produced two miniature bottles of Scotch, the kind mortals steal from hotel minibars, and poured them into glasses older than the concept of glass. "How's the sea?" he asked. She kept a place by the Red Sea, which was crowded with demons she admitted to having mothered and lonelier than she admitted to being. "Wet," she said. "Have you been playing?" He had not been playing. The piano had become furniture, which is the saddest thing a piano can become. But her glass was empty and his was empty and the afternoon had nowhere particular to be, so he sat down and played something slow, something from Chicago. For eleven minutes the building settled around the music and no one screamed. Downstairs, a supervisor made a note about the screaming, which had dipped below regulatory levels. Afterward, she stood, and took the knife, and looked at it the way one looks at a photograph of a hairstyle. "I have other knives here," she said. "Eleven," said Lucifer. "I keep an inventory." "I'll be back for them, then. One at a time. It could take years." "I'll put the kettle on." "You don't own a kettle." "I'll buy a kettle." She left the way weather leaves, and the hellhound's third head watched the door for some time afterward, and even the two pessimists did not object. It was only when Lucifer went to close the piano that he found the matchbook, set precisely in the center of the music stand, where she could not have dropped it by accident, because Lilith had not done anything by accident since the Garden. He put it in the drawer with the knives, which seemed like the right filing system, and told the little dawn to stay lit a while longer, and it did—not because it had to, but because some lights, once made, are sentimental. The next morning he made two cups. For three hundred years the second had been an accusation. Today it was an arrangement. He set it on the counter opposite his own, steam rising, just in case. In Hell, hope was contraband. He'd hidden worse.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally strong piece that fulfills the brief with precision. The Gaiman-esque register is well-executed: understated irony, domestic mundanity against cosmic horror, and a relationship conveyed almost entirely through objects (the knife, the matchbook, the second cup). The prose is clean and controlled, with standout lines ("Lilith arrived at noon the way weather arrives," "the piano had become furniture, which is the saddest thing a piano can become"). The dark comedy lands—the screaming "piped through the building at a tasteful volume, like a water feature," the supervisor noting screaming below regulatory levels. The emotional arc is earned: the shift from "accusation" to "arrangement" in the second coffee cup is a subtle, well-planted payoff. The matchbook left on the piano stand is a masterful show-don't-tell beat. Minor quibbles: the ending's "hope was contraband" line slightly over-explains the theme the story had already conveyed elegantly, and a few of the purse-contents list items flirt with whimsy-for-whimsy's-sake. Dialogue is sparse but sharp and characterful. The piece is coherent, tight, and never meanders; the ~1000-word target is respected. The transformation (thawing of the relationship) is incremental and earned rather than sudden. Very few amateurish elements; the voice is consistent throughout. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 88.2
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Barley and Ash** I woke before the bell, as I always did on the mornings I was to die. That is how I had come to think of such days, though I had died eleven times now, and yet here was my breath again, fogging in the dawn chill, and through the grille the sky above the practice yard was turning the color of a healing bruise. Below the walls, Rome cleared its throat. Cartwheels on basalt—the wagons roll all night, since the law keeps them from the streets by day—the water-seller's cry, a donkey's outraged bray, and under it all the low sound the city makes even in sleep, like a great animal breathing through its mouth. They fed us barley, always barley. They call us *hordearii*, the barley men, because the fat it lays over a man's muscles turns a shallow cut from a deep one. I ate mine with beans and dried figs and drank the cup of ash and water the medicus swears closes a man's blood. It tasted like licking a hearth. I had learned to love it, the way you love anything that has kept you alive. Lucius sat beside me, spooning his porridge like a man reading a will. He had been a soldier once—a Roman of Rome, free-born on the Aventine—until debt made him what war made me. We liked to say we were the two halves of the Empire: the man it conquered and the man it ate. "Ninety-first day," he said, and nodded at the walls, meaning the games. "They say Trajan means to run a hundred and twenty-three." "Dacia's gold," I said. "My gold. They dragged our king's treasure out of the riverbed where he hid it, and now it buys them their mornings' entertainment." He let me say it. That is what friendship is, in the ludus: a man who lets you say the thing. I worked the palus until my shoulders sang, the wicker shield heavy on my arm, the wooden practice sword a full pound heavier than the iron one they would hand me at the gate—so that the real blade, when it came, would feel like mercy in the hand. Old Castus the doctore walked the line with his stick. He had won his freedom thirty years gone, the wooden sword of the rudiarius, and kept it on a shelf in his cell like an altar. He had never once touched it since. I understood. Some things you win only once, and you do not risk them. Our lanista watched from the shade with his account tablets, valuing us in his head. I had seen him look at a horse the same way, and mourn the horse longer when it died. The night before, they had given us the *cena libera*—the free dinner—where the public files past to watch us eat and wagers on which man gorges like he is stuffing a corpse and which picks at his plate like one already elsewhere. I ate. Zina used to say a man who stops eating has agreed to die, and I was not ready to agree. She was sold east, I think. I saw the auctioneer's finger point, and a man with a Greek beard count out coin. I told myself she was a cook in Antioch, fat and scolding, slapping soldiers' hands from the pot. Some mornings I almost believed it. On the mornings of games, I chose to. In the fourth hour they marched us through the tunnel to the amphitheater, our little silent procession under the road. Above us, the city screamed itself hoarse over the morning's dying. With every surge of the crowd, dust sifted from the vaulting, as though the building itself were shivering. The hypogeum was a stew of smells: lion and lamp oil, the ammonia of old straw, the butcher's-shop reek drifting from the spoliarium where the attendants worked with their hooks. Fifty thousand Romans over our heads—free and fed, their bread cheap with Egyptian grain, their temples fat with the gold of my country—howling for blood that was never Roman. A man in the dole line had told me once, in the Subura, that the people want only two things, bread and games, and having them will forgive an emperor anything. Perhaps that was what Dacia had been for. A treasury to purchase the mob's good mood. I found my place by the gate, in the corner where the wall weeps damp, and did what I had done before every fight since the first. With my finger I wrote her name in the dust—Zina, in the Greek letters a Syrian in the next cell taught me years ago, the only writing I know, and it is hers. I spat on my thumb and pressed it to each letter, sealing it, and then I wiped the name away with my palm. If I lived, I would carry her out with me on my skin. If I died, her name would die hidden, and not be trodden under their nailed sandals. The trumpets. The gate rose, and the light came in like something solid, and the sound came with it—a weather of voices, the whole sky made of throats. Beyond the shadow of the arch the sand waited, pale and raked and thirsty. Somewhere above, the editor leaned forward in his purple, and the Emperor too, they said, the conqueror of my country, eating figs. I set my left foot forward first, as I had done eleven times, because I had done it the first time and lived, and a gladiator does not question his laws. Her name was on my palm. I closed my fist around it and went out into the sun.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished piece of historical fiction that meets nearly all the prompt's requirements with confidence and craft. The scene avoids combat, focusing instead on the pre-fight rituals of a Dacian gladiator under Trajan, and embeds the political and social context (the Dacian Wars, Trajan's massive games, the grain dole, panem et circenses, debt-slavery of freeborn Romans) organically through the narrator's perspective rather than as info-dumps. The sensory details are excellent and specific: the ash-water drink, the barley diet of the hordearii, the heavier wooden practice swords, the damp wall of the hypogeum, the dust sifting from the vaulting. The voice is the piece's greatest strength: a plainspoken, wry, fatalistic first-person narrator with genuine literary sensibility ("like a man reading a will," "the two halves of the Empire: the man it conquered and the man it ate," "friendship is, in the ludus: a man who lets you say the thing"). These aphoristic lines mostly land because they feel earned by character rather than performed by the author. The Zina thread—writing her name in dust, sealing it with spit, wiping it away, carrying it out on his palm—gives the piece emotional architecture and a resonant closing image. The final line ("I closed my fist around it and went out into the sun") is earned lightness-in-darkness, satisfying the "slice of a larger story" requirement. Weaknesses are minor. The piece runs roughly 850 words against the 1000 requested—a modest adherence shortfall. The dialogue, while functional and characterful, is sparse; Lucius exists mainly as a vehicle for exposition about Dacia's gold. A few lines flirt with over-polished cleverness ("spooning his porridge like a man reading a will" is doing a lot of work), but nothing tips into purple prose. The final paragraph's "eating figs" is a small invention that gestures at cruelty without being heavy-handed. Occasional historical shorthand (bread and games spoken almost verbatim by a man in the dole line) is slightly convenient but forgivable. Coherence is strong, no meandering, no amateurish mistakes, consistent past tense and first person throughout. The piece is emotionally complex—love, grief, superstition, resentment, dark humor braided together without sentimentality. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 81.8
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Lighthouse Keeper **Sgeir nan Ròn Lighthouse — 14th March 1991** Well Ma, I'm here, and the island's smaller than the garden. Eighteen mile out, nothing but sea and skuas. The landing's a crane and a rope, and I near left my dinner on the rocks. MacAulay the Principal is a Lewisman — says nothing that doesna need said. Davie the third man's a Rangers supporter, worse luck. My room's wee and the bed's dry-ish. Everything smells of paraffin and Brasso. The lens is a wonder, Ma, like a great glass jewel. It's lit at half four. I'll mind it. Your son, Alec **Buckie — 20th March 1991** Son — parcel awa the day: tablet, oatcakes, twa pairs o socks, your good vest. The Jags won Saturday, 2-1, I mind you asked. Mrs Gauld's cat's had kittens again. Is the damp in your chest? Are they feeding you proper? Your Da's photy's on the telly and I tell it the news. I never liked the sea, you ken, but a tower o stone is no a boat. Keep it lit. Ma **Sgeir nan Ròn — 2nd June 1991** Ma — you'll ask how I'm sleeping. I'm no. We've had the haar nine days and the horn goes every ninety seconds, night and day. You feel it in your fillin's. On watch I wind the clockwork that turns the lens, log the weather for the Coastguard, polish, wind again. Off watch I lie and count the horn till I give up. Bread moulds in twa days here; my socks dry on the stove and smell o diesel. There's a grey seal I've named the Provost, for he's fat and disnae answer when spoken to. I'm no scunnered, Ma. Just wabbit. Alec **Buckie — 10th June 1991** Wabbit's what comes o daft hours. I'm ower at the surgery masel the now — it's just my blood, Dr Petrie says, nothing for you to fash ower. The rhubarb's away like anything, and Mrs Gauld's had the minister in twice, so we'll hear the news o that soon enough. Is there no a wumman atween the three o you on that rock? A mermaid would do. Ma **Sgeir nan Ròn — 4th October 1991** You'll have seen the gale on the forecast. Dinna fash — we're built for it. Tuesday a sea came the full height o the tower and put a stone through the weather door, sixty foot up. The water cam doon the stair like a burn in spate. We lashed it and baled. The light never blinked the whole nicht, Ma. That's the job. For one meenit, though, wi the tower groaning, I thought on Da. Dinna tell Maureen that bit. The Provost's awa somewhaur sensible. Alec **Buckie — 11th October 1991** I sat up half the nicht after your letter, and your Da would call me daft for greeting ower a man on granite. I've cast on a gansey for you — I'm putting the wave pattern in it, same as his. It'll be on the November boat. Alec — I'm glad the light never blinked. That's my laddie. Now you blink while you're able. Ma **Sgeir nan Ròn — 28th December 1991** The relief boat was three weeks held, so Christmas dinner was tinned ham and the last o the tatties, black-eyed and sorry. MacAulay and me fell oot ower the logbook and never spoke for twa days — there's naewhere to storm aff to on a rock, you just glower out different windows. We shared a dram at midnight and shook hands. Your parcel got in on the 23rd: the gansey fits braw, the tablet went in twa days. Davie says to tell your mother he's available. He's no. Alec **Buckie — 14th February 1992** Son — I had a wee turn in the Co-op queue and Maureen's made a great carry-on. They're sending me to Aberdeen for tests. It's nothing, and you're no to think o coming hame: you canna climb aff a rock every time an auld wumman grumbles. The Jags are oot the cup. The bairn's lost a tooth. Ordinary days, son — that's what I've got for you the day. Ma **Sgeir nan Ròn — 9th March 1992** Ma — Maureen wrote. Tell me true what they said at Aberdeen. None o your wee turns. News here, sic as it is: the Board's modernising, and Sgeir nan Ròn's to be automated in '94. A machine's to mind the light. A machine'll no scrape the salt aff the glass nor smell a bearing going. MacAulay says he'll tak the money and fish. I dinna ken yet. The sea's no done wi me, or I'm no done wi it. Write true, Ma. Alec **Buckie — 20th March 1992** Aye, well. It's the cancer, son, and they've to operate in April, and I'd have kept it frae you but for Maureen's mouth. I'm no feart. I've had a good life and the best o it was you and the lassie. I telt the surgeon I'm a fisherman's widow and he's no to bother me wi odds. Just you mind the light and come on your proper relief, no afore. I'll be here when you land. I've nae plans to be anywhere else, I promise you that. Ma **Sgeir nan Ròn — 31st March 1992** The Board's granted me compassionate leave — there's a word I'd rather not need. The relief boat's due the 12th and I'll be at your door by the 14th if the wind's kind. MacAulay's covering my watches, and Davie's baked you a cake. It's terrible, Ma, but he's proud o it, and I'll carry it careful. The Provost came back the day, which I'm taking as a sign, though o what I couldna tell you. Haud on. Alec **Buckie — 8th April 1992** Operation's fine. I'm hame already, sitting up like a lady while Maureen spoons soup at me. The rhubarb's through, the bairn's lost anither tooth, and the man next door's painted his door purple, which is the talk o the street. Bring your wet gear on the 14th — it's dreich here and set to stay. Ordinary days, son. That's what I've got for you the day, and I'm glad o every one. Ma **Sgeir nan Ròn — 30th March 1994** Ma — you'll no get this one. I'll put it in the biscuit
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary piece is a strong execution of the brief. The Scottish working-class dialect is rendered convincingly ("wabbit," "fash," "dreich," "greeting," "scunnered") without becoming pastiche. The two voices are well differentiated: Alec's letters carry the concrete textures of lighthouse work (clockwork winding, haar, paraffin, the horn every ninety seconds), while Ma's letters deflect worry through domestic detail — the rhubarb, the Jags, Mrs Gauld's cat — with her illness revealed gradually and plausibly through euphemism ("just my blood") until the cancer is named. The pacing across three years is well judged: isolation, storm, automation threat, illness, near-tragedy averted, and finally the automation's arrival. Humor (the Provost the seal, Davie's terrible cake, "he's available. He's no.") balances darkness effectively, and the recurring motif "Ordinary days, son" is a satisfying emotional anchor. The main flaw is that the response is cut off mid-sentence — "I'll put it in the biscuit" — so the intended final letter, which should provide resolution, is missing. The prompt explicitly required a final letter with a satisfying resolution and ~1000 words; the truncation means instructions are only partially met, and the emotional climax is implied but not delivered. Also, the mother's cancer operation going smoothly is a slightly convenient swerve, though her letter's voice ("I'm no feart") keeps it grounded rather than sentimental. Otherwise, prose is clean, restrained, shows rather than tells, avoids cliché and purple excess. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 79.5
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Hacker Mindset I catalogued the exits before I catalogued her smile. Old habit, old code, still running in the background no matter how many times I patch it. Two doors, one kitchen pass-through, a camera dome over the register that is absolutely a dummy, and a point-of-sale terminal whose admin password I would bet twenty dollars is still "password." Table for two. I took the seat facing the door without asking. Reformed doesn't mean relaxed. Then she smiled and the whole threat model blue-screened. So. Progress. It fell out of her tote between the paperback and the Tupperware: a deck box, scuffed, matte blue sleeves. "Oh thank god," she said. "I was trying to figure out how to bring it up." Magic. She plays Magic. Ten minutes ago I was drafting an internal memo about the QR code on the table tent—could resolve anywhere, scan at your own risk—and now we're arguing about whether Counterspell is a feels-bad and I am, against all odds, having a wonderful time. I catalogued that too. I catalogue everything. People are just systems with better lighting. That's the problem. Her deck: Azorius, blue-white. The colors of rules and of the people who enforce them. *Teferi, Hero of Dominaria.* Note: untaps two lands at end of turn. She likes to look tapped out and not be. *Supreme Verdict.* Note: a board wipe that can't be countered. When she's losing she doesn't negotiate. She resets the world and rebuilds faster than you. *Cyclonic Rift,* overloaded. Note: patience. She will sit behind a pillow fort for an hour waiting to cast one spell that turns your army into a rumor. *Rhystic Study.* She actually said the words—"do you pay the one?"—with a little smile like a customs agent. Note: she taxes you for existing and lets you decide whether it's worth it. I told her what I play, because honesty is the whole exercise, the entire rehabilitation program: Lantern of Insight, Codex Shredder, Ensnaring Bridge. "Lantern," she said. "The surveillance deck. You like seeing the top of my library and deciding what I'm allowed to draw." "I like information," I said, which is the confession and the alibi at once. "Of course you do," she said, and something behind her eyes got filed. Note: so does she. Dinner went the way good dinners go. She did a terrible impression of her playgroup's resident Timmy. I admitted I sleeve my deck with my back to the room. Habit. She said "opsec" like it was a diagnosis, and I laughed, and I did not check the exits once for almost nine minutes. A personal record. Then she went to show me a photo of her cat, and her thumb traced the unlock pattern, and the old code executed before the new code could vote. An L. Top-left corner, down, across. The smudge trail was legible from where I sat—from orbit, honestly—and my mouth, my traitor mouth, said: "Top-left. Everyone starts top-left. There are four hundred thousand possible patterns and half the planet draws a letter from the top-left corner, and yours is an L, and I watched you do it, and I would give anything to unsay all of that." The silence had a texture. Like waiting on a penetration test report you already know is bad. *Exit vectors,* whispered the old code. *Bathroom. Window—no window. Fake text from a contact named "Mom Emergency." She's pattern-matching you as a creep anyway. Cut losses. Ghost. Reformat. Relocate—* Shut up. I don't run that build anymore. "Okay," I said. "Full disclosure. I used to get paid to think like this—the bad kind of paid. Now I get paid to write reports about it instead. The looking doesn't stop; it's a background process, I can manage it, I can't kill it. But I don't use what I see. That's the deal I made. And you are not a target. You're the first person in two years who made me forget the exits for nine minutes, and I'm sorry I made you feel audited. That is the opposite of what I want." She looked at me for a long time. Control players can do that. They let the timer run. "You took the seat facing the door before you asked if I minded," she said. "I—yes." "You checked the window reflections when we sat down. You've touched your phone twice all night, both times screen-down. Your one question to the waiter was whether the Wi-Fi is a captive portal." She turned her phone over slowly, deliberately, like a queen moving to a square you'd been assured was safe. "That pattern opens a decoy partition. Empty gallery. Boring texts. One photo of my landlord's cat, who is real, and ugly, and whom I love." I stared. "I play control," she said. "You think I'd walk around with a readable smudge trail? I wanted to see if you'd say something. Everybody sees. Almost nobody says. It's a filter." The customs-agent smile came back. "Do you pay the one?" I paid the one. I'm paying it still. Note, revised: she is not the vulnerable system. She is the admin, and she has been logging my traffic since the door. "For what it's worth," I said, "I play Lantern. Watching the top of someone's library and *not* shredding the card they need is, for me, an act of genuine affection." "Noted," she said, and flagged the waiter. "Two spoons." We split the crème brûlée. I cracked the top with the back of my spoon—one clean tap—and told her, mostly truthfully, that it was the only thing I'd broken all night.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a tightly executed piece that hits nearly every prompt requirement: first-person internal monologue dominates, the reformed hacker's compulsive vulnerability-scanning is rendered as intrusive "background processes," the MTG fandom discovery lands early and organically, the phone-pattern faux pas occurs on cue, and the fallout negotiation follows. The word count is close to the 1000-word seed. Strengths: The voice is the piece's engine—clipped, self-aware, technical metaphor deployed with wit ("People are just systems with better lighting," "the confession and the alibi at once"). The MTG integration is genuinely clever: the deck-listing section does double duty, characterizing her through card choices while showing his inability to stop profiling. The reversal—she's running a decoy partition and has been observing him all along—is well-earned rather than arbitrary, since her Azorius control identity foreshadows it ("she likes to look tapped out and not be"). The "Do you pay the one?" callback as a relationship filter is an elegant thematic bow. The crème brûlée closer ("the only thing I'd broken all night") is a strong final image. Weaknesses: The twist flirts with wish-fulfillment—the date being a fellow security-conscious operator who was testing him is a fantasy of being perfectly understood, and it slightly deflates the tension the prompt asked for (negotiating fallout with a normal person would be harder and more interesting). The "Note:" structure, while charming, is used a touch mechanically. A few metaphors strain ("turns your army into a rumor" is good; "blue-screened" is stock). The emotional stakes resolve a bit too smoothly; the date's forgiveness arrives quickly, robbing the ending of some earned friction. Dialogue is functional and occasionally aphoristic to a fault—characters speak in polished epigrams more than people do. Still, the prose flows well, the tone is consistent, imagery is economical and effective, and the piece is coherent and engaging throughout. It is not a masterpiece—the reversal is a little too neat and the emotional complexity, while present, resolves without real cost—but it is well above competent.
