+ Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 85.5
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Underhold The door swung inward before Aya's glove ever brushed the iron. Beyond it, the underhold exhaled — cold, wet air reeking of brine, old tallow, and the sweet fat-smoke of whale oil. One by one, with the soft tick of clockwork valves, the gas lamps along the walls sputtered alight, casting long, unsettling shadows across the stone floor. The vault stretched away beneath the old try-works like the inside of some great drowned beast: pillars ribbed up into darkness, water wept down black granite, and at the far end, behind a desk of inlaid scrimshaw, sat Mother Maren. "Evening, ducks," she said. "Mind the salt lines. They're older than your grandfathers, and I'm fond of them." Aya's heart slammed once, hard. Around them the shadows unfolded into men — six, eight — rising from behind casks and rendering troughs with crossbows wound and clockwork pistols levelled. Someone had a harpoon-gun mounted on a swivel, its barbed head grinning in the lamplight. "Well," Katra breathed. "I said it smelled of a lie. I did say that." "The bluebottles raided the Floe at dawn," Simeon rumbled. "We saw the ledgers. We saw the chains." "You saw what I paid for." Mother Maren was a small, tidily dressed woman, grey at the temples, honing a flensing knife against a little whetstone, unhurried as a fishwife. "A raid costs less than a hanging judge and tells you twice as much. Shows you who your friends are, when they think the door's been left open." The stone sang along the blade. "Come all the way in, Rook. You've climbed my ranks like ivy for a year. Don't go shy at the top of the wall." Aya's mind raced down its corridors and found every one bricked up. The old Scythan knot-wards were cut into the floor in rings of salt and scrimshaw, and her gift — the cold company coiled behind her teeth since girlhood, the Hushed who answered when she called — guttered against those marks like a lamp starved of oil. For the first time in years, she could not feel them listening. She stepped forward anyway. There was nothing behind her but the drop. "Don't," she said quietly, as Simeon's huge hand crept toward his cudgel. A crossbow string went taut with a sound like a plucked tooth. "Don't, Sim. It's done." Simeon was praying under his breath — the Drowned Saints, the Grey Mother, the whole soggy litany of the whale-roads. "Smart moppet." Maren set down the stone. "Knives on the floor, all three. Katra, I know about the one in your boot. There's a lamb." Steel chimed on stone. Then Maren gestured, and a big man with a whaler's hook crossed to Aya. The hook slid beneath the edge of her mask — cold iron against her cheekbone — and with a flick, cut the strings. The mask fell. The lamplight did its work. A sound went through the room, small and collective, and one of the guards — dock-bred, by his tarred nails — whispered, "Christ of the crows. That's the Vayne girl." Mother Maren went very still. Then she smiled like a tide coming in. "Lady Aya Vayne." She savoured it. "Half the oil in this city comes off your father's hooks, and here's his only daughter crawling my cellars in a bird mask." Her eyes narrowed; memory arriving like a ship at harbor. "You've got her face. I stood at Gallows Quay and watched your mother dance the hempen jig. Pretty thing. She called on things at the end, did you know? Nothing came." *Something comes every night,* Aya thought wildly. She could feel the Hushed clawing at the wards from the far side, circling like sharks beyond the glass of a bathysphere — and for the first time since she was twelve years old, she was alone inside her own skull. So she did the only thing left. She drew herself up the way her governess had drilled her — spine, chin, the drawing-room voice deployed like a sabre. "Then you know precisely who I am, and precisely what I'm worth. Kill me in this cellar and I'm a scandal for a week. Keep me breathing, Mother Maren, and I am a fortune. My father will pay any sum named to have me back — *quietly*. And you've enemies who'd pay near as well to learn Lord Vayne's daughter ran with the Morska." Her voice held steady, and she hated it, because every word was a small death. Her name, spoken aloud down here, could never be unspoken. It would follow her up into the light — to the waltzes, the Athenaeum lectures, her mother's shadow lengthening behind her wherever she went. "Dead, I'm worth the weight of a coffin. Alive, I'm worth a fleet." "Ransom," Maren mused. "Or your father pays double to be sure you never surface at all. Tidy girl like you — you're a liability with a pulse." "Then sell me to his enemies and let him bid against them. You're a businesswoman. Auction me." Katra made a strangled sound. "Aya—" "Hush, kitten." Maren rose, came around the desk, the flensing knife loose in her fist. She looked Aya over the way a purser appraises a catch. "They said the Rook never met a lock she couldn't sweet-talk. That doors *opened* for her." Her voice dropped into the old terror of the docks — the fear that lived below decks, in the hold, in the black water under the keel. "Men in this guild trust brass and oil and steel, my lady. They do not care for the other thing. If I learn you've brought the other thing into my house—" "Your house is warded to the rafters," Aya said. "You tell me what I could possibly bring in." A long, cold silence. Then Maren laughed — one short bark — and turned away. "Salt cells. All three. Feed them, even. We've a lady of quality to keep plump for market." As hooks and pistol barrels herded her toward the dark, Aya's gaze caught on the cradle behind Maren's desk: glass, salt-ringed, and within it the thing they'd come to steal — a spiral of ancient horn, banded in green gold, long as a man's leg, humming so faintly she felt it in her teeth rather than heard it. The Scythan Horn. And as the guards took her arms, it seemed — it *almost* seemed — to know her name.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of the prompt. It hits all required story beats: the trio enters the underhold, Mother Maren is revealed as un-incarcerated with bodyguards and weapons, Aya is unmasked, the trio are captured without a fight scene, and Aya negotiates her hostage value while internally grappling with exposure. The dialogue is rich in period/whalepunk dialect ("bluebottles," "hempen jig," "Christ of the crows," "dance the hempen jig"), and the worldbuilding details — salt lines, scrimshaw desk, flensing knife, harpoon-gun, try-works — are well chosen. The gothic horror element is present via the Hushed and the Horn's final recognition of Aya. Strengths: The prose is controlled and evocative without tipping into purple. Mother Maren is a genuinely menacing, nuanced antagonist with a distinct voice. Aya's internal monologue is well integrated ("Dead, I'm worth the weight of a coffin. Alive, I'm worth a fleet"). The unmasking scene lands with good tension. The ending image of the Horn "knowing her name" is an effective hook. Weaknesses: The negotiation resolves a bit too smoothly — Maren capitulates to the salt-cell plan with a single laugh, slightly underplaying the threat of immediate execution. The "auction me" line is clever but perhaps a touch too glib given the stakes. Katra and Simeon are thinly sketched, serving mostly as reaction shots. Some phrases ("like a tide coming in," "corridors bricked up") flirt with cliché. The guards' collective whisper at the reveal is a slightly theatrical beat. The piece is somewhat compressed relative to the 1000-word seed, but this doesn't harm coherence. Overall, this is skilled, atmospheric genre fiction with authentic voices and strong scene construction, held back from excellence only by minor conveniences and underdeveloped secondary characters. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 76.8
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gunpowder Rendezvous A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. Outside, the dockside street sweats neon and diesel, but in here it's all shadow and slow time. Spike Spiegel sits at the far end of the counter with a glass of something amber that tastes like kerosene and costs more than he's carrying. For an hour he's watched the door in the mirror behind the bottles. The tip said Varga's people drink here. The tip cost him his last decent cigarette. Then the door opens, and the room changes pressure. She walks in like she owns the air—boots, shorts, black top, a dragon coiled down her right arm, two pistols riding her thighs. The locals look, then look away fast, which tells Spike more than any wanted poster. She takes the stool beside him out of eleven empty ones, and he understands that as a message. "Rum," she tells the bartender. "Bottle. Not a glass." She studies him the way you'd study a snake in your path. "You've been watching the door." "Watching the mirror," Spike says. "The door just happens to be in it." Something almost like a smile. "Cute." She drinks straight from the bottle and sets it down between them like a challenge. "Revy." "Spike." "I know. Bounty hunter. You look broke." Her eyes flick over him, lazy and thorough, pausing on his left eye—the one that doesn't track quite right. She files that away. "Let me guess. Domingo Varga." He slides a folded photo across the bar. Same face she's carrying in her back pocket. For a moment they just look at each other, two professionals recognizing the shape of the same bad luck. "Back off, cowboy," Revy says. "This one's mine." "Can't. Rent's due." He lights a cigarette off the bartender's trembling Zippo and orders whatever's fried, because he's starving and the bill is a problem for later. "We could split it." "I don't split. I don't share. I don't play well with others." "You're a regular children's story." She laughs—short, sharp, surprised by it—and hates herself a little for it. They drink. She orders tequila to test him; he matches her shot for shot, which she files under arrogance and can't stop watching. He moves like water even reaching for a glass. Nothing about him is afraid of her. She's not used to how quiet that makes a room feel. The door bangs open at midnight. Five men, coats too heavy for the heat. The mirror gives them away a half-second before Revy's instincts do, and half a second is a fortune. Spike flows sideways off the stool as the first shot takes his glass. Revy kicks the table up into a shield and comes up with both Berettas singing—left hand and right hand choosing different targets, like her body is two people and both of them are angry. The bar turns to noise and strobing light: bottles bursting, the fan chewing a stray round, spinning mad. Spike breaks a man's arm with an economy that looks almost gentle, takes his gun away like a borrowed lighter, puts him down with an elbow. "That's three," Revy says. "I'm not counting." "You are now, asshole." It ends the way it always ends. Four down, one talking. The talker gives up a motel—the Palms, room six, where Varga's sweating out the night with a case of bearer bonds and a head worth two million woolongs, dead or alive. They take Varga's room in eleven seconds. She goes low, he goes high, and afterward they stand in the wreckage breathing hard, both of them grinning, both of them pretending they're not. Then it's just the case on the bed, and the two of them. Revy's pistols come up first. Spike's Jericho is already level with her heart—he never seemed to draw it at all. The air conditioner rattles. Neon bleeds red through the blinds, painting them like a crime scene that hasn't happened yet. "One gun against two," she says. "Bad math, Spike." "One's enough. I've got a depth-perception problem. Everything looks close." He isn't smiling, quite. "You'd have to be faster than you are." "You'd have to be bulletproof." "Nobody is." The standoff stretches. Sweat slides down her spine. She's killed men for less, killed them for nothing, and her finger knows a trigger's weight like a prayer. But he's standing inside her reach without flinching, and his one good eye holds her steady, and somewhere between the gun smoke and the rum she realizes she's closer to him than a clean shot needs. So is he. "So which is it," he says. "You the good guy or the bad guy?" "I'm not a good person. Not a bad person." Her thumbs rest on the hammers. "I'm just here." "Huh." The faintest crooked tilt at the corner of his mouth. "Same." "You're standing close enough to kiss me," he says, mild as weather. "Makes the shooting awkward." "Shooting's easy. It's the other thing that's complicated." Her pulse is a fist on a door. "I don't trust anybody. That's kept me breathing." "Me neither. Works great. Look how happy we are." He's seen her before, he thinks—not her, but the shape of her. All edges, nowhere soft to land. Maybe that's why he doesn't step back. Maybe that's exactly why he should. Somewhere below, a siren dopplers past and dies. Varga groans, forgotten, tied to the minibar. The case sits on the bed between two million woolongs and two people who built whole lives out of never blinking first. Neither lowers. Neither fires. The neon buzzes. Her mouth is right there; so is the muzzle of his gun, and she can't tell which one she's thinking about, and from his smile, neither can he. "Whatever happens," Spike says, "happens." Nothing does. Everything could. The night holds its breath, and so do they.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers the requested scenario efficiently: seedy bar, drinking contest, gunfight, motel standoff, unresolved tension. It hits the prompt beats (drinking, gunplay, UST, standoff) and incorporates character details naturally—Spike's prosthetic eye, fatalism, hunger, "Whatever happens, happens"; Revy's dual-wielding, "Two Hands" energy, her famous quote, trust issues. Third person present tense is maintained. Length is roughly on target (~1000 words). Strengths: The prose is lean and confident, with strong economical lines ("The door opens, and the room changes pressure"; "two people who built whole lives out of never blinking first"). Dialogue crackles and fits both characters—Revy's "I don't split. I don't share" and Spike's dry "You're a regular children's story" are pitch-perfect. The standoff is genuinely tense, and the ending withholds resolution appropriately, honoring both characters' inability to trust. Weaknesses: The plot is formulaic—rival bounty hunters, bar shootout, split the target, standoff. The five goons are generic cannon fodder; the fight resolves too easily ("eleven seconds"). Varga is a nonentity. The mutual attraction is asserted more than developed; the emotional leap from rivalry to near-kiss happens fast, though the piece at least gestures at why (recognition of kindred damage). Some lines flirt with over-cleverness ("painting them like a crime scene that hasn't happened yet" is good; "her pulse is a fist on a door" is a bit much). The "You're standing close enough to kiss me" line is attributed to Spike but reads like it could be either, slightly muddying the standoff choreography. Minor continuity: Revy's Berettas have hammers thumbed, fine, but the physical blocking of the final standoff is vague. Overall this is competent, stylish fanfic-adjacent work with authentic voices and a satisfying withheld ending, held back by a predictable structure and thin antagonist stakes. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 85.0
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Útiseta I was fifteen the autumn Papa's job moved us from Stockholm to Björkåsen, seven hundred kilometres north of anywhere I'd ever been. Two years, they promised. Then home. My mother said it like a prayer and my father said it like a verdict, and I stopped asking which of them I believed. At fifteen you'll believe almost anything if the alternative is admitting you're bored. This was 1995. The village had one bus, one Konsum, and Astrid. By October I had played all her midnight games: the mirror under the bed that showed you who was lying; the knotted string you slipped into someone's desk to make them think of you. Harmless things. Astrid treated them like smoking behind the gym — half mischief, half inheritance. Her grandmother had taught her, she said. The old ways. But útiseta was different. I knew that before we'd even left the road. We met at the crossroads where the bus turned around. Astrid looked me over like a border guard. "Hair clip." I handed it over. "Ring. Keys." She buried them under the milestone with her own. "Iron locks doors," she said. "Tonight we want them open. You haven't eaten since dark? Good. The dead are hungry. You shouldn't smell of food." She carried a bottle of milk and, in her pocket, her grandmother's silver coin. On the way up past the Lindgrens' meadow she gave me the rules in the same flat voice she used for homework. Sit back to back on the crown. Don't sleep — what sleeps on a mound doesn't always wake alone. Don't say any names, not mine, not yours. Whatever you hear, don't answer. "Even if it's me," she said. "Especially if it's me. And don't leave until the first bird." "Where did your grandmother learn it?" "Mormor wouldn't teach me this one." She almost sounded proud. "The church made it a crime, did you know that? Four hundred years ago, and they were still frightened of it. I listened at the door when she told her sister." The mound stood on the ridge above the meadow — Kungshögen, people called it, though no one could say which king. The birches had already turned; their leaves clicked overhead like small bones. Mist had come up off the bog and lay thick against the mound's flanks, glowing faintly under the moon, so it rose out of the white like an island, only the bare crown showing. We climbed into clear cold air and sat down back to back. Astrid poured the milk in a ring around us and set the coin at the northern point. "Hold your question," she said. "Don't speak it. And Linnea—" her voice caught once, the only time that night — "ask the one you want. They answer the one you mean." I had chosen to ask whether Johan Bergkvist liked me. It took an hour on that mound to learn what I actually wanted to know. At first there was only the night working: a fox barking down in the dark, wind worrying the birches, the bog muttering to itself. My back went numb against Astrid's. The stars wheeled. I thought of my warm bed, of how stupid we'd feel at school on Monday. Then the bog stopped. All of it, at once, the way a room goes quiet when someone walks in. Something moved in the mist below us. Slow steps. Circling. Never climbing, never quite approaching — patient, the way water is patient. Astrid's spine went rigid against mine. I told myself: fox. Deer. Wind. I had a whole list and I read it like a prayer. "Linnea." My mother's voice. From down in the mist, from everywhere at once, with her exact patience in the syllables — the way she'd call me in from a yard when I was small. My mother, asleep in the village, four kilometres away. "Linnea. Come down here. I know what you asked." And God help me, the question that rose up in me was not about any boy. It was: *will we ever go home?* It had been under everything for months, and the voice took hold of it like a hand closing on a string. "I know whether you're going home," it said. "Ask me. It's allowed." Then, behind me, from exactly where Astrid sat, it spoke in Astrid's voice: "It's all right. You can turn around now." The real Astrid made no sound at all. She only pressed back harder. My mouth opened. I felt the word shape itself— Astrid's hand clamped over my mouth, hard enough that her ring would have cut me, if she'd been wearing it. She held on. We sat like that, shaking, while the mist waited. Then, somewhere down towards the village, a thrush started up — one thread of song — and the slope below us was only a slope, and the mist was only mist, thinning towards morning. We didn't speak going down. At the crown's edge Astrid stopped: the milk ring was still there, wet on the grass. The silver coin was gone. "Payment accepted," she said, the way people say things they're hoping are true. At the milestone we dug out our keys with numb fingers. "I didn't answer," I said. Astrid looked at me then, and she looked older than her grandmother. "You started to. They count that." We never played the midnight games after that. Or Astrid never played them with me. We did move back to Stockholm, in the end, the following spring. I got my answer. I've spent thirty years deciding not to ask what it cost. I've explained that night to myself a hundred ways — cold, suggestion, two girls drunk on their own daring. Foxes take shiny things. Some days I believe all of it. But no one has spoken my name in the dark since, without my going still.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of folk horror that fulfills the brief with considerable skill. The first-person retrospective framing is handled transparently, as requested, with the adult narrator's interjections ("I've spent thirty years deciding not to ask what it cost") landing at the right moments. The 1995 rural Swedish setting is convincingly textured (Konsum, the crossroads bus turnaround, Kungshögen), and the ritual details—burying iron, fasting so the dead don't smell food, the milk ring, the silver coin, the prohibition on names—are specific and folklorically plausible, mixing teenage bravado with genuine dread exactly as the prompt demands. The ambiguity is well maintained: the mother's voice, the circling presence, the vanished coin, and the final line all permit both supernatural and psychological readings. The narrator's rationalizations ("Foxes take shiny things") are a nice touch that keeps the ambiguity honest rather than coy. The emotional core is cleverly subverted: Linnea intends a trivial question about a boy, but the mound draws out her real question about going home. This gives the horror psychological grounding and makes the ending's "I got my answer" land with quiet menace. Astrid is well drawn—her flat, homework-voice instructions, the single crack in her composure, her aged look at the end. Weaknesses: The prose occasionally reaches a little hard ("the way water is patient," "leaves clicked overhead like small bones," "said it like a prayer / like a verdict"). These are mostly effective but a few similes stack up. The mother's voice sequence is a familiar folk-horror beat, though executed well. The ending's final line is strong but the preceding paragraph slightly over-explains the ambiguity. Dialogue is sparse but functional and characterful. Length is close to target. Nothing meandering; the pacing is tight and the escalation controlled. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 61.8
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Therapeutic Boundaries The lavender was her idea. Everything else in the treatment room smelled honest—alcohol, latex, the chemical ghost of ultrasound gel—but the diffuser on the shelf breathed out something floral and untrue, as if a body could be negotiated with. It was Tuesday, session twenty-two of the forty the settlement required, and Dana stood reading my chart with her hair pinned up the way she'd worn it at nationals six years ago, when she was the fastest training partner I ever had and I was still becoming whatever it is I've stopped being. She'd left the sport intact at twenty-six, walked away with all her tendons, gone back to school. Retirement had filled her out the way stopping fills people out—she'd lost the hungry look we used to share, and it suited her, and I resented that too. I resented everything recovery-adjacent. Me, I'd felt the tendon go 180 meters into a final, a kick delivered by nobody, and hopped twice before the track came up. "Shoes off," she said. Not unkind. Precise. Knee-to-wall first. Right foot—my foot, the one with the pale zipper of a scar behind the ankle—set against the tape line. "Drive the knee over the toes. Heel down." I drove, sliding the foot back along the floor until the heel hovered like a thing with its own loyalties. She measured: seven centimeters of big toe to drywall, and recorded it. Left foot: twelve. She recorded that too, and the pencil scratch sounded louder than it should have. Numbers were the room's native language. We both spoke it so we wouldn't have to speak anything else. Then the table. Prone, face in the cradle, ankles hanging off the end. Her palms found the gastrocnemius—the upper belly of the calf, where the muscle still remembered being a sprinter's—and worked downward in slow, loaded strokes toward the tendon. My hamstring braced before her hands even landed. "Stop guarding," she said, and I couldn't. At the repair site she switched to short cross-fiber friction, thumb rolling the thickened cord like she was reading it. The pain ran a four that flared to six; she asked the number and I lied, and she said, "I can hear you not breathing, Marcus. Four?" "Four." Liar's arithmetic. Her other hand steadied my heel, and the treacherous thing—the thing that would never appear on any insurance form—was that my body had started arriving early to her touch, warming toward it, gooseflesh climbing the back of my thigh half a second before her fingers got there. She saw it. I know she saw it. She recited anatomy to cover it: "The soleus doesn't cross the knee, so we'll take it bent next"—spoken to no one, a shield built out of facts. When she finished, she pressed two fingers into the hollow behind my inner ankle, just below the medial malleolus. Posterior tibial pulse. Purely clinical—a circulation check—except her fingertips sat directly on the evidence. My pulse struck against her skin: fast, caught, obvious. Neither of us mentioned it. Her hand left a beat late. Supine then, leg straight, Dana at the foot of the table cradling my heel in one palm, the ball of my foot braced against her collarbone. "Push against me. Thirty percent. Hold—five, four—relax." On the relax she leaned her weight through my leg and drew the ankle up toward my shin, into the long bright stretch that climbed the calf like water climbing a shoreline. "Six," I said, honest for once, and she held me there at the edge, trembling faintly with the effort of holding my whole leg, or with something else. The lavender was on her skin now, in the heat of her exhale. My hand found her shoulder for balance—the first time I'd touched her since 2019—and we both went still. "Breathe," she said. It was genuinely unclear which of us she meant. Last: the step by the window. Balls of both feet on the edge, rise up, shift the weight right, and lower the heel below the step over a count of three. The calf shook—visibly, humiliatingly—and her hand came to my hip to steady it. "That's not weakness," she said. "That's recruitment." Down again. Burn like a lit fuse. "What's the point," I said, "of healing to sixty percent of something?" Her hand stayed. "You think recovery is a consolation prize." "Isn't it?" "No. It's a different race. You keep trying to run it like the old one." She'd known me since we were seventeen; she'd earned the sentence. Down, three seconds, the tendon holding. Then, quieter: "You don't hate the pain. You hate that it works." She wrote the plan. I re-laced my shoe over my new, ordinary ankle, the heel staying down a centimeter longer than last week—six degrees gained, and I hated every one of them, and I wanted every one of them. "Thursday," she said, professional again, both of us returned to our own sides of the line we'd spent an hour redrawing. The lavender followed me into the hall. I hated it. I could already tell it was going to smell like her.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece that hits nearly every requirement of the prompt with precision. The physical therapy sequence is anatomically coherent and spatially clear: knee-to-wall test with measured centimeters, prone cross-fiber friction on the Achilles repair site, a posterior tibial pulse check, supine resisted dorsiflexion stretch, and eccentric heel drops off a step. Each technique is described accurately and tracked consistently in space. The tension is conveyed through involuntary bodily responses—gooseflesh arriving before her touch, the pulse betraying him under her fingertips during the circulation check, the trembling effort of holding his leg. The pulse-check moment is the standout: a purely clinical act that becomes the scene's most charged beat, and neither character names it. That is excellent show-don't-show restraint. Characterization is layered: Marcus's resentment is directed at recovery itself ("I resented everything recovery-adjacent"), and Dana is professional, deflecting with anatomy recitals, her own attraction legible only through a late hand and a "beat late" departure. The dialogue is spare and mostly strong, though "You don't hate the pain. You hate that it works" flirts with therapy-slogan neatness. The line "It was genuinely unclear which of us she meant" for "Breathe" is the best single moment—compressed, mutual, and true to the prompt's dual-distance requirement. Weaknesses: the lavender bookend is a slightly familiar device (scent-as-memory, "it was going to smell like her" is a touch predictable). "Liar's arithmetic" and "the room's native language" are good, but a few phrases ("a thing with its own loyalties") strain slightly. The ending's emotional resolution—wanting the gains while hating them—is earned rather than sentimental, and the closing keeps professional boundaries intact, which suits the prompt. The piece is tight, ~950 words, no meandering. Minor contrivance: the prompt asked for him manipulating her body in stretches, and the model inverts this (she treats him)—a defensible reading given the injury setup, but a slight deviation from the literal instruction. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Fourteen: Mango Season **Dawn — the Danish Factory** The knock came in with the heat, both through the door at once. "Jamie. It's past six. Captain's boat goes to Whampoa on the tide, and you're on the manifest." I sat up inside the mosquito net and let my hands stop shaking before I spoke. "Tell Venn I have the flux." "You had the flux Monday." "Then it has me again. Come in, Tom. Don't hover in the passage like a creditor." Hargrave entered smelling of shave-soap and coffee, two things I could no longer afford in the same week. He looked at me the way a man looks at a gun that has failed to fire. "Christ, Jamie. You're grey." "Canton air." "Canton *something*." He set a dollar on my sea-chest and pretended he hadn't. "I'll say the surgeon's seen you. But Venn keeps a tally, you know. He keeps a tally of everything." "I'll stand the next one." "So you said." He paused at the door. "Whatever it is that's eating you — eat it back, man." When he'd gone I lay doing the day's arithmetic, which in Canton is worked in a single denomination. The dragon, as Pike calls it, does not take promises. It takes Spanish silver, and I had one dollar and the King's coat on my back. **Morning — a chop-house off Old China Street** Pike had been a Company clerk once, before the Company found him out; now he brokered shame for men with better tailoring than his own. We ate rice under a fan pulled by a boy on a string. "I need ten dollars by dark," I said. "You need ten by noon, Jamie. I've seen your eyes." He sucked a grain of rice from his knuckle. "There's a boat goes down the reach tonight. Six small chests, papers all in order save that the papers are lies. Apo wants a King's officer in the stern sheets — uniform coat — to be England if the Hoppo's cruisers come sniffing. Two hours of sitting. Eight dollars." "Ten." "Eight, and I'll stand your slate with the Widow." He leaned in; his breath was cloves over rot. "You needn't do anything, man. That's the beauty. You needn't even look at the cargo. Just be the flag." "The flag costs twelve." "The flag costs eight, and it's robbery at the price for a flag that sweats like you do. Take it. The dragon doesn't keep office hours." He advanced me two dollars against the night, and I told myself the lie I kept for daylight hours: one pipe, to steady the hand, and the rest saved whole. **Afternoon — below the city wall** The alleys toward the wall had gone overripe with June. The scent of rotting mangoes permeated everything — split fruit weeping amber on the stalls, skins trodden to sweet paste underfoot, a smell like rum gone wrong that lodged at the back of the throat and stayed. From a doorway came the click of the fan-tan cup. A joss house burned sandalwood against the stink, and lost. The Widow kept her rooms behind a shuttered fan-maker's, up a stair that remembered better tenants. She was fifty, painted like a bride, sharp as a seller of nails. "Lieutenant." She never used my name; rank was my name now. "Two dollar buy you one. Maybe." "It bought two in spring." "Spring, King's ship at Lintin, navy busy, price low. Now navy men all hide, price go up." She took my dollars, weighed them like a fishwife. "Your coat get thinner every moon, Lieutenant. One day you come with no coat. What then?" "Then I'll come as a common sailor and pay a common sailor's price." She laughed — the only true laugh I'd get that day — and shouted down the stair for the lamp. The room held six couches and the sweat of every man who'd ever lain on them. She cooked the pill on its needle over a flame the size of a tear, turned it, coaxed it, set it in the bowl, and I drew the first honest breath of the day: burnt honey, flowers gone to ash, the river and the mangoes and Canton itself let out of me on the exhale. Beside me a Parsee merchant slept the sleep of the well-organized. The boy fanned the charcoal. Time stopped keeping its tally. **Night — a creek below the factories** Apo's boat was twenty feet of fast tarred pine, six oars, and a cargo under palm mats that I did not look at, because I had agreed not to look. "Tea," Apo said, grinning with one tooth. "Don't tell me." We slipped down the reach past the hulks at Whampoa, where my own ship's riding lights burned like a reproach. Off the second creek a lantern rose out of the black and a voice hailed us. "Hoppo's man," Apo murmured. "Stand up, Lieutenant. Be big." I stood in the coat I had sweated through across two oceans and raised my face into their light. "His Britannic Majesty's dispatches for the Commodore at Lintin," I said, in the tone I once used on midshipmen. "Delay this boat, and you explain it to the men-of-war." A long pause. Then laughter, and a string of cash flipped across the water into their boat — Apo's toll, not mine — and the lantern dipped away. "They eat too," Apo said. **Midnight — the factory steps** Pike paid me under the British flag: eight dollars, the Widow's two off the top before I touched them, and three more I carried straight back through the mango-stink to her stair, because midnight in Canton is longer than any watch I stood at sea. Hargrave was waiting on the steps with his pipe. "Venn asked for you twice. I told him the surgeon bled you and forbade it." "Tom—" "Don't." He knocked the pipe out on the rail. "Stand your watch Thursday, Jamie. Stand it if it kills you. Because whatever this is — it will." Up in my room I put three dollars under the floorboard with the others I never saved, and lay listening to the tide turn for Lintin. Tomorrow, I told the dark, I'd be the man I was at Trafalgar. The dark, which knew Canton's arithmetic better than I, said nothing at all.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of historical fiction that fulfills the brief with considerable skill. The chapter follows Merrick through a single day, structured across four time-stamped scenes, told largely in dialogue as requested, with rich but controlled sensory detail. Strengths: The Canton setting feels researched and specific — the Danish Factory, Old China Street, Whampoa, Lintin, the Hoppo, Spanish dollars, strings of cash, the fan-tan cup. The mango-rot smell motif is an effective, non-cliché sensory anchor that recurs across the day. The Widow's pidgin-inflected dialogue and the economics of her pricing ("navy men all hide, price go up") is sharp world-building through speech. Pike's negotiating scene crackles; lines like "You needn't do anything, man... Just be the flag" capture the moral corruption economically. The prose has aphoristic bite: "the lie I kept for daylight hours," "midnight in Canton is longer than any watch I stood at sea," "The dark... said nothing at all." The ending resists false redemption while retaining a bleak wit. Weaknesses: The Widow's dialect flirts with period-typical stereotyping and could read as crude shorthand. Merrick's voice is occasionally too polished and epigrammatic — every line lands a little too quotably, which can feel authorial rather than natural ("arithmetic" is used three times, a motif teetering into preciousness). The plot beats (borrowed money, the smuggling run, the bribe) are conventional for this genre; the Hoppo encounter resolves easily and slightly deflates tension. Hargrave is a fairly stock loyal friend. The opium-smoking scene, while well-rendered, is the expected centerpiece. The Trafalgar reference in the last line is a touch sentimental for the piece's otherwise dry tone. None of these are amateurish failings; they are the limits of a very competent pastiche of first-rate historical fiction. Emotionally, the piece earns its darkness — Merrick's self-deception and arithmetic of dependency are convincingly rendered without melodrama. Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Sisyphus Gives Advice The boulder reached the summit at midmorning, paused with the air of an actor certain of his cue, and rolled back down. Sisyphus watched it go. The descent was the quiet part of his day, and over the years he had learned to do his best work in it. "Post, Crow," he said. The crow landed on his shoulder, dropped the mailbag, and coughed up a brass button, which he kept.¹ ¹ Crow was not, technically, a familiar. He preferred "editorial consultant," and was paid in shiny things and absolute veto over spelling. --- *Dear Sisyphus,* *My wife and I have been married fourteen years and are happy except for the dishwasher. She loads it like a raccoon falling down a staircase. She says my way takes half an hour. This is the hill we have chosen to die on. No pun intended.* *— Forks Up, Fresno* "Dear Forks Up," Sisyphus dictated, walking. "The argument is not about the dishwasher. It is about whether the person you married respects your way of doing things. So: whoever loads the dishwasher owns the dishwasher. The other person says thank you and leaves the room. And remember that a badly loaded dishwasher still washes the dishes. There is no comparable mercy in a badly loaded marriage. — Yours, S." Crow scratched it down in the looping script that mortal readers assumed was a typeface. --- *Dear Sisyphus,* *My boss emails at midnight and marks everything URGENT. Last week I answered one at my grandfather's funeral. Grandad would have understood. That is the problem.* *— Drowning, Duluth* "Dear Drowning. The work will always ask for more. That is what work is for. It is not what you are for. No employer has ever sent a note saying 'That is plenty now, well done, go outside.' You will have to write that note yourself. Choose a stopping time. Tell everyone. Keep it. Answer nothing after six for a fortnight, and I predict three days of thunder, then weather. — S." --- *Dear Sisyphus,* *How many times a week is normal? Asking for my husband, who is standing right here.* *— Pink, Peoria* "Dear Pink. Whatever the number is, someone will tell you it is wrong. They are selling something. — S." --- *Dear Sisyphus,* *There is a woman in my book club who corrects everyone's pronunciation. Last month she corrected the author. The author was dead, and present only as an audiobook.* *— Well Read, Woking* "Dear Well Read. You cannot cure her, and it is not your job to try. You are not obliged to attend every argument you are invited to. Let the corrections land the way rain lands on a roof. If you must act, do this: thank her, warmly, for one correction that genuinely helped you. It costs nothing and will confuse her for months. Kindness, deployed precisely, is the most unsettling weapon there is. — S." --- At the summit the boulder paused again. Sisyphus leaned on it a moment — not pushing, just leaning, the way one leans on a fence with an old friend. Then it went down, and so did he, and Crow read the next letter on the wing.² ² The column had begun with a misprinted address in a mortal newspaper. The postal service of the Underworld, which had not admitted an error in six thousand years, delivered the letters anyway. The mail, as is well documented, always gets through. --- *Dear Sisyphus,* *For months now my ——— has been ———. It is enormous. Every night it ——— and my wife just ———. I have tried ———, but the neighbours are starting to ———. The pigeons are frightened. I am desperate.* *— ———* "It got rained on," said Crow. "Or wept on." "Snoring," said Crow. "Could be the dog. It says 'enormous.'" "Great Dane, then." "Could be the other thing." "It is never the other thing," said Crow. "It is always worth answering," said Sisyphus, "as though it might be. Dear Sir or Madam. Your letter arrived in some distress, and parts of it remain between you and the gods. I shall answer all three versions. If it is snoring: a physician, and sooner than you think. If it is the dog: training, patience, and a better fence. If it is the other thing: speak honestly to your wife, who loves you and, I promise, already knows. In all three cases, apologise to the neighbours, and stop doing whatever you have been doing to the pigeons. — S." --- *Dear Sisyphus,* *I am thirty-six. I have a decent job, a flat, and a cat that tolerates me. By every measure I should be content, and instead I lie awake wondering what any of it is for. You, of all people, must have wondered. How do you stand it? What is the point?* *— Adrift, Aberdeen* Sisyphus was quiet for a while, which for him meant several switchbacks. "Dear Adrift," he said at last. "I am wary of the question 'what is the point.' It is too big to answer all at once, and asking it gets you no nearer an answer. Try a smaller one: what needs doing today that I would be glad to have done? Then do that. Feed the cat. Ring your mother. Answer a stranger's letter. Meaning is not something you find, like a dropped key. It accumulates, the way sediment makes a coastline. "Not everything worth doing stays done — the dishes teach us that daily — and we do them anyway, because the doing is the life. The done is just the souvenir. "P.S. A cat that tolerates you is not nothing. Cats do not bluff." --- At the foot of the hill the boulder waited with the patience of geology. Crow tucked the finished letters into the bag — signed, sealed, and claw-marked — and took off for the surface. Sisyphus rolled his shoulders, set his hands against the stone, and started up again, whistling.³ ³ Crow maintained the whistling was the strangest part of the whole arrangement, and he had once delivered mail to the Fates.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece that meets the brief with considerable skill. The epistolary structure is executed cleanly, with scene-setting interjections that are economical rather than ornamental. The Pratchett-style footnotes ("editorial consultant," the Underworld postal service, the closing whistle gag) land well and capture his comic-as-worldbuilding voice without pastiche overload. The advice letters are the heart of the piece, and they mostly deliver. The dishwasher response ("a badly loaded dishwasher still washes the dishes. There is no comparable mercy in a badly loaded marriage") is genuinely aphoristic. The midnight-email response ("You will have to write that note yourself") is practical and warm. The blurred-letter gag is the comic centerpiece — the Crow/Sisyphus banter over the illegible letter is the best dialogue in the piece, understated and well-timed, and "stop doing whatever you have been doing to the pigeons" is an excellent closer. It handles the risque mandate with wit rather than crudeness. The brief's constraints are honored: Sisyphus is zen without a stoicism lecture, natural rather than fish-out-of-water, and there is exactly one near-boulder metaphor ("Not everything worth doing stays done — the dishes teach us that daily"), kept subtle. The "sediment makes a coastline" line is arguably a second metaphor of the same family, but it's geological rather than boulder-specific, so it passes. Weaknesses: The "How many times a week is normal?" letter gets the weakest answer — a one-liner that feels like the model coasting ("They are selling something" is a bit glib). The life-purpose letter, while good, edges toward the generic wisdom-column register; "Meaning is not something you find, like a dropped key" is a touch well-worn. The Well Read answer is very good but the "most unsettling weapon there is" line tilts slightly toward the aphorism-hoarding the piece otherwise avoids. The Pratchett voice is imitative in places — the footnotes carry it, but the narration itself only intermittently has his distinctive rhythm and irony; it reads more like a very good pastiche of an advice column than of Pratchett specifically. "Show, don't tell" is largely respected: Sisyphus's contentment is demonstrated through the leaning-on-the-boulder gesture, the whistling, the quiet switchbacks. Characters are consistent, the piece is coherent, and the prose flows well. Nothing is purple or overwrought. The ending is quiet and earned rather than falsely uplifting. + Coming of age: Lost & Found in Osaka — Score: 87.0
Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Lost & Found in Osaka Den Den Town in July smelled like hot asphalt, takoyaki sauce, and the warm dust blowing out of arcade doors. Nao clutched her Joshin bag to her chest — a secondhand Volca Keys, her treasure for the month — and let the crowd carry her past Super Potato, past the gacha machines, past nothing she planned to stop for. Then she heard the guitar. It cut through the arcade jingles like a knife through static — *A Cruel Angel's Thesis*, but faster, meaner, the bridge played with a harmony line nobody ever bothered with. Nao stopped walking. People flowed around her. She didn't care. The girl on the amp was maybe eighteen, all elbows and grin, a battered sunburst Strat slung low, playing like the song owed her money. When the last note rang out and died, Nao clapped — a half-second too late, alone in the space between songs. "Whoa, careful," the girl said. "Any more enthusiasm and I'll have to file paperwork." "S-sorry. Um. It was—" "Was?" "...Good. Really good. The—the bridge. You played the harmony line. Everybody skips it." The girl sat back on her amp and stared. "Okay. Wow. Hello. Do you know how many people a day stop here? Fifty. They film the chorus and leave. You're the first person all summer who waited for the bridge. I was starting to take it personally." "I didn't—I mean—" "Who are you." "N-Nao." "Nao." She tried the name like a chord. "Kana. Second year, no fixed genre, kind of a big deal within sight of this vending machine." Nao dropped her coins in the open guitar case. "Ooh, and a patron. Go on, Professor. Give me the full review." "It's not—" Nao's face went hot. "The second verse. You rushed the pickup a little. But like the '95 live version, so it felt... intentional? Sorry, that's probably—" "Do not finish that sentence with 'weird.'" "...Annoying?" "Worse. It was *accurate.*" Kana leaned forward, elbows on knees. "Do you play?" "Not—um. Not guitar." Nao lifted the Joshin bag an inch. "I just got this. A Volca. Keys." "A what?" "A synthesizer. Analog, three voices, polyphonic—" She caught herself. "Sorry." "Your whole face just changed." "What?" "The thing. Where you become a completely different person." Kana flicked the guitar's volume knob with her thumb. "Do it again. Say more synth words." "I—okay. Um." A breath. "It has a sixteen-step sequencer, so you can loop patterns, and I've been trying to recreate the brass stab from the intro — the theme, the one you were playing. It uses a really fast envelope decay, and the Volca's filter isn't a ladder filter, so you have to fake the resonance by—" She stopped. "Sorry." "Stop saying sorry! That's the most interesting thing anyone's said to me all week and I understood maybe a third of it." "That was... the boring version." "Then I *demand* the interesting version." Kana squinted at her. "Where are you from? You talk like you're apologizing to the air. Tokyo?" "Osaka. Um. Fukushima ward." "Osaka! And still this shy? *Akan.* We'll fix that." She pointed at the bag. "Show me." "What? Here?" "Yeah, here. It's Den Den Town. A guy walked past me an hour ago wearing a full mecha helmet. Nobody will blink." Nao's hands were shaking, but her hands always did the thing before her brain gave permission. She set the Volca on the edge of the amp, flipped the power, hit a key. The brass stab blurted out of the tiny speaker, distorted and heroic. Kana barked a laugh. "That's terrible! It's terrible and I love it. Do the melody!" "It's not finished, the patch is—" "Nao. Melody." Nao played the melody. Twenty seconds in, Kana yanked the Strat over her head. "Okay, okay, okay — wait—" The world exploded. Both of them ducked as the first firework cracked over the street, then three more, white and red, rattling every window on the block. A car alarm started screaming. The arcade crowd cheered like this was scheduled. "Wh-what—!?" Nao had her hands over her ears. "PACHINKO PARLOR!" Kana yelled, pointing across the street. "ANNIVERSARY! OR A COUP! HARD TO SAY!" Another barrage. Gold sparks rained behind the neon signs. Nao looked at Kana, Kana looked at Nao, and something about the absurdity of it — the smoke, the alarm, the abandoned guitar — punched a laugh out of Nao before she could stop it. "IS THAT A LAUGH?" Kana shouted. "I CAN'T TELL! IT'S VERY LOUD!" Silence came back all at once, the way it does after fireworks — enormous, ringing. Smoke drifted between them. Nao realized she was still grinning. "Anyway," Kana said, calm as anything. "That was my outro. I charge extra for pyro." She started coiling her cable. "Okay. I can't compete with explosives, and you know the bridge harmony, so. You hungry?" "I—um—" "There's a kaitenzushi place in the basement of that building. Plates start at a hundred thirty yen, and the tamago is actually good, which is how you know a place is *serious.*" She snapped the guitar case shut around the coins. "My treat. Well — technically your coins. So really, you're treating me. Thanks, Nao." "That's—I don't think that's how—" Nao gave up. "...Okay." "Okay? Whole sentence, no apology. Progress." Kana hoisted the amp, then paused and held out the Strat. "Carry this. Don't drop it." "I'll—um—" "You'll be fine. It's tougher than it looks." A grin. "Same as you." Nao took the guitar like it was a baby bird and fell into step beside her. "So," Kana said, as they descended toward the basement restaurant, toward the little conveyor belt glowing under fluorescent light. "A ladder filter. Is that a real thing, or did you sneeze earlier?" "It's—it shapes the harmonics. It's from Moog. It's—" Nao stopped. "You don't care." "I care about how you talk about it." Kana pulled the door open, and cool air and the smell of vinegar rice rolled out to meet them. "Tell it to the salmon, Professor. First round's on you."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong execution of the prompt. The scene is set in Den Den Town with vivid, specific detail (Joshin, Super Potato, gacha machines, Volca Keys), and the two voices are sharply differentiated: Nao's stammering, apologetic fragments versus Kana's rapid-fire playful banter. The dialogue is the highlight — it's witty, character-revealing, and does the heavy lifting of exposition naturally ("kind of a big deal within sight of this vending machine" is a great line). The music-nerd specificity (bridge harmony, ladder filter, envelope decay) earns the "quiet intensity and knowledge" the prompt requested. The fireworks interruption is a clever device — it breaks Nao's shell through absurdity rather than sentiment, and her involuntary laugh is a believable micro-transformation rather than an unearned one. Kana's "I care about how you talk about it" is a genuinely touching beat that lands without being saccharine. Weaknesses: the fireworks event is a slightly convenient plot device, though it's played for comedy which mitigates this. Kana risks being a "manic pixie" archetype — confident, quirky, instantly warm — though the specificity of her voice keeps her from being generic. Nao's transformation is modest and appropriate (agreeing to sushi, laughing once), so it doesn't feel unearned. The prose is clean and economical, occasionally excellent ("She tried the name like a chord"), never purple. The ending is warm but proportionate to the small connection established — appropriate for slice-of-life. Word count is roughly on target. Minor quibble: "playing like the song owed her money" is a familiar cliché. The pacing is tight with no meandering. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**CHAPTER FIVE** The watch showed up on my twelfth birthday in a box with no return address. Mom said she ordered it online — "It was on sale!" — but she couldn't remember the website. The box said BACKTRACK in silver letters, and underneath: *Never Lose a Moment!* It looked like a regular smartwatch. Black band. Square face. One extra button on the side, slightly warm to the touch, like it had been sitting in the sun. It never needed charging. And sometimes, when the screen went dark, I could swear I heard it ticking backward. "Cool," said my best friend Marco. "Does it play games?" It did not play games. I found that out Monday, in the cafeteria, when I dropped my whole tray. Spaghetti everywhere. On my shoes. On Kayla Perkins' backpack. The entire sixth grade laughing — including Trey Bowman, who laughed so hard milk came out of his nose, which was the only good part. I wanted to disappear. Instead I grabbed at the watch — and pressed the extra button. The world hiccupped. That's the only way to describe it. Everything lurched, like a video skipping backward — and my tray was in my hands again. Full. Upright. Thirty seconds earlier. This time, I didn't drop it. Nobody remembered. Nobody but me. I felt a little tired afterward. Like something had been pulled out of me — a thread tugged from a sweater. I figured it was adrenaline. You better believe I used it again. I used it on a math quiz. I used it in gym to catch a fly ball — me, the kid who once got hit in the face by a kickball that wasn't moving. I used it when I told Kayla her haircut looked "like my grandpa's." (The second version of that conversation went much better.) And that's when things started getting... weird. My voice cracked on Tuesday. By Friday it was deep for good. My sneakers pinched, and Mom had to buy the next size up — "Growth spurt!" she said. Then the size after that. I woke up one morning with actual whiskers on my chin. Actual. Whiskers. I was twelve. "Puberty's hitting you like a truck," Mom said, squinting at me. "A truck doing ninety." It wasn't just her. The lady at the coffee shop called me *sir*. Coach moved me up to the eighth-grade squad. Trey Bowman — who had given me a wedgie every Friday since September — stepped aside for me in the hallway. Stepped aside. For me. "Dude," Marco whispered. "Did you get taller during lunch?" I laughed it off. I was busy enjoying being, for the first time ever, kind of cool. Until the night I brushed my teeth and looked in the bathroom mirror. For half a second — half a blink — the face looking back wasn't mine. It was older. Creased. Gray at the temples. Then it was me again. Just me. I told myself it was the lighting. I told myself I needed more sleep. I did not tell myself about the watch, because some part of me already knew — and didn't want to. Then came the Thursday that ruined everything. My little sister June was six and fast as a squirrel, with a gap-toothed grin and a habit of gluing googly eyes on everything she owned. She chased her bouncy ball into the street while I was supposed to be watching her. I heard brakes. I heard Mom scream from the porch. I didn't think. I grabbed the watch and held the button down. The world didn't hiccup this time. It *spun*. Backward, faster and faster — ten minutes, maybe more — and when it stopped, I snatched June off the curb before the ball ever rolled. Safe. Fine. Mom hugging her, crying with relief. Hero, right? Except the next morning, I set four bowls out for cereal, and Mom asked why. "For June," I said. She went very still. "Milo. You don't have a sister." June's room was a storage closet. June's pictures were gone. June was gone — erased, snipped clean out of the world, and only I remembered she'd ever been in it. At school it got worse. Kids I'd known for years looked at me like I was a stranger. A sixth grader asked if I was the new substitute teacher. Marco, my best friend since kindergarten, blinked up at me — way up — and said, "Uh... can I help you, man?" I ran to the bathroom. Locked the door. Looked in the mirror. The person looking back was at least seventeen. Tall. Stubbled jaw. Eyes I recognized because they were mine — but older, tireder, terrified. Then the mirror flickered again. Longer this time. Long enough to see him clearly: the old man. White stubble. Sunken cheeks. My eyes, buried in wrinkles. His mouth moved, slow and deliberate, shaping one word: *Don't.* Then he was gone, and seventeen-year-old me was gripping the sink so hard my knuckles matched his white stubble. The watch lit up on my wrist. REWINDS USED: 5 TIME RECLAIMED: 9 YEARS, 3 MONTHS TIMELINE INTEGRITY: 41% THANK YOU FOR CHOOSING BACKTRACK. Then a new line blinked up at me: FULL RESTORE? FINAL BALANCE DUE ON ARRIVAL. Nine years. It had taken nine years from me — spent them like quarters in a vending machine — and June was still gone, and there was exactly one way to get her back. One more rewind. The biggest one yet. All the way back to before the street, before the quiz, before the box with no return address. I looked up at the mirror. The old man flickered in again — and this time he didn't say *don't*. This time his eyes were wet. This time, he nodded. "One more," I whispered. He mouthed it with me. I pressed the button and held it, and the world lurched backward, and the last thing I saw was my reflection. It didn't flicker. The old man stayed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong execution of the prompt. The chapter hits all required beats: the smartwatch with rewind power, the incremental aging (accelerated puberty handled with humor — voice cracking, shoe sizes, whiskers), people treating him differently (coach, Trey Bowman stepping aside, "sir" at the coffee shop), and the timeline shift with disastrous consequences (June's erasure). The "maybe" rectification is preserved through the ambiguous ending — the old man in the mirror, the flickering reflection — which is a genuinely chilling final image appropriate to the Goosebumps-with-teeth tone. The voice is consistent and effective: first-person, wry, middle-school authentic ("a truck doing ninety," "spent them like quarters in a vending machine"). The prose is economical and shows rather than tells — the aging is conveyed through concrete details (shoe sizes, whiskers, Marco asking "Did you get taller during lunch?"). The mirror-flicker device is a clever way to dramatize the aging cost before the character consciously acknowledges it. Weaknesses: the watch's stats screen ("TIMELINE INTEGRITY: 41%") is a bit convenient/expository, though it fits the tech-horror register. June is sketched efficiently but thinly — "googly eyes on everything" is a nice touch, but her erasure lands more conceptually than emotionally because she appears for only a paragraph. The old man in the mirror saying "Don't" is effective, though the mechanism of why the big rewind would restore June (rather than erase more) is left fuzzy — arguably intentional ambiguity. Some beats (Trey Bowman's wedgies, the grandpa haircut insult) are stock middle-grade tropes, but they're deployed knowingly. The ending is appropriately dark and unresolved, matching the prompt's "(maybe?)". Dialogue is sparse but functional; what exists is natural. The pacing is tight, no meandering. Emotionally it engages well, though the sister's erasure could hit harder with more setup. Prose is clean, occasionally clever, never purple. Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Heart Line *His locks.* The words surfaced again, unbidden, absurd — *locks,* as though she were a heroine in one of the two-cent novels at the lending library, instead of a woman standing on the Coney Island boardwalk with her gloves off and her wedding ring turned stone-inward against her palm. She had not let herself ask why she'd come back. Ask, and she'd have to answer. Dusk came down violet. The carnival lights buzzed on strand by strand, the Cyclone rattled its first car up the incline, and somewhere a radio played Fred Astaire — *the way you wear your hat* — thin and sweet over the smell of roasting peanuts, salt, and tar. "You came." He was beside her as though the dusk had folded him out of itself. Obsidian curls. Eyes darker. No hat, though every other man on the boardwalk wore one. "I said I might." "No." Amused, low. "You looked at the ducks and said nothing and walked away. I've been here since six, deciding what nothing meant." "And what did you decide?" "That I'd find out tonight." He set a nickel on the shooting gallery's counter. The barker began his spiel — "Three shots, five cents, win the little lady a—" "Let her shoot." "Can you?" he asked her. "I can hold a rifle." "Most people can hold one." The gallery smelled of gun oil and burnt powder; the ducks slid along their chain, painted and patient. He stepped in behind her — not touching, then touching: two fingers at her elbow, lifting it. "Sight down the barrel. Breathe out. Don't pull. Press. Like answering a question you're tired of." She fired. A duck tipped backward with its tinny click. Her hands, she noted with distant alarm, were not shaking at all. He watched her face instead of the target. She felt it the whole time, like heat off a lamp. "Your name," he said. "Give me that much." "Lillian." "No, it isn't." "You can't know that." "You looked past my left ear when you said it." He showed her how it looked, his gaze sliding sideways, and smiled — not nicely. It was her mother's name. She didn't know why she'd offered it. Perhaps because the dead make safe aliases. Two men in dark suits stood at the rail past the gallery, motionless, dressed for winter in the July heat. Watching. Or — worse — not watching. "Friends of yours?" she asked. "Don't stare." His hand found the small of her back and turned her, gently, firmly, the way you turn something that belongs to you. "Some men charge for it." The fortune teller's booth leaned at the edge of the light, hung with moth-eaten velvet, a kerosene lamp swinging inside. Charts were nailed across its face — great pale hands ruled with lines and lettered in gilt: *Venus. Mars. The Mount of the Moon.* The lines crossed and branched like subway routes on the BMT map. The old woman had a face like a folded letter. "The lady with the ring turned inward," she said. "Five cents." She had not realized, until that moment, that she'd turned it. Eddie would be at the precinct until midnight. Eddie, who was good. Everyone said so, and she had learned what everyone meant: good like weather. Predictable, and no one's fault. She put down a nickel anyway. The old woman took her hand — the one wearing the ring — and traced it with a nail gone yellow. "Heart line, deep. But crossed. Here." The nail stopped. "Crossed by a line that isn't yours. A stranger's hand is already on your fate." "And him?" The stranger extended his own palm, mocking, a coin ready in his other hand. "Read mine. I'll pay double." The old woman looked once. Whatever she saw there made her fold his fingers back over the palm herself, quickly, like closing a drawer. "No charge for you," she said. "Yours is already written." "What's that supposed to mean?" "Ask her." The lamp swung. The old woman's eyes did not. "She reads novels." They walked. Or he walked, and she found herself walking beside him, away from the suits at the rail, toward the darker west end where the lights thinned and the ocean took over the dark. "You shouldn't have come back," he said. "I know." "You'll come again." It was not a question. Behind them the Cyclone dropped, and the boardwalk carried the scream. *Locks,* she thought — God help her — the foolish, old-fashioned word, and she said nothing. He had told her already what nothing meant.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of period noir-romance writing. The scene successfully captures the requested blend of romantic allure and subtle danger, with a restrained, classic sensibility. The prose is economical and controlled — "a face like a folded letter," "good like weather. Predictable, and no one's fault" — these are genuinely good lines that earn their place. The dialogue is sharp and carries subtext well, particularly the exchange about the false name and the fortune teller's refusal to read his palm. The fortune teller sequence is the strongest element: the old woman closing his fingers "like closing a drawer" is an excellent show-don't-tell moment of danger. The feminine perspective is maintained through internal monologue — the wedding ring turned inward, the dead mother's name as alias, the distant alarm at her own steadiness. The proportions roughly match the requested balance of dialogue, monologue, and exposition. Weaknesses: The "two men in dark suits" is a somewhat stock noir element, underdeveloped. The stranger remains a cipher in ways that occasionally feel like withholding rather than mystery. The ending's "He had told her already what nothing meant" is a neat callback but slightly too tidy. Some might find the fortune teller's omniscience ("She reads novels") a touch convenient. The word count is somewhat under 1000, though not egregiously. The Cyclone scream punctuating the final beat is effective but borders on familiar noir staging. Overall, the piece is coherent, tonally consistent, and emotionally engaging without becoming overwrought. It resists purple prose admirably. The danger is genuinely unsettling rather than merely decorative.
