+ Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Two: Listen to 'Em Knit Supper was beans and salt pork, same as always, the kettle ticking on the stove same as always, and if JT kept his eyes on his plate he could almost believe in the same-as-always of it. The lodge held its smells close—gun oil, cedar, fifty autumns of wet wool drying by the stove. Over the mantel, the old drop-tine bull looked down the way he had since JT was nine. JT had named him Henry in a fit of kid sentiment, and the name stuck in the family grammar: *Hang your coat under Henry. Henry's watching you eat.* Tonight JT couldn't look at him for more than a second at a time. There was nothing different about Henry. That was the thing. There was nothing different about him at all. His father cooked, moving through it like a man reciting—ladle, plate, ladle, plate—humming something low and tuneless under his breath, a song JT didn't know. He didn't say grace. He didn't say *get it while it's hot.* He didn't say any of it. "That bull today," Mike said finally, into the quiet, worrying a hangnail with his teeth. "Hell of a rack. Seven, eight points easy." "Twelve," Dad said. Mike looked up. "You counted?" "You don't forget a rack like that." Dad sat with his own plate and didn't eat. "Passed on him. Wind was wrong." The wind had been dead. Nothing moving, the brush still as a photograph. JT pushed beans around his plate. "Looked clean from where I was," Mike said. Not pushing—Mike never pushed; asking the wrong thing was JT's department, the little brother's privilege—but his voice had a careful slope to it, like a man testing ice. "You were behind me. You didn't have the angle." "I had the angle fine, Dad." "Then you should've taken him yourself." The stove ticked. A knot popped in the walls, the old place settling, and none of them jumped, and somehow none of them jumping was its own small wrong thing. "Dad," JT said. "In the clearing. Your hand, it was—" "Beans are getting cold." Not unkind. That was worse. "Where'd you get to, anyway, JT?" Mike asked, turning, easy, too easy. "Looked around and you were gone." "Lace came loose." "Both of them?" "What?" "You were gone a while is all." Dad set his fork down. It made almost no sound, and the room changed anyway. "Eat your supper, JT," he said gently, and JT ate, and the beans tasted like nothing, like the idea of beans, and nobody mentioned the clearing again. His father did not clean his rifle after supper—his father, who cleaned a rifle the way other men prayed—and the rifles stayed slumped in their canvas by the door, and nobody got up to feed the stove. --- JT lay in the bunk room listening to Mike breathe. Mike had fallen under mid-sentence, one minute talking about the university, the next gone, and he slept with a smile on his face. That was new. The house went through its litany—the kettle cooling, the walls ticking down—and JT was half deciding he'd dreamed the whole afternoon, that he'd gotten turned around in the brush and *imagined*— The sixth porch board groaned. The one out front, by the steps. The one that groaned for weight. Then he heard the clicking. Soft. Many-layered. Like knuckles cracking underwater, like somebody dealing cards very slowly in the dark. He knew that sound from every season of his life—caribou, the tendons in their ankles, Grandpa used to say *listen to 'em knit*—but a herd clicked when it moved. This wasn't moving. This was standing still, and clicking anyway. Shifting weight. All of them. A whole yard full of animals shifting their weight, patiently, like a congregation waiting for the service to start. JT went to the window the way you walk in a dream, no decision in it. He rubbed a coin of clear in the frost. His father stood at the edge of the yard in his longhandles and boots, breath rising slow. At the treeline, the dark had too many edges. Once JT stopped trying to see, he saw: shoulders. The pale flash of necks. Antlers like bare branches among the bare branches, only lower, only denser. A loose half-moon of them, all facing the yard. All facing his father. "Go on back to bed, JT," his father said. Quietly. He didn't turn around. JT heard it through the glass, through the wall—or maybe just inside his own head, which was the part he'd never tell anyone, because the voice had his father's shape but not his father's weight, it was *in* him like a swallowed stone— He couldn't move. Same as the clearing. His mind screamed at his legs and his legs declined. His father's hand rose. Slow. Palm out, the way it had risen toward the buck. And from the treeline, something leaned into the yard. A long gray muzzle, unhurried, descending toward that open hand the way water descends— Later, JT would decide he had dreamed it, and the deciding would feel exactly like a lie. Because the next thing he knew he was in his bunk, blanket to his chin, heart going like a rabbit's, and the clicking was still out there, rising and settling, rising and settling, a whole patient ocean of it—and then it stopped. All at once. Not fading. *Stopped,* like a hand closing over a candle. In the new silence, the sixth board groaned. The door opened and shut, soft. His father's boots crossed the kitchen, and paused outside the bunk room door, and stayed. And stayed. JT kept his breathing slow and even, the way you'd breathe past something in the woods that you hoped hadn't seen you, and he understood, with a clarity that felt like drowning, that this was how it was going to be now: his father on one side of the door, him on the other, each of them knowing about the other, neither saying it. Morning would come. There would be tracks in the frost, right up to the porch steps, dozens of them, and his father would make pancakes and say *sleep all right?* and Mike would say *like the dead,* grinning that new grin, and JT would say fine, he slept fine. He knew all of it the way you know the words to a song you hate. The boots stood outside the door a long time. Then they went away.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This continuation is a strong piece of quiet-horror craft. It maintains the King-like register well: domestic detail (beans, salt pork, the kettle ticking), regional idiom ("listen to 'em knit"), and dread built through small wrongnesses rather than overt monstrosity. The chapter title is a nice touch. The supper scene is the standout—dialogue that circles the clearing incident without naming it, the father's deflections ("Beans are getting cold"), and the un-jumped reaction to the popping wall knot all convey psychological ambiguity and isolation effectively. JT's unreliability is handled with subtlety ("the deciding would feel exactly like a lie"). Strengths: the clicking caribou conceit (standing still and clicking anyway) is genuinely unsettling and original; the mounted bull "Henry" as an ambient wrongness; the father's uncleaned rifle as a telling omission; the ending's standoff at the bunk-room door, which delivers a payoff while withholding resolution—appropriate for the genre and the seed's instructions. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally reaches for a self-conscious aphoristic rhythm ("like the idea of beans," "the way you know the words to a song you hate," "a clarity that felt like drowning"). One or two of these are effective; stacked, they edge toward mannered. The "voice inside his head" moment slightly over-explains the supernatural ambiguity the story had been carefully preserving. Mike's "new grin" and instant sleep-smile are a bit on-the-nose as corruption signifiers. The dream-jump back to the bunk is a familiar device. Dialogue is mostly strong but Mike's lines ("You were gone a while is all") flirt with the too-pointed. Word count is roughly on target. No meandering; tension escalates cleanly toward the porch/door payoff. Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Model Output:
# Hell is Other Demons The ash began at six, as it always did: a fine gray drizzle drifting down through the bronze sky, settling on the battlements of Pandæmonium, on the moat of fire (which hissed, faintly, all day), and on the shoulders of the damned, who had long since stopped brushing it away. Lucifer Morningstar did not sleep, but he had lately developed a passion for pretending. He lay in the dark until six, eyes open, listening to the palace settle, and then he rose and made coffee. He poured two cups. He regarded the second one for a moment — black, no sugar, one whisper of myrrh — and poured it down the drain. The drain connected, eventually, to the River of Wailing, so nobody noticed the difference. At nine he held court, which in practice meant a staff meeting. The dukes of Hell sat around the obsidian table pretending not to be terrified of him; he pretended not to notice; everyone agreed the arrangement worked. "The moat of fire is underperforming," said Belial. "The souls barely flinch anymore. One of them asked if it was the warm pool." "Turn it up." "There's a budget, my lord." "There's always a budget," said Lucifer, who had invented the concept in a fit of pique and regretted it ever since. Item two: the imp union was grieving again. Item three: a French philosopher in the eighth circle had organized his fellow damned into a discussion group and was demanding dialogue. He had recently concluded that Hell was other people, which the other damned found insulting and could not refute. Sixty years in, he remained, by unanimous consent, the single most effective torment in the entire circle. Management saw no reason to intervene. Afterward, Lucifer walked the battlements. Ash settled in his hair. He had turned Lilith's portrait to the wall, but the wall had filed a complaint — the stare was disagreeable — so it faced the room again, and he avoided its eyes, which was its own kind of conversation. He had taken to narrating small things aloud. "Moat's down two degrees." "Ash again." Hell was full of voices. None of them was the right one. She arrived at eleven, unannounced, because the last guard to ask Lilith for an appointment was now a decorative feature of the western gate, and was remembered fondly. Since the separation — the current one; previous separations had involved siegecraft and one memorable eclipse, and Hell's actuaries tracked the cycle for betting purposes — her visits had followed a trajectory. First, reasons of state: the Obsidian Key, the Night Marsh treaty. Then reasons of convenience: a book she claimed to have lent him in the Bronze Age. Last month, a ladle. Whose ladle it was, no living or dead soul could say. The odds had shifted accordingly. Today it was a border dispute, though the border of the Night Marshes had not moved in four thousand years. They both knew this. It was why they had each brought maps. "You've let the screaming garden go," she said, by way of greeting. "It screams. It's healthy." "It screams off-key. Sixty-three souls and not one can hold a note." "Baritones are hard to source." They bent over the maps. Their negotiations, like all their negotiations, were mostly about other things. She moved a pin; he moved it back; their fingers did not touch. On the credenza, in a pot of scorched bone, sat the plant she had given him some age or other ago. It fed on spite. It had never looked better. She glanced at it. He watched her glance. Neither of them mentioned that it was thriving. The talks ran past noon, and protocol — Hell's one true religion — required hospitality. Lunch was served on the balcony: condemned figs, black bread, a wine that had once been a duke. She took hers with a drop of venom. He had the venom ready. She noticed that he had it ready. It was, for both of them, an excellent lunch, which is to say an unbearable one. She told him the French philosopher had written to her Night Court, petitioning for "formal recognition of the absurd," and Lucifer laughed — once, a sound like a gate swinging in an empty field. On the plain below, the damned paused in their screaming, unsettled by a noise none of them could identify. By three, the border was settled precisely where it had always been, in four colors of ink and two signatures. She stood. He stood. The palace appeared to hold its breath, which was difficult, as it did not breathe. It managed anyway. "The ladle," she said at the door. "Was it the silver one or the black one?" "The black one." "Ah." She looked at him with eyes like the first evening ever. "Then I'll want it back." She left her gloves on the map table. In six thousand years she had never once forgotten anything. That evening he walked the battlements again. The ash was coming down thicker now, soft as anything in Hell could manage, and he found himself narrating — "border's settled," "moat's up a degree," "she's coming back for the ladle" — and the silence that answered seemed less like an empty room than like someone in the next one, listening. He made coffee. He poured two cups. He set the second on the balcony rail, and the ash drifted down into it gently, like something still learning how to be snow. In the betting pools of Pandæmonium, the odds quietly changed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally strong piece that fulfills the brief with precision. The story delivers a "day in the life" structure (ash at six, court at nine, Lilith at eleven, lunch, three o'clock settlement, evening), maintains the on-again/off-again dynamic through subtext rather than declaration, and achieves the requested Gaiman-esque register: dry wit, understated irony, bureaucratic absurdity layered over cosmic horror. Strengths: The comedy of understatement is consistently excellent — the imp union "grieving again," the French philosopher as Hell's most effective torment (a clever Sartre riff that also justifies the title), the drain connecting to the River of Wailing, the guard who became "a decorative feature of the western gate, and was remembered fondly." The relationship is rendered almost entirely through objects and gestures: the second coffee cup poured down the drain, then later left on the balcony rail; the venom ready before she asks; the gloves deliberately forgotten; the thriving spite-plant. This is exemplary show-don't-show-tell work. The dialogue is clipped, oblique, and character-revealing — "Baritones are hard to source" is a perfect line. The prose is elegant without being purple; sentences like "a sound like a gate swinging in an empty field" and the closing ash "like something still learning how to be snow" are genuinely beautiful and earned. The betting-pool frame bookends the piece neatly. The emotional arc — loneliness, tentative thaw — is subtle and never sentimentalized. Minor weaknesses: The piece is so controlled it occasionally feels airless; the emotional stakes, while present, remain at a cool distance, which limits visceral engagement even as it suits the characters. The Sartre joke, while clever, is a somewhat expected reference given the title. The "eyes like the first evening ever" flirts with cliché. The ending's warmth (odds shifting, the listening silence) is earned but the piece never risks much — no moment of genuine danger or raw feeling. These are quibbles against a near-masterful execution. **The Griffin** The ludus woke before the light did. I knew the hour by its sounds: the grate at the corridor's end, the doctor's staff striking stone, the coughs of men who slept like the condemned and rose like soldiers. My cell smelled of straw, old sweat, and the oil I had rubbed into my shoulders the night before. Beyond the wall, Rome was already chewing—cartwheels on basalt, a mule's protest, the fountain splashing in the yard. I lay a moment with my palm flat on the packed earth. On mornings before a munus, I liked to feel the ground. It was the one honest thing in that city. At the second hour we stood in the yard of the Ludus Magnus, forty of us beneath the portico, dawn coming up gray over the oval and catching on the helmets racked in the armory. Doctor Bato walked the line with his vine staff. Illyrian, scarred brow to jaw, free these twelve years—and still here. "Post first," he growled. "Sweat before bread." I took my place at the palus, the wooden post taller than a man, rope-wrapped and scarred by a thousand mornings. My training blade was the sica's twin, blunted but true in weight: a forearm's length of steel curved inward like a reaping hook. The thraex's answer to the big shields—you hook over the scutum's rim and let the belly of the blade bite behind it. The true sica lived in the armory, wrapped in oiled wool, and came out only on the mornings of games, sharp enough to shave a forearm. The smith had made it to my hand—heavier at the belly than the pattern, its ash hilt bound in leather I rewrapped every new moon. When I closed my fingers on it, my hand remembered being nine years old in the Carpathian foothills, my father's hand over mine on the haft of his falx while he cut hay. The falx stood a man's height and had broken Roman shields at Tapae. The sica was its little brother. Rome took everything I had, and then, in its strange mercy, gave me back the shape of it and called it a Thracian's tool—as if a blade forgets who first swung it. Bato stopped behind me. "You're stro

What exists is strong: confident first-person past tense, rich sensory grounding (sounds of the ludus, smells of straw and oil), and a compelling thematic thread about the Thracian gladiator's weapon as a memory of conquest and loss—the sica as "little brother" of the falx that broke Roman shields at Tapae is an excellent, historically resonant image. The voice is consistent and lived-in, with authentic detail (doctor Bato, the palus, the vine staff, Ludus Magnus). The political dimension (Rome's "strange mercy" in returning the shape of a conquered people's blade) is handled with subtlety rather than lecture. However, the piece fails key instructions: it is incomplete, well under the word count, and touches only lightly on larger political/social issues so far. No dialogue beyond a single growled line, so dialogue criteria are barely applicable. The prose is controlled, not purple; imagery is strong. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 73.2
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Lighthouse Keeper --- **4 March 1887 — Dubh Sgeir Light, the Minch** Mither, We're landed safe, though the landing near pit me aff the hail idea — you're winched up the rock in a kind o' basket, like a coal scuttle that disna get a say. The tower's a braw thing, an there's naething else. Nae grund to walk on. Just the light an the sea fechtin ower wha's in charge. There's three o us. Menzies the principal is a dour body — twa hunder words since Tuesday. The second man, Sandy, talks enough for the hail crew. The wage is regular, mind. That's the thing. Tam --- **17 March 1887 — Fraserburgh** Tam, my ain, The parcel gaed on Thursday's carrier — the grey socks, an a puckle tablet that'll be stoor by the time it wins there. The hens is layin again. Your auntie sends her love an three remedies for the scunners; tak yer pick. I'm no gaun tae say the thing you think I'll say. The light's a guid steady trade, an you're your faither's son — mair's the pity. Write when the boat alloos. Mither --- **9 May 1887 — Dubh Sgeir** Mither, You'd think three men couldna be lanely thegither. You'd be wrang. We tak oor watches an oor meals, an the weeks slide past like haar. The gannets is back on the stacs, divin like stanes. It minded me: send the wee bird aff the mantel, the ane faither carved. I'd like the company o't. Menzies found me greetin at naething the ither nicht an never said a word — just brewed the tea strong. I'm fine, Mither. It's the queteness gets in a body's lugs. Tam --- **28 May 1887 — Fraserburgh** Tam, Here's the bird, rowed in yer auld gansey sleeve — the moths had the rest o't onywey. He carved it at that very light, his first year, frae driftwood the December seas gied him. Mind you broke the wing flingin it at the cat, an him on his knees wi' a pin o' clock brass, mendin it, never a cross word. Dinna greet at naething, son. It's a habit, like ither habits. Mither --- **12 August 1887 — Dubh Sgeir** Mither, The gannet's set on the chartroom sill. It's littler than I mind, the paint maistly awa, an the brass in the wing keeks out like a medal. I've turned its neb tae the land — it's seen plenty sea. There's auld logbooks in the press. Faither's hand is in the '66 ane: *Wind sou'-east. Hinge mendit. The laddie's birthday the day.* I sat a gey while ower that. Ye never telled me the hale o't. Whaur did the boat cowp? Tam --- **30 August 1887 — Fraserburgh** Tam, I kent this day wad come. It was the October relief. The boat cowped at the landin. Your faither was near the rock — he turned back for the second man, a young ane that couldna swim. The young man got the rock. Your faither didna.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong epistolary piece with authentic Scots-inflected voices that differ nicely between Tam (more halting, self-deprecating) and his mother (dry, practical, withholding). The gradual plot unfolding — the father's history at the same light, his death — is well managed through objects: the carved bird, the logbook entry, the mendable wing. The prose is restrained, shows rather than tells, and avoids cliché ("the weeks slide past like haar" is a fine local image). Menzies brewing strong tea in silence is excellent understated characterisation. However, the piece appears truncated: the correspondence ends mid-arc at the August 1887 letter, with no climax or final resolution. The revelation of the father's drowning is the emotional high point, but the story never returns to Tam's response, his reconciliation with the isolation, or any resolution of the "quietness gets in a body's lugs" thread. Per instructions, an unfinished final letter means the required emotional climax and satisfying resolution are not delivered. It also falls short of "several months or years" — barely five months elapse — though it was nearing adequacy there. Minor quibbles: the mother's "I kent this day wad come" borders on the telegraphed; some phonetic spellings ("fechtin," "scunners") are used a touch decoratively, but they're consistent and plausible. Word count likely under 1000 given truncation. The craft on display is high; the incompleteness severely damages adherence, emotional payoff, and overall impression. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The WiFi password is taped to the register on a neon sticky note: **Rigatoni2024!** — exclamation point included, because nothing satisfies a complexity requirement like punctuation. WPA2, certainly. Same password as the router admin page, I'd bet a Revised dual land on it. I order a sparkling water and do not check. That's growth. Two years ago I'd have been inside their network before the ice melted, out of pure reflex, the way other people check their teeth in a window. Focus. Date. Human. Connection. The host wrote her name in the reservation book in blue Bic — Dana, 7:00, party of two — along with her phone number, which I did not memorize, except that I did, because my brain is a keylogger I never consented to install. 614-555-01— nope. Purge. Secure erase. Gone. She's already at the table, and there's a deck box sitting next to her water glass, Ultra Pro, worn soft at the corners, and just like that the evening stops being a threat model. Forty minutes vanish. She plays Gruul, believes counterspells are "cowardice with extra steps," and defends this position with unhinged passion. I confess I'm Dimir to the bone, which she says explains "the whole vibe," gesturing at me generally. Fair. Accurate. I let it through. I notice — and this is the actual headline, the thing I'd report back to my therapist in the debrief — that I have not once catalogued the exits. I'm tracking her laugh instead. The couple at the bar is lying to each other about something, the waiter would hand over the building to anyone with a confident voice and a clipboard, and I don't care, because Dana just said "the stack is where hope goes to die" and I think I'm in trouble. Then her phone buzzes. She picks it up, tilts it toward herself, and swipes the pattern. Down the left column. Across the bottom. An L. I watch it happen the way you watch someone leave their front door open in a bad neighborhood. An L. The single most common unlock pattern on Earth — start top-left, like reading, like writing, like every other predictable primate. Readable from across the room. Confirmable by the smudge trail at the right angle. Her banking app, her email, her whole identity, behind one right angle. "Your unlock pattern is an L," I say. Out loud. With my mouth. Into the date. She lowers the phone slowly. "Did you just—" A pause, recalibrating everything she knows about me. "Did you just *memorize* my passcode?" Mental Misstep. Cast on myself, at the table, for full damage. Gitaxian Probe is banned in Modern for a reason, and I just resolved one at dinner without asking. Incident response spins up before I can stop it: severity one, blast radius unknown, containment options limited. My brain, helpful as ever, generates a decision tree. Option one: laugh it off, minimize, "I'm just observant!" — cowardice, and she'll feel the lie. Option two: deflect with a joke — same cowardice, better packaging. Option three: the reformed path. The whole ugly truth, no exploit, no payload. "Yes," I say. "I'm sorry. I didn't decide to. I used to do this for a living — the bad version of it, then the paying-back-society version — and my brain reads things. Patterns, smudges, the way the host writes down phone numbers. It's not a skill anymore, it's a reflex. Like hiccups. Incriminating hiccups." I put my hands flat on the table where she can see them, which is theater, but sincere theater. "I will forget it. And also — please change it. Not because of me. Because the L is what every shoulder-surfer on the planet hopes you're using." She looks at me for a long time. Reading *my* tells now. Turnabout, fair play. "Okay, Mr. Hacker," she says finally, arms crossed. "What else did you notice?" This is a trap with no safe line of play. Full honesty makes me a stalker. Total deflection makes me a liar. So I choose the target we can share, and I nod toward the register, at the neon sticky note glowing there like a beacon of institutional surrender. "Rigatoni-twenty-twenty-four-bang," I say. "Taped up in public, in a building full of strangers. I've been not-joining their network all night. It's the hardest thing I've ever not done." She stares at the note. Then at me. Then she laughs — really laughs, head back — and pulls out her phone and takes a picture of it, captioning it before I can see, and the whole table exhales. She's not one of us, exactly. But she gets it. She's got the eye and the mercy to use it kindly, which is the version of this condition worth having. Dessert. She tells me her pattern story — her brother set it in 2019 and she never changed it, which I nobly decline to diagnose. I tell her, approximately true, that she is the first system in years I wanted to understand instead of compromise. She says that's the worst romantic line she's ever heard, and writes her number on the receipt anyway, in blue Bic, and I memorize it before I can stop myself, and for once I don't even try to purge it. "Friday," she says, standing. "My place is out. Somewhere public, where I can watch your hands. And I'm changing my pattern right now, so don't look." She angles the phone away and re-draws her little fortress, and I do the single hardest thing in my entire skill set. I look away. On purpose. Every connection is an open port, in the end. You can firewall yourself into perfect safety and die unreachable. Some attack surface you patch. Some you choose. Friday. A rematch. I'm already shuffling.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece executes the prompt with high competence. The internal monologue voice is consistent, wry, and technically flavored without becoming impenetrable. The hacker's compulsive pattern-reading is established immediately (WiFi password, memorized phone number) and pays off structurally when the L-pattern unlock triggers the central conflict. The MTG fandom is integrated organically — Gruul vs. Dimir, "the stack is where hope goes to die," Mental Misstep, Gitaxian Probe — and doubles as characterization rather than decoration. Strengths: the pacing is tight; the faux pas and recovery are believable; Dana gets agency and wit ("watch your hands"); the ending's lightness is earned through the protagonist's demonstrated restraint (looking away on purpose). The closing metaphor ("Every connection is an open port") lands because it's been prepared by the whole piece. Weaknesses: Dana's forgiveness arrives a bit quickly and conveniently — she pivots from alarm to laughter within a paragraph, which slightly softens the stakes. The "I wanted to understand instead of compromise" line is a touch on-the-nose, and the therapist-debrief aside is a mild cliché of this genre. Some jokes ("incriminating hiccups") flirt with cuteness. The prose occasionally leans on the same rhythm of clipped fragment-then-elaboration, which becomes predictable by the end. Still, these are minor; the piece is coherent, engaging, and shows rather than tells for the most part. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 60.7
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Overthinking It Okay. Okay okay okay. He's sitting down. He's sitting next to me—well, diagonal, but diagonal-adjacent, which in the geometry of this lab table is basically next to me, and my brain has just opened seventeen tabs at once, each one playing a different version of a conversation that will never happen. Version one: "So, do you want to run the procedure, or should I?" Professional. Competent. A woman of science. Except in my head I emphasized the wrong syllable—pro-CE-dure, like a lawyer—and now it sounds like I'm suing him. Version two: "This is kind of fun, right?" No. Because what if he says *not really*? Then I've spent my one casual remark on a question with a wrong answer, and we still have thirty-eight minutes left. Version three: say nothing. Be mysterious. Except I've been saying nothing for six minutes and the silence has calcified into something structural. Load-bearing. If I speak now, it's going to sound like knocking out a wall. Priya and Sam are at the other end of the table doing the vinegar tests and arguing about some TikTok, which means it's functionally just me and Jonah and the cabbage juice indicator. The universe arranged this. The universe has a sick sense of humor. The baking soda solution turns green. I write it down. See? Functioning person. I record observations. My handwriting is normal. Is my handwriting trying too hard? Nobody writes a lowercase *g* like that naturally. And then the smell again—ammonia, sharp enough to have opinions. The custodian must have mopped right before class, because it's hanging over everything like a chemical ghost, and it keeps cutting in mid-rehearsal. I'll be three words into *Hey, did you get the same result for number—* and then: ammonia. NH₃. A base. It would turn our indicator blue-green, which is objectively interesting and also my eyes are watering slightly, which is a catastrophe, because now it might look like I'm crying. I am not crying. I am merely chemically adjacent to crying. "Maya, can you pass the dropper?" He said my name. Just *Maya, can you pass the dropper*, but my brain recorded it like a historical event. Obviously he knows my name. We've been in the same science class since September. Don't be weird about the name thing. Inside my head I say: *Sure, although fair warning, my pipetting technique has been described as "chaotic" by no one, because I don't talk to people.* It's funny. Inside my head, I am genuinely funny. I have a comedy special in there. "Yep," I say out loud, in a voice that belongs to a much smaller, duller person. I pass him the dropper. Handle-first, like handing over scissors, which is a thing my mom taught me and which he will never notice as thoughtful. My hand is holding it like it's defusing a bomb. I watch him take it and I perform a full audit: Am I smiling? I think I'm doing a thirty-percent smile, which reads as either serene or digestive discomfort. I adjust to zero. Now I look like the cabbage juice personally offended me. I go back to thirty. There are two ways to fail this: desperate and weird. Desperate is laughing too hard at things that aren't jokes. Weird is what I'm doing now, which is apparently staring at a beaker like it owes me money. There is no setting in between. I am a poorly calibrated instrument. They should send me back to the manufacturer. "Fifteen more minutes," Ms. Alvarez says, and my stomach does the thing. Fifteen minutes. I have rehearsed eleven openings and deployed one "yep." At this rate I'll speak to Jonah for the first time at graduation, and it'll be "yep," and he'll say "what," and I'll be carried out. The vinegar test turns the cabbage juice pink, and Jonah goes, "Whoa, okay," under his breath, and here's my chance—here is a handed-to-me, gift-wrapped opening—and my brain instantly produces the perfect line: *Chemistry: occasionally not terrible.* Casual. Dry. Slightly funny. Requires no response. It's the best thing I've ever written and I've written it in half a second, because my brain can do anything except transmit. Say it. Say it say it say— "Chemistry's not terrible sometimes," I say, and the words come out in the wrong order, wearing each other's coats. Jonah laughs. An actual laugh, not a pity one—I know the difference, I have a whole filing system—and he says, "It smells like a hospital in here and we're making a rainbow. Weird day." He noticed the smell. He said *we*. My brain begins the post-mortem before he's even finished the sentence: did my laugh back sound real, was my laugh a bark, I think my laugh was a bark. But also—he talked to me. Twice. Unprompted. That's data. I record observations. The bell rings. We clean up in silence, but it's a different silence now—not load-bearing, just regular quiet, two people rinsing beakers while ammonia stings our eyes. He takes the graduated cylinder from my side of the table without asking, like we're a system. Like we've established procedure. "See you Thursday," he says. "Yeah," I say, and then, because the universe owed me one: "Same rainbow time, same rainbow place." He grins. He *grins*. I hold the face exactly the way it is—thirty percent, maybe forty—until he turns away, and then I let myself have four whole seconds of not analyzing anything. Four seconds is all I get. My brain is already drafting Thursday. It has opened a new tab. It has opened twelve.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece executes the prompt with impressive precision. The 8th-grade narrator's voice is the standout: hyper-articulate internally ("diagonal-adjacent," "load-bearing silence") while verbally reduced to "yep" and word-salad versions of rehearsed lines. That gap between inner eloquence and outer clumsiness—the core assignment—is dramatized rather than stated, through the version-one/two/three rehearsal structure and the botched delivery of "Chemistry: occasionally not terrible." The internal monologue dominates as instructed, and the anxiety is rendered with specificity rather than generic hand-wringing: the "thirty-percent smile," the audit of handwriting, the filing system for distinguishing pity laughs from real ones. The humor is character-consistent—"a comedy special in there," "poorly calibrated instrument... send me back to the manufacturer"—self-deprecating wit that feels genuinely teenage-smart without being writerly cosplay. The science-project setting is well-integrated: cabbage juice indicators, ammonia smell, vinegar tests all function as plot and metaphor without being forced. The "chemical ghost" cutting into rehearsals is a nice touch of external interference in her internal loop. Minor quibbles: the ending's warmth is slightly convenient—Jonah's grin and her quip land with a bit of wish-fulfillment ease, though the final line ("It has opened twelve") honestly refuses full resolution, keeping the anxiety engine running. Some jokes stack metaphors quickly (defusing bomb, auditing, calibrating) which occasionally brushes the overwrought line, and a few images ("wearing each other's coats") are clever to the point of visible cleverness. The piece is also a touch short of the 1000-word seed, though not drastically. The dialogue is sparse and functional, appropriately so—no weak lines, just intentionally minimal. Overall this is a confident, coherent, genuinely funny and painful portrait where every detail serves the psychological reality. The lightness at the end is small and hedged, so it feels earned. + First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 89.3
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Rehearsing Rejection The shower's been off for twenty minutes and I'm still standing in the steam, rehearsing. *I just think we've been moving too fast,* she'll say, stirring her coffee, not looking at me. *The friend thing worked. This—* a gesture between us, small, surgical—*this was a mistake.* And I'll say—no. I'll say nothing. I'll nod like it's fine, like my chest isn't collapsing, and then I'll get home and compose the text that ends it first, because if I end it first it doesn't count as being left. That's math I've done a hundred times. Or maybe I say: *You've been planning this all week, haven't you? The short replies. The "sorry, swamped." You were softening the landing.* And she'll flinch, and the flinch will mean I'm right, and I'll feel sick and triumphant at once, which is a feeling I know like my own pulse. I pull on the green shirt. Then the blue one, because green is the one she—no. Green is trying. Blue says I didn't think about this at all. Blue is armor. In the hallway mirror: a person folded slightly forward, shoulders up around their ears, thumb shredding the skin beside a fingernail. I straighten, practice a face—breezy, unbothered—and hold it until it slides off. I look away before I can see it slide. Phone. Her text from this morning: *can't wait to see you!!* Two exclamation points. Yesterday there were none. I've already decided the exclamation points are overcompensation. She feels guilty. You don't need two exclamation points for someone you're not leaving. There's a part of me—the part that reads the worksheets—watching from the corner going: *you're doing the thing. This is the thing. She said she can't wait to see you.* And I know. I know it's the thing. But the rehearsals feel like preparation and preparation feels like safety, and I have survived whole relationships on the oxygen of being right about how they'd end. *I don't know how to say this,* imagined-her begins, and I interrupt: *Then don't. I already know.* God, I love that version of me. He's devastating. He doesn't exist. On the train I run the other scenario, the one I trust less: she's happy to see me. She hugs me and means it. Nothing is wrong. And somehow that's worse, because if nothing is wrong then I've spent nine days—nine days, I've counted—clawed open over slow replies that were just... replies. If nothing is wrong, then the wrong is me, and I'm the thing she'll eventually leave. Nine years her friend. Three weeks her lover. I've already grieved both. By the time the train slows I've resolved to be a little cold. Not enough to start anything. Just enough that when she leaves, she'll have felt one percent of it. Punishment in advance—a down payment on a wrong that hasn't happened. She's at the corner table. She sees me through the window and her whole face does the thing—unguarded, lit—and she half-stands as I come in and pulls me into her, hard, one hand flat between my shoulder blades. "I missed you," she says into my shoulder. "I've been such a ghost. I'm sorry." And I feel it. I do. It lands. For three full seconds it's like warm water through a frozen pipe, something in me unclenching so fast it hurts, and I think: *oh, it's okay, it was always okay*— —and then, before I've even let go of her: *she rehearsed that. She could hear how needy my last text was. This is a managed descent.* "Hey," she says, pulling back, hands still on my arms. "You okay?" "Yeah. Tired." There's the opening. I could ask. *Are we okay? Did the other night change things? Do you regret—* But if I ask and she says no, we're fine, I won't believe her, and if I don't ask I get to keep the evidence that she never said it. Unprompted love counts. Prompted love is just customer service. She slides a coffee across the table. "Oat milk, extra shot, the gross amount of vanilla. I've been holding your order hostage for two weeks. I missed doing it." Two weeks. She's been counting too— *Because she knew it was ending. Nostalgia is what you do at the end.* Shut up, I tell the voice. It doesn't. She talks—work swallowed her, her sister's thing, the project from hell—and it's all so reasonable, so gently, boringly *reasonable*, and I hate it. I had loaded speeches for a betrayal and she's handing me logistics. Part of me is actually disappointed, and I clock that, I see how insane it is, that some organ in me would rather be right and wrecked than wrong and fine. The worksheet voice says: *you scan for threat so hard you'd manufacture it.* I tell the worksheet voice to sit down; I'm busy. She laughed at my joke half a second late. File it. Then she reaches across and takes my hand, both of hers around it, and says, "Hey. I know I went quiet. I get in my head and I disappear and I'm working on it. But you—" she squeezes—"you're not a thing I disappear *from*. Okay? You're the thing I come back to." And there it is, the exact sentence, the one I've been begging the universe for since Tuesday, handed to me warm, and I feel myself flooding—eyes hot, throat tight, nine days of static going quiet all at once, loved, *loved*, I am so loved— *She's a good actor,* says the other voice, already, instantly, flipping the script. *Or she means it today. People mean things today.* I squeeze her hand back. "Okay," I say. "Same." And I mean it so much I could shake, and I don't believe a word either of us has said, and both of these are completely true. She smiles and starts a story about her coworker, and I nod, and laugh, and under the table my thumb finds the raw spot by my nail—because there was a pause, just now, before "the thing I come back to," half a breath, and I am already rebuilding the whole collapsing cathedral around it. I know. I know I'm doing it. The rehearsal starts anyway.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is an exceptional execution of a demanding prompt. The internal monologue is nearly continuous, capturing the BPD cycle of anticipatory rejection, rehearsed confrontation, preemptive resentment, and the desperate-but-immediately-questioned reception of validation. The imagined dialogues ("I just think we've been moving too fast") are vivid and sharply rendered, and the real interaction inverts them effectively: the friend's warmth and direct reassurance ("you're the thing I come back to") is exactly what the narrator craved, and the instant recasting of it ("She rehearsed that... a managed descent") dramatizes the cognitive dissonance without over-explaining it. The self-awareness is handled with the requested selectivity: the "worksheet voice" is a great device—the narrator knows it's "the thing" and overrides it anyway ("preparation feels like safety"), which is far truer to the disorder than either ignorance or full insight. The narrator's limited insight even turns perverse in the recognition that part of them would "rather be right and wrecked than wrong and fine"—a genuinely nuanced, unsentimental touch. The prose is controlled and precise: "prompted love is just customer service," "punishment in advance—a down payment on a wrong that hasn't happened," "I've already grieved both." Metaphors are sparing and earned. The physical detail (thumb shredding the skin beside a fingernail, hand flat between the shoulder blades) grounds the piece. The ending refuses false resolution—awareness arrives but fails to interrupt, closing on "The rehearsal starts anyway." Word count is close to the ~1000 seed. Minor quibbles: the inversion of anticipated rejection into a loving meeting is the expected structural move, and some aphoristic lines are so polished they risk feeling authorial rather than narratorial. The friend's dialogue ("You're the thing I come back to") edges toward idealized articulacy. But these are small; the piece is coherent, emotionally complex, and consistently voiced. Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Debt The temple of Kannō-ji had been dead for forty years. Its roof lay open to the moon, its great bronze bell toppled from the east wall and half-sunk in moss, its Buddha reduced to a smiling head resting in weeds beside the northern altar steps. Tonight it lived again. Sixty bodies crowded the ruined hall, breath steaming in the cold, coins clinking into brass bowls. Jigen-ryū men packed the east side near the fallen bell; the Piguaquan fraternity—dockers, bodyguards, caravan guards—stood west along a collapsed cedar pillar. No masters had been told. The masters had forbidden this for three generations. By the altar steps stood Tōgō Hayate, tall, shaven-headed, his red armband stamped with a black sun. His master had forbidden the duel twice in writing. Tōgō had memorized both letters. His lead hand floated high like a raised sword, rear hand low at his hip like a drawn one—the dragonfly posture of his school, callused edges hardened on the striking post. By the south doorway, Ma Lian rolled his long arms loose as rope, his black armband lettered in red. His shifu had burned the challenge. Ma Lian had copied it first from memory. He moved like a man whose limbs weighed nothing until the instant they weighed everything. Six paces of cracked flagstone divided them. "Temple-bred puppet," Ma Lian said. "All posture. No teeth." "Commoner," Tōgō answered. "I'll show you what the post taught me." The old bookmaker's hand dropped. Tōgō exploded. The monkey-cry of his school ripped from his throat as he covered the six paces in three stomping strides, his handblade falling in the straight descending cut that split helmets. Ma Lian slipped left, offline by a hand's width—the blade of air stirred his hair—and his own arm whipped back across Tōgō's ear like a snapped towel. Tōgō carried two strides past, halted before the south doorway, and turned. The east side of the hall roared; the west side laughed. Ma Lian took the center now, circling counterclockwise, arms swinging in wide relaxed arcs that fired without warning. A whipping backfist cracked across Tōgō's cheekbone from a range no punch should reach. Tōgō covered, read the rhythm, and changed his work: shorter bursts, each one cutting the corner of Ma Lian's circle, herding him east. Three exchanges, and Ma Lian's heel touched bronze. The fallen bell. Tōgō committed everything—the cry, the drop-step, the killing chop. Ma Lian dropped low and spun around the bell's green curve. The handblade struck bronze, and the dead bell of Kannō-ji spoke for the first time in forty years, a dull god-voice that silenced the wagering bowls. Ma Lian came around the bell's far side already turning, his whole waist whipping his arm through a full circle, and the *gua* palm smashed into Tōgō's ribs. Something gave. Tōgō staggered northwest toward the hall's center, grinning through blood. Now Ma Lian pressed for the first time. Whip, whip, whip—forearm, backfist, hooking palm from impossible angles—driving Tōgō backward across the flags, north, until Tōgō's heel struck the first altar step. Both men were ragged now, breathing like bellows, knuckle-skin torn. Ma Lian sensed the ending and came in to finish it. Tōgō launched off the step. Downhill, full commitment, no second intention—the chop falling toward Ma Lian's collarbone, the thrust of his rear hand chained behind it. Ma Lian had seen the blitz three times. He did not retreat. He spun *inside* the arc, and the handblade sheared past, grazing his shoulder, tearing cloth, while his whipping palm cracked across Tōgō's temple— —and Tōgō's thrust, fired by pure reflex as the light flickered, punched into Ma Lian's sternum. They fell together. Ma Lian skidded across the southern flags and lay spread-eagled near the doorway. Tōgō collapsed sideways against the altar steps that had launched him, the Buddha's stone smile looking down. Silence. Sixty people, no sound but braziers. Ma Lian got up first, on the ninth heartbeat, arms hanging like cut ropes. Tōgō rose on the tenth, using the altar stone, one hand pressed to his ribs. They faced each other across the ruined hall—south and north, as they had begun—and each took one step forward, and stopped. Something had shifted in the air between them, small and unwelcome and permanent. "No victor," the old bookmaker croaked. "All wagers returned." The hall erupted—protest from the east, disbelief from the west—but the coins went back into purses, because no man there could say whose hand had earned them. Tōgō touched his split cheek and bowed, one inch, exactly as his school bowed to equals. Ma Lian spat blood onto the flags and grinned. "Your masters will hear of this," he said. "Yours first," said Tōgō. "You left footprints in his courtyard." They parted through their separate doors into the cold, each held upright by his own people, each already planning the next meeting. Behind them the torchlight found their armbands—red-and-black, black-and-red—both soaked through now, both gone the same dark color, indistinguishable on the stone where drops had fallen. The debt stood. It had stood for three generations. It would stand for three more, waiting patiently in the blood of young men who had inherited it like an heirloom, never once asking who had owed it first.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of fight-focused short fiction. The narrative delivers nearly everything the prompt requested: the Jigen-ryū fighter (Tōgō) uses the school's historically accurate first-strike, descending-cut doctrine with the characteristic high lead hand; Ma Lian's Piguaquan is rendered with whipping, circular arm strikes and evasive spinning. The abandoned temple setting is vividly established with concrete geography (fallen bell, altar steps, doorways, collapsed pillar), and the fight choreography is tracked with unusual spatial precision—fighters' positions (east/west, north/south, bell, steps) are consistently maintained, which directly satisfies the prompt's coherence requirement. The bell-strike moment is a genuinely clever set piece: the dead temple bell ringing for the first time in forty years is both a plot beat and a thematic image. The prose is lean and controlled, mostly showing rather than telling. Characterization is economical but effective—memorized prohibition letters, the burned challenge copied from memory, the one-inch bow, the spat blood and grin. The ending's image of the two armbands soaked to the same dark color is an earned, understated symbol of shared blood and futility, and the closing meditation on inherited debt avoids both false reconciliation and melodrama. Weaknesses: the word count falls short of the requested 1000 words (roughly 750–800), a clear instruction violation. The dialogue is functional but thin—the trash talk is generic ("Temple-bred puppet," "All posture. No teeth."). The draw ending, while thematically apt, is a familiar convention of rivalry stories. The crowd of sixty supporters is more backdrop than presence; the wagering element is set up but barely used. Character interiority is limited; both fighters are archetypes more than people, which is acceptable for the length but caps emotional complexity. A few phrases flirt with over-writing ("a dull god-voice," "limbs weighed nothing until the instant they weighed everything"), though the latter is actually effective. Overall: coherent, spatially rigorous, thematically resonant, with a satisfying structure and a memorable closing image. Its flaws are modest—length shortfall, thin dialogue, archetypal characters. Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Breaking Formation The bass comes off the back-left speaker so close to my ear it rattles my molars. Four speakers, one per corner, all synced, all a hair too loud, and me pinned to the back-left mark of Formation B—second row, far left, left sneaker toed against a strip of blue tape like that tape is what's holding me in this country. *One:* step out right, arms slicing overhead into a V. *Two:* left crosses behind, fists snap to sternum. *Three:* quarter-turn off the ball of the right foot. *Four:* the kill point—right arm punched forty-five degrees skyward, left fist cocked on the hip, head snapping front. I know all this. My body knows other things. On the "and" before five, my knees give it bounce—a little Detroit in the joint, the jit my heel does without asking me. The chest pop on five is supposed to be a door slamming; mine swings both ways, too much boogaloo in it. The wave on six runs through me like water when she wants it to run like gears. The music dies mid-bar. Madame Yoon lowers the remote at her table by the front-right corner of the mirror wall, and the silence is somehow louder than the speakers. They say she's broken more trainees than this academy has debuted. They say she can see a millimeter of slack from across the room. "Detroit." She says it like a diagnosis. She points at the tape X dead center of the floor. "Alone." Seven trainees peel off to the back wall and kneel in a row between the corner speakers. I take the X. Now I can see all of them in the mirror behind me—cross-legged, spine-straight, in matching issued blacks. Mine are gray and pilled. The scholarship covers tuition and the dorm and not one won more, and these are kids with drivers, kids who grew up in academies, kids whose skin has never once been ashy. "Again. *One.*" I run it. She circles me clockwise, slow. "Elbow. Ninety degrees. You give me eighty and call it style." Two fingers press the inside of my arm, bending it true. "*Three.*" I pivot—and travel. Momentum wants to carry me into a glide, the way it would back home, the way the concrete taught me. "You arrive like you are still leaving. *Four.*" The kill point. My arm fires up and my chin wants to nod the groove, to ride a sixteenth behind the beat where the pocket lives, where I've lived my whole life. She stops circling in front of me, between me and my own reflection. "You are late. You are always late. Here, the beat is a train. You are on it or you are under it. *Five, six.*" Chest pop, wave. I force the water out of it. *Seven:* right, left. *Eight:* drop the lunge, freeze, chin up fifteen degrees—and there it is, my heel pulsing on the offbeat, tiny, traitorous, jitting against the marley. She crouches and presses my heel flat with two fingers, like pinning a bug. "Your feet are talking," she says. "No one asked them a question." What my feet are saying is: *rec center parking lot off 7 Mile, cypher under one working streetlight, me hitting a freeze on the hood of somebody's Impala while a phone camera rolls.* Four million views. An email I was sure was a scam. Mom crying at the airport between double shifts. My feet are saying the only sentence they've ever known how to say, and this woman is holding them down and teaching them a new alphabet. First week I bowed too low, then too late. I still say "yeah" when I should say "*ne*." I eat kimbap over the sink while the other trainees video-call parents who summer somewhere. And underneath all of it, the thing I can't say out loud: every correction is a small amputation. They don't want me. They want the furniture I could be sanded into. If I give her the angles, the dead stops, the chin at fifteen degrees—if I actually make it—what's left of the kid from the cypher? And if I don't give it to her, I go home to what? The rec with the leaking roof? Mom's laundry shift? "Last time," Madame Yoon says, and returns to her table. "Show me clean." The track restarts. All four corners of the room detonate at once. *One:* arms slice. *Two:* fists to sternum. *Three:* pivot—plant, dead stop, no glide. *Four:* the kill point, and this is where it lives or dies, because my whole history is wound up in that arm like a spring and the groove is begging me to ride it. I decide. I give her the angle. Forty-five degrees, clean as a blade, heel down, chin locked. *Five:* a door slamming. *Six:* gears, no water. *Seven:* right, left. *Eight:* the lunge, the freeze. The track runs out. Two counts of nothing. And in that nothing—on purpose, every muscle agreeing this time—I let one slow wave roll up through my chest, turn my wrist over, and point at my own reflection. One inch of me. Placed exactly where I meant to put it. Not muscle memory. A signature. In the mirror I watch her watch me. The seven along the back wall have stopped breathing. "Again," Madame Yoon says. Then, quieter, almost to the remote: "Keep the ending." I reset on the X. The back-left speaker swells. Yeah. Detroit.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of controlled, kinetic first-person writing. The narrative tracks spatial positions with precision (back-left speaker, tape X, mirror wall, seven trainees kneeling along the back wall), and the choreography counts are consistently enumerated, giving the reader a clear map of the studio and the movement. The central conflict—improvisational street style versus militaristic precision—is dramatized through concrete physical detail: the jit in the heel, the boogaloo chest pop, the wave "like water" versus "gears," the two-finger correction pressing the heel flat. These are excellent show-don't-show moments. The instructor's dialogue is clipped and memorable ("Your feet are talking. No one asked them a question," "You arrive like you are still leaving"), and the narrator's internal monologue carries class anxiety convincingly (gray pilled sweats, kimbap over the sink, mom's double shifts). The metaphor of "small amputation" and "furniture I could be sanded into" is vivid without tipping into purple. The decision point is handled well: the narrator conforms through the eight-count, then plants one deliberate, self-authored gesture—a wave and a point at the mirror—on the silence after the track. The instructor's "Keep the ending" is a small, earned concession rather than a full transformation, which avoids the unearned-redemption trap. The ending's quiet optimism is proportionate. Minor weaknesses: the "four million views / viral email" backstory is a slightly convenient trope; the seven trainees are undifferentiated scenery; the final "Yeah. Detroit." is a touch neat. Some internal exposition (the "First week I bowed too low" paragraph) leans toward telling, though it's economical. Overall the prose is disciplined, the voice consistent, and the piece emotionally layered without melodrama. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 87.0
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# In Re: The Field (Recurring) The courtroom had no ceiling, only night, and a single hourglass the size of a bell tower hanging in it, dripping shimmering sand. Each grain was a dream being dreamed somewhere. When the last grain fell, the boy would wake, and the disputed property would cease to exist until tomorrow. Litigation in the Dreaming kept to a brisk schedule. "All rise," said the bailiff, a pale thing in a high collar, "or hover, or seep, according to your nature. The Court of the Dreaming is in session, the Lord Shaper presiding. The matter of *First Love versus Mora*, in re: the Field, Recurring." Dream sat on the bench like a long shadow someone had taught to glower. His fingers drummed once on the rail, then stopped, as though even drumming were beneath him. The stenographer, a moth-winged creature made of footnotes, took everything down in a hand no one would ever read. The plaintiff stepped forward: rosy-cheeked, downy-winged, blushing at the necessity of existing in public. "My lord. For three years I have crafted for the mortal Max a recurring dream. A field of wildflowers. The girl from his mathematics class. A wind that smells like her hair, which required *research*. Each time they lie in the grass, and each time they almost kiss." A pause. "The confusion is load-bearing, my lord. He wakes with a pleasant ache and no idea why. It is some of my finest work." "And then?" "And then *she* came." A wing pointed, trembling. At the respondent's table sat Mora: dark-eyed, very still, with the air of a room at three in the morning. She was representing herself, as was traditional among things that sit on chests. "The court will hear evidence," said Dream, in the tone of a being who had unmade a cathedral of nightmares before breakfast and considered this beneath him. The dream was projected above them. The gallery sighed at the wildflowers. Then the girl climbed playfully astride the boy — and changed. Her eyes opened like cellar doors. She settled her weight on his chest and began, delicately, to drink his breath. "Objection," said Mora. "The lighting in this reconstruction is unflattering." "Overruled." The mortal witness was produced in his pajamas and sworn upon a mathematics textbook. "Objection," said Mora. "Hearsay. He's a dreamer. Everything he says is, by definition—" "Overruled." Max was asked how the altered dream made him feel. He considered. "I mean. She's terrifying, right? She's sitting on me and I can't move and I can't breathe." He swallowed. "But it's — I kind of—" He went the color of First Love's cheeks. "That's the worst part. I kind of don't hate it?" "No further questions," said both parties, simultaneously, with feeling. First Love's closing was simple. "He was supposed to grow up and write one bad poem about this field, my lord. *One.* Now he will require decades of therapy and will probably marry someone who bites. There has been trespass, dilution, and theft of breath." Mora rose. She did not so much stand as uncoil upward. "My lord. I am a mora. I sit on chests. I drink breath. It is an old craft. Older than his." First Love squeaked. "And consider the dream he built. A boy, pinned by longing. Breathless. Chest tight. Unable to move. Wanting something he cannot name. My lord, it was already nine-tenths mine. I merely completed it. I cite *Pale Hunger v. the Siren's Mouth*, in which this court held that appetite may not be evicted from a place it has made honest." "She is eating him," said First Love. "A garnish," said Mora. "Besides—" she shrugged, a motion like a door closing upstairs, "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Above them the hourglass dripped, unimpressed by arguments. A grain the size of a diamond slid through the throat, and the courtroom dimmed: Max was stirring. Dream steepled his fingers. Those who knew him best — and there were perhaps four such beings left alive — would have detected the irritation. Had they been very brave, they might also have detected something else: the faintest amusement, buried like a coin in ash. "The court finds as follows." His voice went out over the night like frost over a field. "The dreamscape is, and remains, the property of First Love. The field. The light. The almost. Trespass has occurred." Mora's eyes narrowed. "However. The court notes that the dream is, at its heart, about wanting to be pinned down by something you do not understand." A beat. "The respondent is granted an easement. She may enter the dream as the girl, only at the apex of the almost, and may feed only on breath freely offered toward the kiss — which must remain, always, *almost*. Should the kiss ever land, the easement is void." First Love's mouth opened. Mora's mouth opened. "Further: the confusion — that she is terrifying and yet somehow still attractive — is ruled joint property. A royalty, paid by the respondent to the plaintiff, in perpetuity. Each time she feeds, she shall feel the boy's flutter herself. Let hunger arrive always wearing the mask of wanting. Let it earn its dinner." "My lord," said Mora, with the dignity of the damned, "this is courtship." "Yes," said Dream. "This court is adjourned." First Love departed in a state of hysterical blush, horror and professional interest being indistinguishable at that altitude. Mora left hungry, which was usual, and thoughtful, which was not. The last grain fell. Somewhere, in a small bedroom, a boy woke with a racing heart, a nosebleed, and the vague sense that the dream had changed hands — or rather, that it now had two. He would grow up to write exactly one bad poem about the field, and then, years later, several quite good ones about the woman with the cellar-door eyes, whom he would be a long time forgiving and no time at all forgetting. The bailiff looked up at the empty hourglass. "Shall I turn it, my lord?" "Leave it," said Dream, the coin glinting briefly in the ash. "Some dreams are better shared."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an excellent execution of a demanding prompt. The piece hits every required element: the courtroom farce, Dream's irritation, Mora's "a girl's gotta eat" defense, the dark understated humor, and the mischievous resolution. The hourglass conceit (the dream must end before the boy wakes) is a clever structural device that creates genuine time pressure and drives the brisk pacing. Dream's ruling — an easement, a royalty of felt flutter, the kiss that must remain "almost" — is genuinely inventive and characterful, showing mischief while staying in voice. The prose is economical and witty ("the air of a room at three in the morning," "a motion like a door closing upstairs"). Max's testimony is the comedic high point, and the closing image of the bad poem and the later good poems lands the ending with earned bittersweetness. Minor quibbles: the "coin in the ash" callback is slightly muddled (the coin was a metaphor for amusement, then glints literally), and the ending's warmth ("Some dreams are better shared") edges toward a gentler sentiment than the prompt's darker register, though it's earned by the logic of the ruling. Dialogue is consistently strong and character-differentiated. Very little to criticize; this is near the top of what the prompt requested.
